markerNotes: Judge each resource against the purpose of the report, which is the boiling point trend.
Separate resources with quantitative information on boiling point from those with only qualitative information.
Check that numerical data agree across sources before relying on them.
commonStudentErrors: Selects every resource without deciding which one is relevant to the purpose.
Rejects the graph because it is a visual form of data rather than a list of numbers.
Rejects the text as irrelevant because it has no numbers, without considering what qualitative information it adds.

sampleAnswers.answer: When selecting resources, the tables and graphs provide the most relevant information, because they give quantitative information on the boiling point of each alkane, which is the data needed to show the trend. The graph is especially useful because the pattern is easier to see than in a list of numbers. Other databases are also relevant if they give the same boiling points, but any database entry should be checked against the table so that the values agree. The text on the uses of alkanes contains qualitative information, which is useful background but does not show how boiling point changes, so it should be rejected as a main source. The video of an alkane burning does not provide relevant information about boiling point and should be rejected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing each resource against the purpose of the report, with reasons for selecting or rejecting each one.

sampleAnswers.answer: The table is relevant because it gives boiling points for each alkane, so it should be selected. The video is not relevant to boiling point, so it should be rejected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying relevant resources and giving reasons for the table and the video, without analysing the database or the text.

sampleAnswers.answer: The table is useful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by making a general statement about one resource, with no reasons and no comparison.

dotPoints.description: Apply quantitative processes to data, including unit conversions

prompts.question: Explain why data recorded in different units must be expressed in a consistent unit before they are compared in a table or graph.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two groups in a Year 11 class measure the volume of hydrogen gas produced by the same reaction. One group records its volumes in litres and the other in millilitres, and the class must place both sets of data in one table.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that values in different units cannot be compared directly, and that quantitative processes put the data on one consistent scale
2 marks: Explains that the units must match before the data are compared
1 mark: Identifies that the units of the data differ
markerNotes: Explain why the mismatch matters: the values cannot be compared directly, not just that they look different.
Name the process, such as expressing every value in one common unit, and say that it puts the data on one scale.
Keep the answer conceptual: the marker is looking for reasoning about units, not a worked example.
commonStudentErrors: Says the data must be changed because the teacher said so, without explaining the comparison.
Treats litres and millilitres as different quantities rather than different units of volume.
Says changing the unit changes the amount of gas that was produced.

sampleAnswers.answer: Values in litres and millilitres describe the same kind of quantity on different scales, so they cannot be compared directly in a table or graph. Quantitative processes applied to the data, such as expressing every value in one common unit, put the data on a consistent scale. Once the data share a consistent unit, the class can judge the trend fairly and avoid a misleading comparison.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining why values in different units cannot be compared directly, and how quantitative processes give the data a consistent scale.

sampleAnswers.answer: The units must match before the data are compared. Otherwise the values could be misread.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining that the units must match, but does not say what process achieves this.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two groups used different units.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that the units differ, without explaining why this matters.

prompts.question: Analyse the consequences for a laboratory report of plotting these results on one graph without first expressing all the values in a consistent unit.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student records the mass of a solid product in grams in one trial and in kilograms in another trial, and the teacher asks for all trials to be shown on one graph.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how mixed units distort the graph and the reading of the trend, and explains why quantitative processes must come before the data are displayed
4 marks: Analyses how mixed units would distort the graph, with some reasons for the effect on the reader
3 marks: Explains that the trials would be shown on different scales, so the trend would be wrong
2 marks: Identifies a way that mixed units would affect the graph
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about units in the graph
markerNotes: Trace the consequence from mixed units to a distorted graph, then to a wrong conclusion.
Name the process, quantitative processes, and say why it must come before the data are displayed.
Give a specific effect on the report rather than a general statement that the report would be wrong.
commonStudentErrors: Says the graph would be wrong without saying which feature of the graph is affected.
Assumes that plotting the data on a graph automatically converts the units.
Treats an error in units as a rounding error that does not affect the trend.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a laboratory report, plotting values in grams and kilograms on one set of axes without a consistent unit would place the trials on different scales and make the graph misleading. A reader would see the kilogram value as far larger or smaller than the gram values, so the apparent trend in the data could be wrong. Quantitative processes must therefore be completed before the data are displayed, so that every value on the graph shares one unit and can be compared fairly. The error also affects the credibility of the whole report, because a reader who finds mixed units may doubt the care taken in the practical work and the accuracy of the conclusions drawn from it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing how mixed units distort the graph and the reading of the trend, and explaining why quantitative processes come first.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graph would show the trials on different scales, so the apparent trend would be wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining that the trials would be on different scales, but does not analyse the consequences for the reader or the report.

sampleAnswers.answer: The axes would have mixed units.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by noting that the axes would have mixed units, without explaining the effect on the reader.

dotPoints.description: Select and use a range of representations to organise data and information, including graphs, keys, models, diagrams, tables and spreadsheets

prompts.question: Explain why a table, rather than a graph, is the most suitable representation for recording the raw data from this practical.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class measures the volume of gas produced by a reaction every 10 seconds for three minutes. Students must organise the data so that it can be shared with the class and used to draw a conclusion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains why a table suits raw data by linking its fixed order and units to accurate recording, and contrasts this with the role of a graph in showing the trend
3 marks: Explains why a table is suitable for recording raw data, with some reference to a graph
2 marks: Identifies a feature of a table that makes it suitable for recording data
1 mark: Identifies a representation that could record the data
markerNotes: Compare representations by purpose: a table records raw values, and a graph shows a trend.
Use the scenario's details, such as timed readings and units, to justify the choice.
Mention that diagrams and spreadsheets can support the table, rather than replace it.
commonStudentErrors: Chooses a graph for raw data without saying that the graph is drawn from a table of readings.
Says a table is better because it looks neater, without linking the choice to the data.
Lists several representations without choosing one for the raw data.

sampleAnswers.answer: Tables are the most suitable representation for raw data, because they record each timed volume reading in a fixed order, with units, so no value is lost or misread. Graphs show the trend well, but they are drawn from the readings rather than used to record them. A labelled diagram can show the apparatus, and spreadsheets can organise the data so the class can sort and share it. Choosing the right representation helps students organise data and information clearly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining why a table suits raw data and contrasting its recording role with the trend-showing role of a graph.

sampleAnswers.answer: A table keeps each reading in a fixed order, so the data are easy to check.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a feature of a table that makes it suitable, but does not explain why it matters for the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: A table can record the readings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by naming a representation that could record the data, without a reason.

prompts.question: Distinguish between a line graph and a column graph as representations of these two data sets: the volume of gas collected over time, and the reaction times of five different metals.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has measured the volume of gas collected every 30 seconds in one reaction, and the time taken for five different metals to react with the same acid. The student must choose a representation to organise the data for the report.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes the two graph types by the variable they show, and justifies a line graph for the time data and a column graph for the metal categories
4 marks: Distinguishes between line and column graphs and makes a choice for each data set
3 marks: Describes the features of a line graph and a column graph, with limited reference to the data sets
2 marks: Identifies a line graph or column graph as suitable for one data set
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about graphs
markerNotes: Base the distinction on the type of variable: continuous data joined by a line, and separate categories shown as columns.
Match each graph to a data set, rather than treating the two graphs as interchangeable.
A column graph can show time periods, but a line graph is better for a continuous trend.
commonStudentErrors: Says a line graph is used for categories and a column graph for continuous data.
Says the two graphs are the same, differing only in their colour.
Chooses one graph type for both data sets without giving a reason for either choice.

sampleAnswers.answer: A line graph and a column graph differ in the type of variable they show, and each suits a different set of data. A line graph plots a continuous variable, such as time, on the horizontal axis and joins the points, so it shows how the volume of gas changes steadily. A column graph plots separate categories, such as different metals, with one column for each, so it compares reaction times without implying values between the categories. The student should choose the representations that match each data set, and organise the gas volumes as a line graph and the metal reaction times as a column graph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by distinguishing the graphs by the variable they show, and justifying a line graph for the time data and a column graph for the metal categories.

sampleAnswers.answer: A line graph shows change over time, and a column graph compares separate categories. Both show the data clearly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing both graph types, but does not link either one to the two data sets or justify the choice.

sampleAnswers.answer: A line graph can show the gas volumes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by suggesting a line graph for the gas volumes, without describing the graph or the distinction.

dotPoints.description: Extract data and information from a wide range of sources and acknowledge these sources using an accepted referencing style

prompts.question: Outline the details a student must record from a journal article so that the data and information extracted from it can be acknowledged in an accepted referencing style.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has used a journal article on the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide to extract data and information for a practical report. The report must acknowledge all sources using an accepted referencing style, such as APA.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the authors, year, title, journal name, volume, issue, page numbers and DOI to record from the article, and shows how each supports an accepted referencing style
3 marks: Outlines most of the key details of a journal article needed for an accepted referencing style
2 marks: Identifies two details to record from the article for referencing
1 mark: Identifies one detail of the article that should be recorded
markerNotes: List the details that appear in a reference, such as authors, year, title, journal, volume, issue and pages.
Explain the purpose of recording them during extraction, which is to acknowledge sources accurately.
Name the accepted referencing style, such as APA, rather than writing 'a referencing style'.
commonStudentErrors: Records only the article title, without the authors or year.
Waits until the report is finished to record the details, which risks losing them.
Says acknowledging a source only means writing its name at the end of the report.

sampleAnswers.answer: When a student extracts data and information from a journal article, the details to record are the authors, year of publication, article title, journal name, volume and issue, and page numbers. A DOI, where one is given, identifies the article online. These details let the student acknowledge the journal article in an accepted referencing style, such as APA, so that a reader can find the sources used. Recording the details at the time of extraction prevents later errors and the risk of plagiarism.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining the full set of reference details and showing how they allow the source to be acknowledged.

sampleAnswers.answer: A student should record the authors and the year of publication.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying two details to record, but does not explain how they support referencing.

sampleAnswers.answer: The article title should be recorded.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying one detail that should be recorded, without linking it to referencing.

prompts.question: Analyse the consequences for a scientific report when data are extracted from several sources but only some of those sources are acknowledged.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's practical report draws data from five websites and journal articles, but only two of the sources appear in the reference list.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how partial acknowledgement reduces the checkability, reliability and credibility of the report, and states what full referencing requires
4 marks: Analyses at least two consequences of partial acknowledgement for the report, with some reasons
3 marks: Explains the effect of partial acknowledgement on the checking and reliability of the findings
2 marks: Identifies a consequence of not acknowledging some sources
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about unacknowledged sources
markerNotes: Trace each consequence to the report: from checkability to reliability, and then to credibility.
Link plagiarism to the integrity of the report, not only to breaking a rule.
State the full requirement: acknowledge every source used to extract data, in an accepted referencing style.
commonStudentErrors: Says the report is wrong because it has too many sources, rather than because some are unacknowledged.
Describes plagiarism as a consequence without explaining its effect on the reliability of the findings.
Says the reader is unhappy without explaining why the reader cannot check the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: If a report uses data from several sources but acknowledges only some of them, readers cannot check the work. Without the original sources, they cannot test whether the data were copied correctly, so the reliability of the findings is reduced. The unacknowledged sources also amount to plagiarism, which damages the credibility of the student and the report. A scientific report must acknowledge every source used to extract data, in an accepted referencing style, so that the evidence can be checked and reproduced. Partial referencing therefore weakens the report at every stage, from the data collected to the conclusions drawn from them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by tracing the consequences of partial acknowledgement for checkability, reliability and credibility, and stating what full referencing requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Readers cannot check the data against the original sources, so the findings are less reliable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining the effect on checking and reliability, but does not analyse plagiarism or the credibility of the report.

sampleAnswers.answer: Some sources are not credited, which is unfair.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by noting that some sources are not credited, without explaining the effect on the report.

dotPoints.description: Describe the Cultural Knowledges and observations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and examine how these contribute to the development of scientific knowledge

prompts.question: Describe two examples of Cultural Knowledges and observations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples that relate to the natural environment.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 Science class is studying fire ecology. A local Aboriginal community member visits to talk about cultural burning and how observations of plants and animals guide when burning is done.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two specific examples of Cultural Knowledges or observations and explains how each relates to the natural environment
2 marks: Describes two examples of Cultural Knowledges or observations
1 mark: Identifies an example of a Cultural Knowledge or observation
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
markerNotes: Name the specific practice or observation, such as cultural burning or seasonal indicators, rather than a general statement about culture.
Link each example to the natural environment, for example to fuel loads or the timing of ecological events.
Present the knowledge as held by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, rather than attributing it to a general group.
commonStudentErrors: Treats Cultural Knowledges as myth or folklore, with no observations to describe.
Describes a Western scientific method, such as a controlled experiment, instead of a Cultural Knowledge.
Gives a general statement that Peoples 'care for the land' without a specific example.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural Knowledges of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples include cultural burning, in which small, planned fires reduce fuel build-up and create a mix of burnt and unburnt areas across the natural environment. Observations of plants flowering and animals breeding are used in many seasonal calendars to guide the timing of burning, which adds to scientific knowledge of fire ecology.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two specific examples and explaining how each relates to the natural environment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning uses small, planned fires to reduce fuel in the natural environment. Observations of seasonal change guide the timing of burning.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing two relevant examples, with only brief reference to the natural environment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural burning is one example of a Cultural Knowledge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying one example, without describing it.

prompts.question: Discuss how Cultural Knowledges and observations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples contribute to scientific knowledge, including the protocols needed for respectful use.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 Science unit on fire ecology compares seasonal observations shared by an Aboriginal community with the results of a modern fire-monitoring study.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how Cultural Knowledges and observations add evidence to scientific knowledge, with specific examples, and considers the protocols that make this use respectful
5 marks: Discusses how Cultural Knowledges and observations contribute to scientific knowledge, with specific examples
4 marks: Discusses at least one way that Cultural Knowledges contribute to scientific knowledge
3 marks: Describes an example of Cultural Knowledges and links it to a scientific idea
2 marks: Identifies a Cultural Knowledge or observation relevant to science
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples' knowledge
keywords: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples
markerNotes: Discuss both the contribution to science and the protocols that make the sharing respectful, since the question asks for the relationship.
Give named, specific examples of practices or observations, rather than general statements about culture.
Present Cultural Knowledges as knowledge in its own right that adds to science, not as raw data to be taken.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the Cultural Knowledges without discussing how they contribute to scientific knowledge.
Says Cultural Knowledges are myths or stories with no evidential value.
Treats Cultural Knowledges as free public data, with no mention of consent or acknowledgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural Knowledges of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples contribute to scientific knowledge through long-term observation of ecosystems. Seasonal indicators, based on flowering plants and animal behaviour, record environmental change over many generations, which can add evidence about timing and patterns that short-term studies miss. Cultural burning is a documented example: planned, low-intensity fires reduce fuel loads, and Western fire ecologists have studied its effects on vegetation. Scientists can test these observations with their own methods, which strengthens the scientific knowledge produced. However, these contributions depend on protocols of respect: knowledge should be shared with the consent of the community, acknowledged to its Peoples, and never treated as free public data. Where a research project draws on this knowledge, the community should be consulted from the start, credited in any published work, and offered a share in the benefits of the research. Used in this way, Cultural Knowledges enrich science without being taken from their owners.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by discussing how Cultural Knowledges add evidence to science with specific examples, and considering the protocols that make this respectful.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cultural Knowledges, such as seasonal observations of plant flowering, can contribute to scientific knowledge about timing in ecosystems. Scientists can test these observations using their own methods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by discussing one way Cultural Knowledges contribute to scientific knowledge, with one example and no discussion of protocols.

sampleAnswers.answer: Seasonal observations of plants are one example of Cultural Knowledges.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one relevant Cultural Knowledge, without explaining how it contributes to science.

dotPoints.description: Describe qualitative and quantitative relationships between variables

prompts.question: Describe the qualitative and quantitative relationships between the concentration of the acid and the time taken for the magnesium to disappear.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student reacts identical pieces of magnesium ribbon with hydrochloric acid at four concentrations and times how long each piece takes to disappear. At 0.5 mol L⁻¹ the time is 240 s, at 1.0 mol L⁻¹ it is 120 s, at 2.0 mol L⁻¹ it is 60 s and at 4.0 mol L⁻¹ it is 30 s.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the qualitative relationship that time decreases as concentration increases and the quantitative pattern that each doubling of concentration halves the time, referring to the data
2 marks: Describes the qualitative relationship between concentration and time, with some reference to the data
1 mark: Identifies that the time changes as the concentration changes
markerNotes: Name the qualitative relationship first, then give the quantitative pattern as a specific change, such as each doubling of concentration halving the time.
Quote values from the data to support the pattern, rather than only saying the time gets smaller.
State that the variables move in opposite directions, which makes the relationship inverse.
commonStudentErrors: Says the time increases as the concentration increases, reading the trend backwards.
Describes the time falling without referring to the data or the size of the change.
States that the relationship is linear, although equal steps in concentration do not give equal steps in time.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two variables are the concentration of the acid and the time taken for the magnesium to disappear. Qualitatively, the relationship is that time decreases as concentration increases, which means the variables move in opposite directions. Quantitatively, each doubling of concentration halves the time, from 240 s at 0.5 mol L⁻¹ to 120 s at 1.0 mol L⁻¹. Both qualitative and quantitative relationships therefore show an inverse proportion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by giving the qualitative trend and the quantitative doubling-and-halving pattern, both referenced to the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the concentration of the acid increases, the time taken for the magnesium to disappear decreases. For example, the time falls from 240 s at 0.5 mol L⁻¹ to 30 s at 4.0 mol L⁻¹.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the qualitative relationship with a reference to the data, which meets the 2-mark row. It does not state the quantitative halving pattern, so it cannot reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The time changes as the concentration changes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies that the variables are linked, which is the minimum for 1 mark. It gives no direction and no reference to the data.

prompts.question: Analyse the data to explain whether the student's claim that the time is inversely proportional to temperature is supported, and describe the qualitative and quantitative relationships the data do show.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A second student times how long a fixed mass of sugar takes to dissolve in 100 mL of water at four temperatures. The times are 160 s at 10 °C, 80 s at 20 °C, 40 s at 30 °C and 20 s at 40 °C. The student concludes that the time is inversely proportional to temperature.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the data to show that the claim of inverse proportion is not supported, and describes both the qualitative and quantitative relationships between temperature and time with precise reference to the data
5 marks: Analyses the data to show the claim is not well supported, and describes the qualitative and quantitative relationships with some reference to the data
4 marks: Analyses the data to show that the time changes with temperature, and describes the qualitative relationship with relevant reference to the data
3 marks: Describes the qualitative relationship between temperature and time, with some reference to the data
2 marks: Identifies that the time decreases as the temperature increases
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: A strong answer explains that inverse proportion means the time falls by the same ratio as the temperature rises, then shows that the data do not match this.
Describe the pattern as a halving of time for each 10 °C rise, which is a clear quantitative relationship to state in words.
Do not call the pattern linear, since equal temperature steps produce smaller and smaller drops in time.
commonStudentErrors: Accepts the student's claim of inverse proportion without checking it against the data.
Says the time is directly proportional to temperature, which the data do not show.
Describes the relationship as linear, with equal temperature rises giving equal drops in time.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim that the time is inversely proportional to temperature is not supported. Inverse proportion means that the time falls by the same ratio as the temperature rises. From 10 °C to 20 °C the time does halve, but from 20 °C to 30 °C the temperature rises by a smaller ratio while the time still halves, so the time falls by a larger ratio than the temperature rise would predict. The data therefore do not follow inverse proportion. Qualitatively, the time decreases as the temperature increases, so the two variables move in opposite directions. Quantitatively, each 10 °C rise halves the time, so the time falls by a constant ratio for each equal temperature step rather than by a constant amount. These qualitative and quantitative relationships are not linear, and the pattern can be used to predict the time at a temperature that was not tested, provided the prediction stays within the range of the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by rejecting the claim with a step-by-step check of the data and describing both the qualitative and quantitative relationships precisely.

sampleAnswers.answer: The time decreases as the temperature increases, from 160 s at 10 °C to 20 s at 40 °C, so the two variables move in opposite directions. The data do not show that the time is inversely proportional to temperature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the qualitative relationship with values from the data. It does not analyse why the claim fails, so it cannot reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The time changes as the temperature changes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, with no direction and no reference to the data.

dotPoints.description: Explain patterns and trends, including inconsistencies in data and information

prompts.question: Explain the pattern in the volume of gas collected over time, and suggest a reason why the reading at 90 seconds is inconsistent with the trend.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student reacts excess dilute hydrochloric acid with marble chips and records the total volume of carbon dioxide collected every 30 seconds for 5 minutes. The volume rises rapidly during the first two minutes and then levels off at about 120 mL. The reading at 90 seconds is lower than the readings either side of it, which otherwise fit the trend.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains the rapid rise and levelling off in terms of the marble being used up as the limiting reactant, and gives a specific, plausible cause for the inconsistent reading at 90 seconds
3 marks: Explains the levelling off in terms of the marble being used up, and identifies the reading at 90 seconds as inconsistent with the trend
2 marks: Identifies the rapid rise followed by levelling off, or the inconsistent reading at 90 seconds
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the gas volume readings
markerNotes: Link the rapid early rise to the high concentration of the acid and the many collisions at the start of the reaction.
Explain the levelling off with the marble as the limiting reactant, since the acid is in excess.
Name a specific, plausible cause for the 90 second reading, such as a leaking gas syringe, rather than saying it is simply wrong.
commonStudentErrors: Says the volume levels off because the acid has run out, when the acid is in excess.
Says the 90 second reading is wrong without giving a possible cause.
Explains the rapid rise by saying the reaction is faster, without linking it to collisions or concentration.

sampleAnswers.answer: The data and information show clear patterns: the volume rises rapidly at first, then levels off at about 120 mL. The rapid rise happens because the acid is most concentrated at the start, so there are many collisions with the marble and the reaction is fastest. The volume levels off because the marble is the limiting reactant. Once the marble is used up no more carbon dioxide forms, even though the acid is in excess. The data show few inconsistencies, but the reading at 90 seconds is lower than the trends either side of it. A plausible cause is a leak at the gas syringe, which would let some gas escape and lower the recorded volume.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining both the rise and the levelling off through the limiting reactant and giving a specific cause for the inconsistent reading.

sampleAnswers.answer: The volume rises quickly and then levels off because the marble runs out. The reading at 90 seconds does not fit the trend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the rapid rise followed by levelling off and the inconsistent reading, but gives no explanation or cause, so it meets the 2-mark row only.

sampleAnswers.answer: The volume goes up and then stays about the same.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information about the readings only, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Discuss whether the pattern in the boiling points holds for all four compounds, and explain the inconsistency shown by HF.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student lists the approximate boiling points, in degrees Celsius, of four hydrogen halides: HCl −85, HBr −67, HI −35 and HF 20. The student plots these boiling points against the molar mass of each compound and says that all four show the same pattern.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the increasing boiling point trend from HCl to HI in terms of dispersion forces growing with molar mass, explains HF as inconsistent because of hydrogen bonding, and reaches a supported conclusion about the pattern
5 marks: Discusses the trend from HCl to HI and explains the HF inconsistency in terms of hydrogen bonding, with a sound conclusion
4 marks: Discusses the trend and identifies HF as inconsistent, with some explanation of the forces involved
3 marks: Describes the increasing boiling point trend from HCl to HI with some reference to molar mass
2 marks: Identifies the trend or the inconsistent boiling point of HF
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Explain the rising trend from HCl to HI through dispersion forces, which strengthen as molar mass increases.
Name hydrogen bonding as the force that lifts HF above the trend, rather than saying HF is simply different.
Weigh whether the pattern holds for the whole set before reaching a conclusion.
commonStudentErrors: Says HF is an outlier because it is a gas, without naming hydrogen bonding.
Says the boiling points rise because the covalent bonds get stronger, confusing bonds with intermolecular forces.
Says the trend holds for all four compounds without addressing HF.

sampleAnswers.answer: The patterns in boiling point hold for HCl, HBr and HI, but not for all four compounds. Boiling point rises from HCl to HI as the molar mass increases, because the dispersion forces grow stronger as the electron clouds get larger. This is a clear trend across the three compounds, since the boiling point rises at each step from HCl to HI. HF does not fit it. Its molar mass is the smallest of the four, so the trend predicts it should boil lowest, yet its boiling point is about 20 °C, far above the others. The inconsistencies in the data come from HF alone, and they are explained by hydrogen bonding, which is much stronger than the dispersion forces in the other hydrogen halides. The data therefore support the trends for three compounds, but HF shows that a stronger force can override the trend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by discussing the HCl to HI trend through dispersion forces, explaining HF through hydrogen bonding, and reaching a supported conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point rises from HCl to HI as the molar mass increases, which shows a clear trend. HF does not follow this pattern, so the inconsistency needs an explanation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the increasing trend with reference to molar mass, which meets the 3-mark row. It identifies HF but does not explain it, so it cannot reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: HF has a higher boiling point than the others.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Assess error, uncertainty and limitations in data and include calculations of percentage error, range, mean and standard deviation

prompts.question: Classify each of the three errors described as random or systematic, and justify each classification in terms of its effect on the data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student titrates sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid and notes three problems. The balance used to weigh the solid sample was never zeroed and reads 0.02 g high every time. The student reads the burette meniscus from slightly different eye levels in each trial. The burette was rinsed with water instead of the acid before it was filled.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies all three errors correctly and justifies each by whether it shifts results in one direction or varies between trials, showing how each adds error or uncertainty to the data
2 marks: Classifies two errors correctly with a relevant justification
1 mark: Identifies at least one error as random or systematic
markerNotes: A systematic error shifts every result in the same direction, so the balance offset and the rinsed burette both belong here.
A random error varies unpredictably between trials, such as eye-level differences when reading the meniscus.
Justify each classification by its effect on the data, not only by naming the type of error.
commonStudentErrors: Classifies the balance offset as random because the student did not notice it.
Classifies the meniscus reading as systematic because the same student reads every trial.
Lists the errors without justifying why each is random or systematic.

sampleAnswers.answer: The balance offset is systematic because it shifts every mass in the same direction, so it adds a consistent error to the data. Reading the meniscus from different eye levels is random because it varies unpredictably between trials, which adds uncertainty. Rinsing the burette with water is systematic because it dilutes the acid by the same amount each time. These errors show limitations of the method that the student should report.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by classifying all three errors and linking each to its effect on the data and the uncertainty it adds.

sampleAnswers.answer: The balance offset is systematic because it shifts every reading. Reading the meniscus at different eye levels is random.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies two errors correctly with a short justification, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The meniscus reading is random.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one error correctly, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess how reliable the mean titre is as a measure of the true volume, and explain why a percentage error cannot be worked out from these results.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student titrates 25.00 mL samples of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid three times, obtaining titres of 23.80 mL, 23.85 mL and 23.90 mL. The student's rough trial of 24.60 mL was excluded. The burette reads to the nearest 0.05 mL, and the student states that the mean titre is the true volume needed to neutralise the sample.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the reliability of the mean titre, linking the narrow range and small standard deviation to precision, the burette uncertainty to limitations, and explains clearly why a percentage error needs an accepted value that is not given
5 marks: Assesses the reliability of the mean titre with reference to the range, the standard deviation and the uncertainty, and explains why a percentage error cannot be found
4 marks: Assesses the precision of the titres with some reference to the range or standard deviation, and identifies a limitation of the method
3 marks: Describes the spread of the titres with some reference to the uncertainty of the burette
2 marks: Identifies the range of the titres or the uncertainty of the burette
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: A narrow range and a small standard deviation show that the titres are precise, which is not the same as being accurate.
A percentage error compares a result with an accepted value, so without one it cannot be found; say this rather than inventing a true value.
Name the burette uncertainty as one of the limitations and say how it affects the reliability of the mean.
commonStudentErrors: Says the mean titre is accurate because the three titres are close together.
Invents an accepted value so that a percentage error can be given.
Says the rough trial of 24.60 mL should be averaged in without justification.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mean titre is reasonably reliable as a measure of the volume needed, but it is not shown to be accurate. The three titres lie within a narrow range, and their small standard deviation shows that the titrations are precise and repeatable. However, precision does not guarantee accuracy. The burette reads to the nearest 0.05 mL, so each titre carries an uncertainty of about that size, which is one of the limitations of the method. The rough trial was rightly excluded, since it was not a careful titration, so it should not change the mean. A percentage error cannot be worked out because there is no accepted value to compare the mean against, and the true volume is unknown. The student's claim that the mean is the true volume is therefore unsupported, and a further limitation is that only one set of titrations was carried out, which is a weakness in the error analysis.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by linking the range and standard deviation to precision, the burette uncertainty to limitations, and explaining why a percentage error needs an accepted value.

sampleAnswers.answer: The three titres are close together, with a narrow range and a small standard deviation, so they are precise. The burette uncertainty is one of the limitations of the method.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the spread of the titres with a reference to the burette uncertainty, which meets the 3-mark row. It does not assess the accuracy of the mean, so it cannot reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The titres are close together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Assess the validity, reliability, accuracy and precision of data and information

prompts.question: Define validity and reliability as they apply to these results, and explain why the results are reliable but not accurate.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student weighs a 10.0 g mass on a balance that reads 2.0 g too high. The student records 12.0 g, 12.0 g and 12.0 g in three trials.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Defines validity and reliability correctly and explains that the consistent readings show reliability, while the 2.0 g offset from the true mass shows the results lack accuracy
2 marks: Defines validity or reliability correctly and identifies that the readings are consistent but not accurate
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the balance readings
markerNotes: Define reliability as consistency of repeated results, and validity as whether the measurement measures what it is meant to.
Explain the gap between the readings and the true mass, rather than saying the balance is simply wrong.
A consistent offset is a systematic error, so the readings show precision and reliability but not accuracy.
commonStudentErrors: Says the results are accurate because all three readings agree.
Confuses reliability with accuracy, saying a reliable result must be close to the true value.
Defines validity as the same thing as reliability.

sampleAnswers.answer: Validity means the measurement measures what it is meant to measure, and reliability means repeated results agree with each other. The balance results are reliable because all three readings are 12.0 g. They lack accuracy because they sit 2.0 g above the true mass of 10.0 g, which is a systematic error from the balance. The data show high precision but low accuracy, so the balance is not valid for measuring the true mass.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by defining both terms and explaining the gap between the consistent readings and the true mass.

sampleAnswers.answer: The results are reliable because all three readings are 12.0 g. They are not accurate because the true mass is 10.0 g.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the consistent but inaccurate readings, which meets the 2-mark row. It defines neither term, so it cannot reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The balance readings are all the same.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information about the readings only, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess how far the student's three results can be trusted as evidence that the liquid is methanol, referring to validity, reliability, accuracy and precision.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student measures the boiling point of a sample of methanol three times at standard atmospheric pressure, obtaining 78.1 °C, 78.2 °C and 78.1 °C. The accepted boiling point of methanol at this pressure is 64.7 °C, and the student's thermometer was never checked against a known reference before use.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity, reliability, accuracy and precision of the three results, explaining that they are precise and reliable but not accurate, and makes a judgement about whether they can support the claim that the liquid is methanol
5 marks: Assesses the reliability and accuracy of the results, explaining that close agreement does not show they are accurate, and makes a judgement about the claim
4 marks: Assesses the precision and accuracy of the results, identifying the gap from the accepted boiling point
3 marks: Describes the agreement between the three results and compares them with the accepted boiling point
2 marks: Identifies that the three results agree with each other or differ from the accepted boiling point
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Separate precision, where the results agree with each other, from accuracy, where they agree with the accepted value; here the results are precise but not accurate.
Name the uncalibrated thermometer as the most likely systematic error, and say that it does not show up as scatter between readings.
Let the judgement about the claim follow from the assessment, and say what extra evidence would be needed.
commonStudentErrors: Says the results are accurate because the three readings are close together.
Says the results are valid because the thermometer gives a reading for the liquid.
Treats the offset from the accepted value as random error that averaging would remove.

sampleAnswers.answer: The three results show high precision, because they agree closely with each other, and they show good reliability, because repeated trials give consistent values. They lack accuracy, though. The accepted boiling point of methanol is 64.7 °C, and the readings are well above it, so the thermometer is likely to have a systematic error rather than random scatter. Averaging the three readings would not remove this offset. Because the thermometer was never checked against a known reference, the method has a calibration problem that limits its validity. A boiling point far from the known value does not show that the liquid is methanol, so the results are not valid evidence of identity. The student could strengthen the evidence by calibrating the thermometer, recording the air pressure for each run, and testing a second property of the liquid, since pressure changes the boiling point and an unrecorded change could shift the readings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing all four terms, identifying a systematic error, and making a supported judgement about the identity claim.

sampleAnswers.answer: The three results are precise because they agree with each other, but they are not accurate because they sit well above the accepted boiling point of 64.7 °C.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Compares the results with the accepted boiling point and describes their agreement, which meets the 3-mark row. It does not explain the error or judge the claim, so it cannot reach 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The results agree with each other.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Interpret data and information to identify outliers, make predictions, explain results and draw conclusions

prompts.question: Outline how the 4.1 °C result should be identified as an outlier, and what the student should check before deciding whether to exclude it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student measures the temperature rise when 25 mL of 1.0 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 25 mL of 1.0 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide in a polystyrene cup. Five repeat trials give temperature rises of 6.7 °C, 6.9 °C, 6.8 °C, 4.1 °C and 6.6 °C. The lab notes do not record anything unusual about any trial.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how the result is identified as an outlier by comparing it with the other repeat trials and checking for a recorded cause, and states that it should be excluded only with a documented reason
2 marks: Outlines that the 4.1 °C result differs markedly from the other trials, with some reason for how it should be treated
1 mark: Identifies the 4.1 °C result as different from the other trials
markerNotes: An outlier is judged against the spread of the other repeat trials, not because it disagrees with what the student expected.
A result should be excluded only with a documented cause, such as a spill or a misread thermometer, not because it is inconvenient.
Say that the decision is recorded and that the result is reported both with and without the outlier.
commonStudentErrors: Deletes the 4.1 °C result because it is lower than the others, without checking for a cause.
Keeps the 4.1 °C result in the average without commenting on it.
Calls the result an error without saying how it was identified against the other trials.

sampleAnswers.answer: Compare the 4.1 °C result with the other repeat trials, which cluster between 6.6 °C and 6.9 °C, so it is clearly an outlier. Check the lab notes and procedure for a documented cause, such as a spill or a misread temperature. Exclude the result only if a cause is found, and state why. If no cause is found, keep it in the data and report the average with and without it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying the outlier against the spread of the trials and setting out the check for a documented cause before any exclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: The 4.1 °C result is much lower than the other trials. The student should check the notes for a cause before deciding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the marked difference and a reason for checking it, which meets the 2-mark row. It does not set out how the outlier is identified, so it cannot reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The 4.1 °C result is different from the others.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the different result only, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Extrapolate the trend to predict how the temperature rise for 0.30 g of magnesium would compare with the rise for 0.20 g, and explain the assumptions and limitations of predicting beyond the data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student adds different masses of magnesium ribbon to 50 mL of excess 2.0 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature rise. A mass of 0.05 g gives a rise of 4.6 °C, 0.10 g gives 9.2 °C, 0.15 g gives 13.8 °C and 0.20 g gives 18.4 °C. The student has no data for masses above 0.20 g.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Extrapolates the linear trend to predict that the temperature rise for 0.30 g would continue to increase in equal steps, explains the assumptions needed such as excess acid, and discusses the limitations of predicting beyond the data
5 marks: Extrapolates the trend to predict a larger rise for 0.30 g, with an explanation of the assumptions and some limitation of the prediction
4 marks: Extrapolates the trend to predict a larger rise for 0.30 g, with some reference to the data
3 marks: Describes the pattern in the data, that the temperature rise increases in equal steps for equal masses
2 marks: Identifies that the temperature rise increases as the mass increases
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Show that the rise increases by the same amount for each equal mass step, so the trend is linear, and then extend it in words beyond 0.20 g.
Name the assumption that the acid stays in excess, since the trend stops once the magnesium uses up the acid.
Name limitations such as heat lost to the surroundings, which grows as the temperature rises and can make the measured rise fall below the trend.
commonStudentErrors: Predicts the rise for 0.30 g will be the same as for 0.20 g, ignoring the trend.
Assumes the trend will continue for any mass without checking that the acid stays in excess.
Ignores heat lost to the surroundings when discussing limitations.

sampleAnswers.answer: The temperature rise increases by the same amount for each equal step in mass, so the data show a linear trend. To extrapolate this trend, the rise for 0.30 g would continue the pattern and be larger than the rise for 0.20 g, by a similar step. These predictions assume that the acid stays in excess, which it does at this mass, and that the energy released is proportional to the moles of magnesium that react. The predictions have limitations, however. The data stop at 0.20 g, so the trend is untested beyond that range. Heat lost to the surroundings increases as the temperature rises, so the measured rise may fall below the linear trend. At larger masses the acid would eventually be used up, and the trend would stop. An experiment at 0.30 g would test the predictions before they are relied on.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by extrapolating the linear trend, stating the excess-acid and energy assumptions, and discussing the limitations of predicting beyond the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: The temperature rise increases by the same amount for each equal step in mass, so the data show a linear trend. Extending this trend predicts a larger rise for 0.30 g.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the equal-step pattern and extends it, which meets the 3-mark row. It gives no assumptions or limitations, so it cannot reach 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The temperature rise increases as the mass increases.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate data and information to suggest improvements or further investigations

prompts.question: Outline two weaknesses in this method and a suggested improvement for each, so that the student can improve the reliability of the mass readings.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student investigates how the surface area of calcium carbonate affects the reaction rate with dilute hydrochloric acid. Using one trial each, the student measures the mass lost from an open conical flask over three minutes, once with powder and once with chips, on a balance that reads to 0.1 g.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines two specific weaknesses in the method, such as the reading precision of the balance and the lack of repeat trials, and suggests a clear improvement for each
3 marks: Outlines two weaknesses in the method with a suggested improvement for one of them
2 marks: Identifies one weakness in the method with a relevant improvement
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the method
markerNotes: Name each weakness as something that affects the data, such as the resolution of the balance, and pair it with an improvement that addresses it.
Repeat trials and a controlled temperature are the most useful improvements for a rate investigation.
Avoid general advice such as being more careful; name the specific change to the method.
commonStudentErrors: Says the experiment should be done more carefully, without naming a specific weakness.
Suggests a more accurate balance without saying what it would change in the data.
Lists a weakness that is not in this method, such as the acid being too concentrated.

sampleAnswers.answer: One weakness is that the balance reads only to 0.1 g, so small mass losses from the chips are hard to tell apart from noise. An improvement is to use a balance that reads to 0.01 g, which would give more reliable mass readings. A second weakness is that only one trial was done for each surface area, so there is no measure of repeatability. Repeating each trial three times and reporting the average would show whether the difference between powder and chips is consistent. The method also does not control the temperature of the acid, which can change the rate and limit the comparison.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by naming two specific weaknesses, each with a clear improvement that addresses it.

sampleAnswers.answer: One weakness is that the balance reads only to 0.1 g, so a more precise balance would give better mass readings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one weakness with a relevant improvement, which meets the 2-mark row. It does not outline a second weakness, so it cannot reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The method could be more careful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives general advice without a specific weakness, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Evaluate the data and the method, and suggest improvements and further investigations that would strengthen the conclusion about surface area.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares how the surface area of calcium carbonate affects the reaction rate with dilute hydrochloric acid. The powder reaches a steady mass after about 90 seconds, and the chips take about 3 minutes, with one trial each on a balance reading to 0.1 g. The flask was open to the air and the temperature of the acid was not recorded.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Evaluates the data and the method, judging the reliability and validity of the results and the significance of the weaknesses, and suggests specific improvements and further investigations that would strengthen the conclusion
7 marks: Evaluates the reliability of the data and the method, with clear and sound suggestions for improvements and a further investigation
5-6 marks: Evaluates some weaknesses of the data and the method, with suggestions for improvements that relate to them
3-4 marks: Discusses the data with some weaknesses identified, and suggests an improvement
2 marks: Identifies a weakness in the method or the data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Judge which weaknesses matter most, for example that one trial per surface area cannot show the difference is reliable, rather than listing every possible flaw.
Link each improvement to a named weakness and say what it would change in the data.
Suggest a further investigation that extends the question, such as testing whether the same effect holds at a different acid concentration.
commonStudentErrors: Lists weaknesses without judging which matter for the conclusion.
Suggests an improvement that does not address the weakness named, such as a more accurate balance when the real problem is one trial.
Says the results are valid because the powder reacted faster, without assessing the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: The data show a clear difference: the calcium carbonate powder reached a steady mass after about 90 seconds, while the chips took about 3 minutes, which fits the idea that a larger surface area speeds up the reaction rate. However, the evidence for this conclusion is weak. Each surface area was tested in only one trial, so there is no measure of repeatability, and a single unusual run could explain the difference. The balance reads to 0.1 g, which is too coarse for the small mass losses in the early stages, and the readings were taken too infrequently to define the early reaction rate of the powder. The temperature of the acid was not recorded or controlled, and temperature affects the reaction rate, so the comparison is not fair. The open flask could also lose spray or acid mist, which would show up as mass lost and inflate the readings. Overall, the data are reasonably valid as evidence of a surface area effect, but they are not reliable enough to measure its size. These are the main improvements: repeat each trial at least three times and report the mean and range, and record mass every 10 seconds on a balance that reads to 0.01 g, or collect the carbon dioxide in a gas syringe. Further investigations could test whether the same surface area effect holds at a second acid concentration, and whether a water bath that holds the temperature fixed removes that variable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-8 mark row by judging the reliability of the data, identifying which weaknesses matter most, and suggesting specific improvements and a further investigation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The powder reacts faster than the chips, which fits a larger surface area. The result comes from one trial each, so it is not reliable, and the balance is not precise enough. Repeating the trials would help.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a weakness in the data and a suggested improvement, which meets the 3-4 mark row. It does not judge how far the weaknesses affect the conclusion, so it cannot reach 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The powder reacts faster than the chips.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Use appropriate significant figures to express quantitative solutions

prompts.question: Explain why the reported concentration should not be given to seven significant figures, and why its precision should match that of the least precise measurement.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's report gives the final concentration of a solution as 0.0832645 mol L⁻¹. The volume was measured with a measuring cylinder that reads to the nearest 1 mL, and the mass was measured on a balance that reads to 0.001 g.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the reported value cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement used to obtain it, so extra digits imply false precision, and links this to the measuring cylinder reading
2 marks: Explains that the reported value should match the precision of the measurements rather than the calculator display
1 mark: Identifies that the value should be given to fewer significant figures
markerNotes: The number of significant figures in a result follows the precision of its measurements, not the number of digits a calculator shows.
Name the least precise measurement, here the measuring cylinder, and link it to the number of significant figures reported.
Explain false precision: extra digits claim a certainty that the measurements do not support.
commonStudentErrors: Says the answer should keep every digit from the calculator because more digits are more accurate.
Says significant figures depend only on how many decimal places the answer has.
Explains the rule without linking it to the precision of the measurements.

sampleAnswers.answer: A result cannot be more precise than the measurements used to obtain it. The volume was read to the nearest 1 mL with a measuring cylinder, which is the least precise measurement, so the concentration should be reported to a similar number of significant figures. Giving seven significant figures implies a certainty the measurements do not support, which is false precision. Extra digits from the calculator are not more accurate, so the reported value should match the least precise measurement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by linking the measuring cylinder to the number of significant figures and explaining false precision.

sampleAnswers.answer: The answer should match the precision of the measuring cylinder, not the calculator. Seven digits suggests too much precision.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the link to measurement precision briefly, which meets the 2-mark row. It does not explain why extra digits are misleading, so it cannot reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The answer should have fewer significant figures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the need for fewer significant figures only, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify the number of significant figures the chemist should use when reporting the concentration, given the precision of the measurements, and assess the consequences of reporting four significant figures for readers comparing batches.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A quality-control chemist measures sodium chloride in a drink by weighing about 0.5 g on a balance that reads to 0.001 g, then making the solution up in a 100 mL volumetric flask that is accurate to about 0.1 mL. A colleague suggests reporting the concentration to four significant figures so that it looks more precise on the public website.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a specific number of significant figures by linking it to the precision and uncertainty of the measurements, and assesses clearly how reporting four significant figures would mislead readers comparing batches
5 marks: Justifies the number of significant figures by linking it to the precision of the measurements, and assesses the risk of false precision for readers
4 marks: Justifies a number of significant figures with some reference to the precision of the measurements
3 marks: Describes the effect of measurement precision on the number of significant figures reported
2 marks: Identifies that the number of significant figures should reflect the measurements
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Name the precision of the balance and the flask first, then state the number of significant figures that matches it, rather than choosing the number first.

Four significant figures would imply an uncertainty far smaller than the measurements support, so readers could read a small difference between batches as real when it lies within the method's uncertainty.
Suggest a practice such as stating the uncertainty beside the value, which helps readers judge differences.
commonStudentErrors: Chooses four significant figures because it looks more precise, without reference to the measurements.
Says more significant figures are always more accurate, so the reporting choice does not matter.
Justifies the number of significant figures by counting decimal places only.

sampleAnswers.answer: The chemist should report three significant figures, because the balance reads to 0.001 g and the volumetric flask is accurate to about 0.1 mL, so the precision of the measurements limits the result to about three significant figures. The number is set by the measurements, not by how it looks on the page. Matching the reported figures to this precision shows the real uncertainty of the concentration. Reporting four significant figures would imply that the value is known more finely than the measurements allow, which is false precision. Readers comparing batches could then read a small difference in the fourth figure as a real change in the drink, when it may fall within the uncertainty of the method. A better practice is to report three significant figures and state the uncertainty beside the value, so that readers can judge whether batches genuinely differ. Reporting fewer figures than the measurements allow would throw away useful information, so three is the best match.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying three significant figures from the precision of the balance and volumetric flask and assessing how four would mislead readers.

sampleAnswers.answer: The chemist should report three significant figures, matching the balance and the volumetric flask. Four would suggest more precision than the measurements have.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Links the number of significant figures to measurement precision, which meets the 3-mark row. It does not assess the effect on readers, so it cannot reach 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The number of significant figures should match the measurements.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Use appropriate scale prefixes for powers of 10: femto (f) = 10⁻¹⁵, pico (p) = 10⁻¹², nano (n) = 10⁻⁹, micro (μ) = 10⁻⁶, milli (m) = 10⁻³, kilo (k) = 10³, mega (M) = 10⁶, giga (G) = 10⁹, tera (T) = 10¹² and peta (P) = 10¹⁵

prompts.question: Describe what the scale prefixes nano and micro tell the reader about each size relative to the metre, and state which item is larger.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A lab report gives the diameter of a virus particle as 100 nanometres and the length of a bacterium as 2 micrometres. Both sizes are written in metres with a scale prefix attached.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes that nano and micro are scale prefixes for powers of 10 relative to the metre, explains that micro is a larger power than nano, and states that the bacterium is the larger item
2 marks: Describes that nano and micro are scale prefixes that give the size of a unit relative to the metre, and identifies which item is larger
1 mark: Identifies that the prefixes give the size of the particles
markerNotes: Explain that a scale prefix is a power of 10 applied to the metre, so the prefix sets the size of the unit.
Compare the two prefixes by their powers of 10, since micro is a larger power than nano.
Name the larger item explicitly rather than leaving the comparison implied.
commonStudentErrors: Says nano is larger because the word sounds bigger.
Says the scale prefixes are only names with no meaning in terms of powers of 10.
Describes the prefixes without stating which item is larger.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scale prefixes are powers of 10 attached to the metre, so each prefix sets the size of its unit. Nano means 10⁻⁹ of a metre and micro means 10⁻⁶ of a metre, so a nanometre is much smaller than a micrometre. The virus at 100 nanometres is far smaller than the bacterium, which is measured in micrometres. The bacterium is therefore the larger item, because micro is a larger power of 10 than nano.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing both prefixes as powers of 10 relative to the metre and stating that the bacterium is larger.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nano and micro are prefixes that give the size of each unit. The bacterium is the larger item.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the prefixes and identifies the larger item, which meets the 2-mark row. It does not compare the powers of 10, so it cannot reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The prefixes show the size of each particle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Justify which scale prefix the public report should use for this concentration, and assess the risk of misreading the symbols milli and mega in a report.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A public report gives the concentration of a dissolved metal in drinking water as 5 µg per litre, using the micro prefix, and a second report gives 5 mg per litre after a typing error. The milli symbol m and the mega symbol M look similar and differ only in case.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the micro prefix for this concentration by linking it to powers of 10 and a readable number, and assesses clearly how confusing milli with mega could misstate the amount by a large factor
5 marks: Justifies the choice of prefix with reference to the powers of 10 involved, and assesses the risk of confusing the symbols m and M
4 marks: Justifies a prefix choice with some reference to the size of the quantity, and identifies the risk of confusion between the symbols
3 marks: Describes what each prefix means in powers of 10, with some reference to the risk of misreading the symbols
2 marks: Identifies a suitable prefix for the concentration or the risk of misreading the symbols
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Justify the prefix by a practical rule: choose the prefix that gives a readable number, so the value is neither very large nor very small.
The symbols m (milli) and M (mega) differ only in case, but their powers of 10 are a billion times apart, so a misread changes the value by a huge factor.
Strong answers recommend a clear convention, such as writing the prefix in full in public reports.
commonStudentErrors: Says the prefix does not matter because the same amount is still present.
Treats the symbols m and M as interchangeable because they look alike.
Justifies micro only by saying it is a smaller unit, without a readable number.

sampleAnswers.answer: The micro prefix is the most suitable here, because the concentration is small and expressing it in micrograms per litre gives a readable number. Milligrams per litre would give a very small value, and grams per litre would be impractical. Scale prefixes are powers of 10 that place a value in a sensible range, so choosing the prefix that matches the size of the quantity keeps the report clear for the public. The risk of misreading is serious, however. The symbols milli for m and mega for M differ only in case, but their powers of 10 are a billion times apart, so a reader who mistakes one for the other could misstate the amount by a huge factor. Writing the prefix in full, such as micrograms per litre, removes this ambiguity. A clear convention for every scale prefix is therefore part of using them appropriately.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying micro from powers of 10 and a readable number, and assessing the serious risk of confusing milli with mega.

sampleAnswers.answer: Micro suits a small concentration because it gives a readable number. Misreading m for milli as M for mega is a risk, because the symbols differ only in case.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the choice of micro and the symbol risk, which meets the 3-mark row. It does not explain the size of the powers of 10 involved, so it cannot reach 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Micro gives a readable number.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Apply scientific principles to address real-world applications and problems

prompts.question: Explain why the magnesium corrodes instead of the steel when the two metals are connected.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council is choosing how to protect a buried steel water pipe from corrosion. One option is to connect a block of magnesium to the pipe, a method called a sacrificial anode, and another is to paint the pipe.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that magnesium is higher in the reactivity series and is oxidised first, giving up electrons that flow to the steel, so the magnesium corrodes as a sacrificial anode
2 marks: Explains that magnesium is more reactive than steel, so it corrodes in preference to the steel
1 mark: Identifies that magnesium is more reactive than steel
markerNotes: Name the reactivity series position as the reason: a more reactive metal is oxidised more readily, so it loses electrons first.
Describe the flow of electrons through the connection to the steel, which is the protected metal, not just the reactivity of the metals.
Use the term sacrificial anode and explain that the magnesium is used up to protect the pipe.
commonStudentErrors: Says the magnesium is protected because it is harder than steel.
Says the steel corrodes because it is connected to the magnesium.
States that magnesium is more reactive without linking this to oxidation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Magnesium is higher than iron in the reactivity series, so it is more readily oxidised. When the two metals are connected, magnesium atoms lose electrons to form ions, and these electrons flow through the connection to the steel. The magnesium corrodes in preference to the steel, so the steel is protected. This is why the magnesium is called a sacrificial anode.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by linking the reactivity series to oxidation, the electron flow and the sacrificial anode.

sampleAnswers.answer: Magnesium is more reactive than steel, so it corrodes in preference to the steel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the preferential corrosion through reactivity, which meets the 2-mark row. It does not describe the electron flow, so it cannot reach 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Magnesium is more reactive than steel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the reactivity difference only, which meets the 1-mark row.

prompts.question: Apply the reactivity series to explain why the zinc coating protects the exposed steel while the tin coating causes the steel to rust faster.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A food manufacturer compares two coatings for steel cans. Zinc-coated steel and tin-plated steel are each deliberately scratched through to the bare steel. After several weeks in a damp environment, the zinc-coated scratch shows little rust, while the tin-plated scratch shows rapid rusting of the steel.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Applies the reactivity series to explain that zinc is more reactive than iron and corrodes first at the scratch, while tin is less reactive so iron becomes the metal that is oxidised and corrodes faster, with clear reference to oxidation and electron flow
5 marks: Applies the reactivity series to explain the protection of steel by zinc and the faster rusting with tin, referring to which metal is oxidised
4 marks: Applies the reactivity series to explain why zinc protects the steel, with some reference to the tin coating
3 marks: Explains that zinc is more reactive than iron and tin is less reactive, with some reference to the scratch
2 marks: Identifies that zinc is more reactive than steel
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: The key is which metal is oxidised at the scratch: the more reactive metal, as the reactivity series shows, loses electrons first.
