For tin, iron is the more reactive metal, so iron is oxidised and rusts faster, which is the opposite of what the coating is meant to do.
Say that electrons flow from the oxidised metal to the other metal, rather than only saying one metal is more reactive.
commonStudentErrors: Says tin protects the steel because tin is a metal that resists rust.
Says zinc is protected by the steel, reversing which metal is more reactive.
Says the scratch matters only because it lets air in, without using the reactivity series.

sampleAnswers.answer: Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so zinc has the greater tendency to undergo oxidation than the steel. At the scratch, the zinc in the coating loses electrons and corrodes instead of the iron, so the exposed steel is protected. The electrons released by the zinc flow into the steel, where they take part in reactions that do not oxidise the iron. Tin is lower than iron in the reactivity series, so iron is the more reactive metal. At a scratch in tin-plated steel, the iron is oxidised, because it loses electrons more readily than the tin does. The iron corrodes faster, and the tin coating gives no protection and may make the rusting worse. The reactivity series, not the appearance of the coating, decides whether a coating protects the steel. This is why galvanised steel can protect for years, while the zinc is gradually used up.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by applying the reactivity series to both coatings, identifying the oxidised metal at each scratch, and explaining the electron flow.

sampleAnswers.answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes at the scratch and protects the steel. Tin is less reactive, so the iron would corrode instead.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the reactivity difference with reference to the scratch, which meets the 3-mark row. It does not explain the electron flow, so it cannot reach 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Zinc is more reactive than steel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only, which meets the 1-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Use modelling and cause-and-effect relationships, including mathematical examples, to make predictions, explain phenomena and solve problems

prompts.question: Predict how the pressure of the gas changes when it is heated, and explain your prediction using the particle model of matter.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A rigid, sealed steel cylinder contains a fixed amount of argon gas at 20°C. The cylinder is heated to 80°C, and its volume does not change.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Predicts that the pressure increases and explains the change using the particle model, linking higher kinetic energy to more frequent and more forceful collisions with the walls
3 marks: Predicts the direction of the pressure change and explains it using the particle model, with some links between temperature and collisions
2 marks: Predicts the pressure change with a limited explanation that refers to the particles
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the gas or the particle model
markerNotes: The prediction must name the direction of change, and the explanation must follow from the particle model rather than restate the scenario.
Strong answers link temperature to kinetic energy, kinetic energy to collision frequency and force, and collisions to pressure, in that order.
Because the volume is fixed, the answer should say why collisions become more frequent, not only that particles move faster.
commonStudentErrors: Predicts that the pressure falls because the gas expands when heated, ignoring that the container is rigid.
Says the particles get bigger when heated instead of moving faster.
Gives a prediction with no reference to the particle model, so the explanation only restates the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pressure of the argon will increase. In the particle model of matter, pressure comes from gas particles colliding with the walls of the container. Heating the gas increases the kinetic energy of the particles, so they move faster. Because the volume is fixed, the faster particles strike the walls more often and with greater force. The rigid container also prevents the gas from expanding to reduce these collisions, so the model predicts a clear rise in pressure. This cause-and-effect relationship is the basis of the prediction, and this use of modelling could be tested by measuring the pressure at several temperatures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts the increase and explains each step of the particle model, including why the fixed volume and rigid container matter. The cause and the effect are both stated clearly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pressure will increase because the particles move faster when the gas is heated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Predicts the correct direction and gives a brief particle reason. It does not explain how faster particles produce more pressure at the walls, so it earns the lower mark.

sampleAnswers.answer: The gas particles are constantly moving and hit the walls of the container.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant particle information, but no prediction is made about the pressure.

prompts.question: APPLY the collision model to explain why the powdered marble produces carbon dioxide faster than the lumps, then use the same reasoning to predict the effect of also heating the acid.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student adds the same mass of marble (calcium carbonate) to two separate flasks of dilute hydrochloric acid at room temperature. In Flask A the marble is one large lump, and in Flask B it is ground into a fine powder. Carbon dioxide gas is produced in both flasks, but it is produced faster in Flask B.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Applies the collision model to explain the faster rate in the powder through surface area and collision frequency, and extends the same reasoning to a sound cause-and-effect prediction for heated acid
5 marks: Applies the collision model to explain the faster rate in the powder with surface area as the cause, and makes a prediction for heated acid with some reasoning
4 marks: Applies the collision model to explain the faster rate in the powder with a relevant link to surface area
3 marks: Explains the faster rate in the powder in terms of more collisions, without clear reference to surface area or the model
2 marks: Identifies that the powder has a larger surface area, with limited explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the reaction or the marble
markerNotes: The strongest answers name surface area as the cause, collision frequency as the mechanism and the faster rate as the effect.
The prediction for heated acid must follow from the same model: higher kinetic energy means more frequent and more energetic collisions.
Describing the powder as more reactive earns no credit unless it is explained through collisions.
commonStudentErrors: Says the powder is more reactive than the lump, with no link to collisions or surface area.
Claims the powder has more marble, when the same mass is added to each flask.
Predicts that heating the acid slows the reaction because the particles move apart.

sampleAnswers.answer: The collision model is a form of modelling that links cause and effect. Chemical reactions occur when reactant particles collide with enough energy. In the lump, only particles on the outer surface of the marble can be reached by the acid, so fewer particles are exposed to collisions at any moment. The powder has a much larger total surface area, so many more calcium carbonate particles are exposed to the acid at once. This increases the frequency of successful collisions, so carbon dioxide is produced faster. The cause is the greater surface area and the effect is the faster rate, a cause-and-effect relationship that the model explains. Heating the acid would increase the kinetic energy of its particles, so collisions would be more frequent and more energetic. More collisions would then have enough energy to react, so the powder in heated acid would be predicted to produce carbon dioxide faster still. This prediction could be tested by repeating the experiment at two temperatures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies the collision model to the change in surface area, links it to collision frequency and the faster rate, and makes a clear cause-and-effect prediction for heated acid. The modelling is explicit throughout.

sampleAnswers.answer: The powder reacts faster because there are more collisions between the marble and the acid. Heating the acid would make the reaction faster too.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the faster rate through more collisions, but does not link the cause to surface area or apply the model in detail.

sampleAnswers.answer: The powder is a different form of marble that reacts more quickly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about the reaction, but the collision model is not applied.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate and modify a scientific investigation in response to new evidence

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two modifications the student should make to the investigation in response to this new evidence.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student investigated how temperature affects the rate of reaction between magnesium ribbon and hydrochloric acid, using one trial at each temperature. The first results suggested that the rate increases with temperature. A classmate then repeated the trials and found that the times at each temperature varied widely, and that the volume of acid had not been measured.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two specific modifications that respond to the new evidence, with a clear reason for each that links it to the reliability or fairness of the investigation
3 marks: Describes two modifications that respond to the new evidence, with some reasons given
2 marks: Identifies one relevant modification to the investigation with a brief reason
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the investigation or the evidence
markerNotes: Each modification should respond to the new evidence, not list general good practice.
Give a reason for each change, such as reducing random error or keeping the acid volume constant.
A change that alters the question being tested, such as the metal used, does not modify this investigation.
commonStudentErrors: Proposes a different hypothesis or a different metal, rather than modifying the existing investigation.
Lists vague changes such as 'be more careful', with no link to the evidence.
Suggests a more precise thermometer without explaining how it addresses the variation in times.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first modification is to repeat each trial several times at every temperature and use the average time, recording each time in a table so the spread can be compared. This shows whether the variation is random error or a real effect of temperature, so the new evidence can be interpreted reliably. The second modification is to measure and keep constant the volume and concentration of the acid, because these are controlled variables that affect the rate. With these changes, the scientific investigation becomes a fair test, and the conclusion about temperature rests on evidence that can be repeated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two specific modifications, each linked to the new evidence and to reliability or fairness. The response is clear and specific.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should repeat each trial to check whether the times are consistent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one valid modification with a brief reason. A second, different change is needed for the higher mark.

sampleAnswers.answer: The variation in the times is new evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant comment on the evidence, but no modification to the investigation is described.

prompts.question: ASSESS how strongly the averaged results support the conclusion that rate increases with temperature, and justify one further modification the student should make before drawing a firm conclusion.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: After the repeated trials, the student found that the average time to produce the same volume of hydrogen gas was shorter at 60°C than at 20°C. The average at 40°C fell between these two values, but the spread of individual times at 40°C overlapped with both other temperatures. Only three temperatures were tested, all using the same batch of magnesium.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the strength of the conclusion using the averaged results and the overlap at 40°C, and justifies a specific further modification that reduces uncertainty in the scientific investigation
5 marks: Assesses the conclusion by commenting on the trend and the overlap, and proposes a relevant further modification with some justification
4 marks: Comments on the strength of the conclusion with some reference to the results, and identifies a relevant further modification
3 marks: Describes the results and the conclusion, with a basic comment on the reliability of the investigation
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the results or the investigation, with limited comment
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the results
markerNotes: The assessment should weigh the evidence for and against the conclusion before judging how strong it is.
A further modification earns full credit only when it targets the uncertainty in the results, such as the overlap at 40°C.
Describing general improvements that do not respond to this evidence earns limited credit.
commonStudentErrors: Says the conclusion is definitely correct because the average times fell, ignoring the overlap at 40°C.
Recommends a different metal, which changes the question rather than refining the investigation.
Judges the results without mentioning their limitations, such as the small number of temperatures tested.

sampleAnswers.answer: The averaged results give moderate support for the conclusion. The average time falls from 20°C to 60°C, which is consistent with collision theory: higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react. However, the overlap at 40°C means the trend is not yet clear, and the new evidence suggests that random error may affect individual times. The evidence is also limited because only three temperatures were tested. A justified further modification is to test more temperatures between 20°C and 60°C, and to repeat each temperature enough times to show whether the overlap is real. Recording each repeat time in a table would also show the spread at every temperature, so the overlap can be judged rather than guessed. Until that extra data is collected, a firm conclusion about how the rate changes between 20°C and 60°C cannot be drawn, and the claim should be stated as tentative. This would make the scientific investigation a more reliable test of the conclusion and a firmer basis for the rate trend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the strength of the conclusion against the overlap at 40°C and justifies a specific further modification that reduces the uncertainty. The evidence is weighed on both sides.

sampleAnswers.answer: The average times fall as temperature rises, so the conclusion seems reasonable. The student should repeat the trials to be more confident.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the trend and gives a basic comment on reliability, but does not weigh the overlap at 40°C or justify the modification.

sampleAnswers.answer: The results show that the magnesium reacted faster at 60°C.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information from the results, but makes no assessment of the conclusion.

dotPoints.description: Explain why current scientific knowledge is both contestable and testable by further inquiry

prompts.question: EXPLAIN why the current model of the atom is both contestable and testable by further inquiry.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student reads a textbook that describes the current model of the atom. The textbook also compares this model with earlier models, such as Dalton's solid sphere model, and notes that the current model may be revised.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that current scientific knowledge is contestable because new evidence can revise it, and testable because its predictions can be checked by further inquiry
2 marks: Identifies that current knowledge can change with new evidence, with a limited reference to testing
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the atomic model or about scientific knowledge
markerNotes: Contestable means the knowledge can be challenged and revised with evidence, and testable means it makes predictions that can be checked.
Naming a specific example, such as the atomic model, makes the explanation concrete and earns credit.
A strong answer ties the explanation to the word current, since the knowledge is the best available and not final.
commonStudentErrors: Says scientific knowledge is contestable because scientists disagree, rather than because evidence can revise it.
Says the atomic model is true and cannot change, which contradicts the idea of contestable knowledge.
Describes the history of the atomic model without explaining why it can be tested.

sampleAnswers.answer: Current scientific knowledge is contestable because it is accepted only while it fits present evidence, and new evidence, such as results from scattering or emission experiments, could require the model of the atom to be revised. The model is testable because it makes predictions, such as the pattern of light emitted by excited atoms, that can be checked by further inquiry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains both contestability, through the role of new evidence, and testability, through predictions that can be checked. The examples make the explanation specific.

sampleAnswers.answer: The atomic model can change if new evidence is found. Scientists can test it by doing experiments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies that the knowledge can change and that it can be tested, but neither point is developed with a specific example or prediction.

sampleAnswers.answer: The atomic model has changed over time, from Dalton's model to the current model.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about the model's history, but it does not explain contestability or testability.

prompts.question: DISCUSS how the changes from Dalton's model to the current model of the atom show that scientific knowledge is both contestable and testable.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class compares Dalton's solid sphere model of the atom, Rutherford's nuclear model and the current electron-cloud model. Students are asked to identify what new evidence led to each change.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how each change to the model was driven by new evidence and how each model made testable predictions, linking both points to the contestable and testable nature of current scientific knowledge
5 marks: Discusses at least two changes to the model, showing that new evidence led to revision and that the models were testable
4 marks: Discusses one or two changes to the model with some reference to the evidence that prompted them
3 marks: Describes the changes to the model in sequence with a basic link to new evidence
2 marks: Identifies one change in the model with limited reference to evidence or testing
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the atomic models
markerNotes: Strong answers follow the sequence of models and state what new evidence changed each one.
Testability needs a named prediction or observation, such as particle deflection, rather than a general claim that models can be tested.
The conclusion should link the history back to the dot point: current knowledge is provisional and open to testing.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the models in order without saying what new evidence caused each change.
Argues that scientists keep changing their minds without evidence, which confuses contestable knowledge with opinion.
Treats the electron-cloud model as final, so the answer does not show that current knowledge is contestable.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dalton proposed that atoms were solid, indivisible spheres. Thomson's discovery of the electron showed that atoms have internal structure, so this model had to be changed. Rutherford's gold foil experiment then showed that most of an atom's mass and positive charge are concentrated in a small nucleus, and his nuclear model replaced the earlier model. Each change shows that the model of the atom was contestable, because it was accepted only while it fitted the new evidence. Each model was also testable, because it made predictions about observations, such as particle deflections or the light emitted by atoms, that could be checked by experiment. The current electron-cloud model is the product of this process. It is the best model available, and it will be revised if future evidence does not fit it, which shows that current scientific knowledge is provisional and open to further inquiry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Traces each change in the model to the new evidence that caused it, shows that each model made testable predictions, and links both points to the contestable nature of current scientific knowledge.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dalton's model was changed when Thomson found electrons, and Rutherford then proposed a nucleus. Each model was tested by experiments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the sequence of changes with a basic link to evidence, but the testable predictions and the conclusion about current knowledge are not developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dalton proposed that atoms were solid spheres.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about one model, but no change, evidence or testing is discussed.

dotPoints.description: Construct evidence-based arguments and recognise the role of peer review in the evaluation of scientific practices, solutions or conclusions

prompts.question: OUTLINE the role of peer review in evaluating the team's conclusion before it is accepted by the scientific community.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A research team submits a paper to a scientific journal, claiming that a new catalyst speeds up a reaction more than the catalysts currently used. Before the paper can be published, it is sent to other experts in the same field for review.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how peer review evaluates the evidence and reasoning behind a conclusion before publication, and explains why this makes it a check on evidence-based arguments
2 marks: Outlines one role of peer review in checking a scientific conclusion, with limited explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about peer review or scientific evidence
markerNotes: The outline should name what reviewers check, such as the methods, the data and whether the conclusion follows from the evidence.
Credit requires the role of peer review specifically, not general statements about the value of science.
commonStudentErrors: Says peer review proves a conclusion is true, rather than testing whether the evidence supports it.
Describes peer review as a vote by scientists, which ignores the checking of methods and data.
Confuses peer review with repeating the experiment in the laboratory of the original team.

sampleAnswers.answer: Peer review is a stage of evaluation in which other experts in the field examine a paper before publication. Reviewers check the methods, data and conclusions, and ask whether the evidence supports the claim and whether the investigation is repeatable. This makes peer review a check on evidence-based arguments in scientific practice, so weak or unsupported conclusions can be identified and revised before they are accepted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the review process and what reviewers check, and explains why this makes it a check on the argument. The answer is concise and specific.

sampleAnswers.answer: Experts in the field check the paper before it is published. This helps identify weak conclusions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one role of peer review, with limited explanation of how it checks the conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scientists share their results with each other through journals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about publishing, but no role of peer review in checking a conclusion is described.

prompts.question: CONSTRUCT an evidence-based argument about whether the student's claim is supported, including what peer review would need to check before the claim is accepted.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student claims that a new iron-based catalyst makes hydrogen peroxide decompose faster than the manganese dioxide catalyst used in the school lab. The only evidence is that oxygen bubbles appeared sooner with the new catalyst in a single trial for each catalyst, and the two peroxide solutions were at different temperatures.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a sustained evidence-based argument that evaluates the single trial and the temperature difference, and explains what peer review would need to check before the claim is accepted
5 marks: Constructs an evidence-based argument that identifies the flaws in the investigation and links them to the strength of the claim
4 marks: Constructs an argument that comments on the evidence for the claim, with some reference to the flaws in the investigation
3 marks: Identifies a feature of the evidence and makes a basic judgement about the claim
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the investigation, with limited comment on the claim
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about catalysts or peer review
markerNotes: The argument must judge the claim, not just list features of the investigation: say whether the evidence supports it and why.
Name the confounding variable, temperature, and explain how it could produce the observed result.
Peer review earns credit when linked to checking the method or repeatability, not as a general statement that science is checked.
commonStudentErrors: Accepts the claim because the bubbles appeared sooner, without noting that only one trial was done.
Says the temperature difference does not matter because catalysts work at any temperature.
Treats peer review as the same as repeating the experiment, rather than checking the argument.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is not yet supported by the evidence. The faster bubbling with the new catalyst is a relevant observation, but it comes from a single trial for each catalyst, so it cannot show whether the difference is consistent or due to random variation. The two solutions were also at different temperatures, and temperature increases the rate of reaction, so temperature may explain the faster result rather than the catalyst. This means the comparison is not a fair test, because a controlled variable was not kept constant. A sound evidence-based argument would need repeated trials for each catalyst, solutions at the same temperature, and the volume of oxygen measured in each case. Peer review would check these points before acceptance, asking whether the method is a fair test, whether the results are repeatable and whether the conclusion goes beyond the evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Judges the claim as unsupported, identifies the single trial and the temperature difference as flaws, and explains what peer review would check. The argument is sustained and evidence-based.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is probably wrong because the student only did one trial. Peer review would check whether the results can be repeated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one flaw in the evidence and gives a basic judgement, with a brief link to peer review. The flaws are not connected to the strength of the claim in depth.

sampleAnswers.answer: Catalysts speed up reactions without being used up in the reaction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about catalysts, but no argument about the student's evidence is made.

dotPoints.description: Select and use appropriate digital, visual, written and oral media to convey scientific arguments

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two features of a visual medium that would help the class see why the outer electron of a larger Group 1 atom is easier to lose.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 student must explain to classmates why reactivity increases down Group 1 of the periodic table, using evidence from a demonstration. The student has to choose a visual medium to show the trend in atomic structure.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two features of a suitable visual medium and explains how each would convey the scientific argument clearly to the audience
2 marks: Describes one suitable feature of a visual medium with some link to the argument
1 mark: Identifies a visual medium that could be used in the presentation
markerNotes: A strong answer chooses features that make the trend visible, such as electron shells, arrows or labels, rather than naming a medium alone.
Credit goes to the link between each feature and the class's understanding of the trend.
commonStudentErrors: Names a medium, such as a poster, without describing any feature that would convey the argument.
Describes decorative features, such as colours, rather than features that show the trend in reactivity.
Suggests a long written report for a short class presentation, without considering the audience.

sampleAnswers.answer: A labelled diagram of lithium, sodium and potassium atoms would show the extra electron shell in each larger atom, which makes the outer electron easier to lose. Arrows drawn beside the diagram would show the increasing atomic radius, so the audience can see the trend. Clear labels make the visual medium support the scientific argument.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two features that make the trend visible and explains how each conveys the argument. The link to the audience is clear.

sampleAnswers.answer: A labelled diagram of the atoms would show the extra electron shell in each larger atom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one suitable feature linked to the trend, but a second feature is needed for the higher mark.

sampleAnswers.answer: A poster could be used to present the argument to the class.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a suitable medium, but describes no feature of it.

prompts.question: RECOMMEND the most appropriate medium for presenting this conclusion to the science fair visitors, and justify why it suits their audience and purpose.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A team has investigated how the surface area of marble chips affects the rate of their reaction with hydrochloric acid, and found that the powdered marble produced gas faster than the lumps. They must now present this conclusion at a school science fair, where visitors read each display for only a few minutes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Recommends the most suitable medium for the science fair audience and justifies it with reference to the purpose, the visitors' limited time and the clarity of the evidence
4 marks: Recommends a suitable medium for the audience and gives sound reasons that relate to the purpose
3 marks: Recommends a suitable medium with some reasons, but the link to the audience or purpose is limited
2 marks: Identifies a medium that could be used, with a basic reason
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the media or the audience
markerNotes: The recommendation should name a specific medium or combination and say why it suits visitors at a science fair.
Strong answers weigh the visitors' limited time against the detail the scientific argument needs.
A justification that only praises the medium, without linking it to the audience or purpose, earns limited credit.
commonStudentErrors: Recommends a long written report, which a passing visitor is unlikely to read.
Recommends an oral talk only, without considering that most visitors will not stay for it.
Justifies the choice by calling the medium professional, without reference to the audience or purpose.

sampleAnswers.answer: A one-page poster with a labelled graph of the results would be the most appropriate medium for the science fair. Visitors are a general audience who spend only a few minutes at each display, so a visual medium can show the trend at a glance. A labelled graph shows that the powdered marble produced gas faster than the lumps, which is the key evidence for the conclusion. A short written caption can state the conclusion and the scientific argument, linking greater surface area to more frequent collisions. An oral explanation would suit a visitor who stops to ask questions, but the poster is understood without a speaker, so the purpose of informing every visitor is met.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Recommends a single poster with a labelled graph and justifies it against the visitors' short time, the purpose of informing everyone, and the key evidence. The oral element is weighed and set aside.

sampleAnswers.answer: A poster is the best choice because it is quick to read at a fair. It shows the main conclusion clearly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Recommends a suitable medium with a basic reason, but the link to the purpose and to visitors' limited time is not developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: A science fair has many visitors and displays.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about the setting only, and no medium is recommended.

dotPoints.description: Apply appropriate scientific notations, language and nomenclature

prompts.question: CLASSIFY each compound as ionic or covalent, and give its correct name using the rules of nomenclature.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's lab report labels three compounds, CuO, CO and FeCl₃, as 'copper oxide', 'carbon oxide' and 'iron chloride'. The report does not say whether each compound is ionic or covalent, and the teacher asks the student to correct it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Classifies all three compounds correctly and names each one correctly, showing the Roman numerals and prefixes where needed
3 marks: Classifies all three compounds correctly and names two of them correctly
2 marks: Classifies at least two compounds correctly and names at least one correctly
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about ionic or covalent compounds
markerNotes: Credit a name only when the Roman numeral or prefix is correct, since copper oxide and carbon oxide are both incorrect names here.
Classification should rest on whether the elements are metals or non-metals, not on the appearance of the compound.
commonStudentErrors: Names CO as carbon oxide, which omits the prefix that identifies the compound.
Calls CuO covalent because oxygen is a non-metal, without considering that copper is a metal.
Writes the formula of iron(III) chloride as FeCl, ignoring the 3+ charge on the iron ion.

sampleAnswers.answer: CuO is an ionic compound, because copper is a metal and oxygen is a non-metal, so electrons are transferred to form ions. Applying nomenclature, its correct name is copper(II) oxide, where the Roman numeral shows the 2+ charge on the copper ion. CO is a covalent compound, because carbon and oxygen are both non-metals that share electrons. Its correct name is carbon monoxide, where the prefix 'mono' shows one oxygen atom. FeCl₃ is an ionic compound, because iron is a metal and chlorine is a non-metal. Its correct name is iron(III) chloride, where the Roman numeral shows the 3+ charge on the iron ion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all three compounds with a reason and names each correctly, using the Roman numeral and prefix. The nomenclature is applied accurately throughout.

sampleAnswers.answer: CuO is ionic and CO is covalent. FeCl₃ is ionic. The names are copper oxide, carbon oxide and iron(III) chloride.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all three correctly and names one compound correctly. The copper and carbon names lack the Roman numeral and the prefix.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ionic compounds form between metals and non-metals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about ionic bonding, but no compound is classified or named.

prompts.question: APPLY the rules of nomenclature and state symbols to correct the student's notes, naming the product and justifying the state symbol for each substance in the equation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student reacts solid copper(II) oxide with dilute hydrochloric acid and obtains a blue-green solution. The student's notes name the product 'copper chloride' and write the equation as CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O, with no state symbols.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies nomenclature and state symbols correctly to name the copper product and justify the state of every substance in the equation
4 marks: Applies nomenclature correctly to name the copper product and gives correct state symbols for most substances, with reasons
3 marks: Names the copper product correctly and gives correct state symbols for at least two substances
2 marks: Gives a correct name or state symbol for at least one substance, with limited accuracy
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about nomenclature or state symbols
markerNotes: The Roman numeral is needed for copper(II) chloride because copper forms more than one ion, so a name without it is ambiguous.
Justify each state symbol from the chemistry, such as solubility, the physical state of the reactant or the temperature, rather than only stating it.
Use (aq) for substances dissolved in water and (l) for the water produced, not (g) or (s).
commonStudentErrors: Names CuCl₂ as copper chloride, omitting the Roman numeral that identifies the copper ion.
Writes H₂O as (g), as if the water were produced as steam at room temperature.
Writes CuO(aq), as if the solid oxide dissolves in the acid.

sampleAnswers.answer: The product is copper(II) chloride, not copper chloride. Applying nomenclature, the Roman numeral (II) is needed because copper forms more than one ion, and the name must show that the copper ion carries a 2+ charge. The state symbol for CuO is (s), because copper(II) oxide is an insoluble solid. The state symbol for HCl is (aq), because hydrogen chloride dissolves in water to form hydrochloric acid. The state symbol for CuCl₂ is (aq), because copper(II) chloride is soluble and its ions separate in solution. The state symbol for H₂O is (l), because water produced at room temperature is a liquid.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names the product with its Roman numeral and gives a state symbol for every substance, each justified from the chemistry. The justification is the key difference from a bare list of symbols.

sampleAnswers.answer: The product is copper(II) chloride. CuO is (s), HCl is (aq), CuCl₂ is (aq) and H₂O is (l).
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names the product correctly and gives correct state symbols for all substances, but gives no justification for them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The blue-green product is a salt that dissolves in water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant information about the product, but no name or state symbol is given.

dotPoints.description: Use evidence and correct scientific language and terminology to address a specific audience and purpose in a variety of contexts

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two changes to the wording of this warning so that it suits a general household audience and uses correct scientific terminology.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A council asks a local chemist to write a short warning for its newsletter about mixing bleach with ammonia-based window cleaner. Mixing these products can release toxic chloramine gases, but the draft warning says only that 'toxic fumes' may form.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes two specific changes to the wording that use accurate terminology and cite the evidence, each clearly suited to the household audience and purpose of the warning
3 marks: Describes two changes to the wording that suit the audience, with some accurate terminology or evidence
2 marks: Describes one relevant change to the wording with a brief link to the audience
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the warning or the household audience
markerNotes: The changes should be about the wording; any change to the content must be justified by the evidence.
Strong answers keep the correct term alongside the everyday one, so the notice is both accurate and understood.
A specific action for the reader earns credit because it serves the purpose of the warning.
commonStudentErrors: Replaces 'hypochlorite' with 'bleach' only, which loses the correct chemical name for the label.
Rewrites the warning as a detailed explanation of chloramine chemistry, which a general audience would not follow.
Suggests changing the colour or layout of the notice, which is not a change to the wording.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first change is to pair the everyday term with the correct terminology, so the warning reads 'bleach (sodium hypochlorite)'. This keeps the scientific language accurate while suiting a general household audience, and it matches the label on the product. The second change is to replace the vague phrase 'toxic fumes' with the evidence that mixing bleach and ammonia-based cleaners releases toxic chloramine gases. A clear action, such as never mixing the products and ventilating the room if they are mixed, serves the purpose of the warning, which is to prevent harm.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes two specific changes, each using accurate terminology or evidence and each suited to the household audience. The purpose of the warning is served by the action.

sampleAnswers.answer: The notice should name bleach as well as sodium hypochlorite. This suits households who read the label.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one relevant change and links it to the household audience, but gives no second change.

sampleAnswers.answer: The warning should be written in plain English so people understand it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relevant but general; no specific change to the wording is described and no evidence is used.

prompts.question: ASSESS how well the newsletter uses evidence and scientific language for its audience and purpose, and JUSTIFY one change that would improve it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's Year 7 newsletter explains why marble fizzes faster when crushed. It says: 'Crushing the marble makes the fizzing quicker because there is more stuff touching the acid. Hotter acid would be even quicker still.' The class results showed that powdered marble produced gas faster than the lumps.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the use of evidence and scientific language in the newsletter against its audience and purpose, and justifies one specific change that keeps the explanation accurate for Year 7 readers
5 marks: Assesses the use of evidence and language for the audience and purpose, and identifies one change with a sound reason
4 marks: Assesses the wording with some reference to the audience, and suggests a change with a brief reason
3 marks: Comments on the evidence or language in the newsletter with a basic link to the audience
2 marks: Identifies one feature of the wording with limited comment on the audience or purpose
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the newsletter or its readers
markerNotes: The assessment should judge the wording against both the audience and the purpose, not only whether each statement is correct.
A correct change keeps the science accurate while making it suitable for the audience, such as replacing 'more stuff' with 'greater surface area'.
Separate a prediction in the newsletter from evidence from the class results when judging the evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Says the newsletter is wrong to use simple language, when simple wording suits a Year 7 audience.
Judges the newsletter only for layout or spelling, without judging the evidence or the scientific language.
Proposes adding a full technical explanation of collision theory, which would not suit a Year 7 audience.

sampleAnswers.answer: The newsletter uses evidence well, because it links the faster reaction in the powder to the class results and gives a cause-and-effect explanation that a Year 7 reader can follow. However, the phrase 'more stuff' is not correct scientific language, and it does not identify what is touching the acid. The newsletter should say 'greater surface area' so that the audience learns the correct terminology and understands that the reaction happens at the surface of the solid. The claim that hotter acid would be quicker is a prediction, not a result from the class, so it should be labelled as a prediction that could be tested. The wording suits the purpose of informing a general audience, but the explanation needs correct terminology to remain accurate. Replacing 'more stuff' with 'greater surface area' is the single most important change, because it keeps the science accurate while staying readable for Year 7 students.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the evidence and the language against the audience and purpose, then justifies one specific change, the replacement of 'more stuff', that keeps the science accurate for Year 7 readers.

sampleAnswers.answer: The newsletter explains the faster rate using the idea of more stuff touching the acid, but this wording is vague. The language is suitable for Year 7 readers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Comments on the language and the audience with a basic link to the purpose, but does not assess the evidence or justify a change.

sampleAnswers.answer: The newsletter is about the reaction between marble and acid.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides some relevant information about the newsletter only, and no assessment is made.

dotPoints.description: Use the physical characteristics of the components in homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures to explain how they can be separated

prompts.question: Explain why a mixture of sand and water can be separated by filtration, but a solution of salt in water cannot.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a student has two beakers. One holds sand stirred into water, and the other holds table salt (sodium chloride) completely dissolved in water. The student pours the contents of each beaker through filter paper held in a funnel.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how the physical characteristics of the sand and the dissolved salt determine what passes through the filter paper, linking particle size and solubility to the result of filtration
3 marks: Explains that the sand is trapped because its particles are too large to pass through the pores, while the salt passes through with the water
2 marks: Identifies that the sand is insoluble and the salt dissolves, with some link to filtration
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about filtration or these mixtures
markerNotes: Compare the two mixtures directly: sand particles are too large to pass through the pores of the filter paper, whereas dissolved salt ions pass through with the water.
A strong answer names the physical characteristic behind each result, particle size or solubility, rather than saying only that the salt is too small.
commonStudentErrors: Says the salt stays on the filter paper because it is a solid, without considering whether it dissolves.
Describes filtration in general terms without linking the result to the particle size of the sand.
Says the salt cannot pass through the filter because it is heavier than water.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sand stirred into water is one of the heterogeneous mixtures, and the salt solution is homogeneous. The sand does not dissolve, and its particles are much larger than the pores in the filter paper, so the sand is trapped while the water passes through. Table salt dissolves to form sodium and chloride ions, which are far smaller than the pores, so the dissolved salt passes through with the water. The physical characteristics explain the result: particle size separates the sand, but solubility means the salt cannot be removed. The filtrate from the salt solution still contains dissolved salt, so filtration cannot separate it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by linking the particle size of the sand and the solubility of the salt to what passes through the filter paper.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sand does not dissolve in water, so it stays on the filter paper. Salt dissolves, so filtration does not separate it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying that the sand is insoluble and the salt dissolves. Explaining why the particles behave this way would meet the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Filtration uses filter paper to separate solids from liquids.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about filtration, but it does not explain why either mixture behaves as it does.

prompts.question: Apply the physical characteristics of each component to describe a sequence of separation methods that recovers the iron filings, the sand and the salt from a heterogeneous mixture of these solids.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a student is given a dry mixture of iron filings, sand and table salt (sodium chloride) and must recover each component in pure form. Available equipment includes a magnet, distilled water, filter paper, a funnel and an evaporating dish.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies the physical characteristics of each component, including magnetism, solubility and particle size, to a logical sequence that recovers all three components
4 marks: Applies the physical characteristics of most components to a sequence that recovers all three components, with some explanation of each step
3 marks: Identifies a suitable separation method for at least two components and links each method to a physical characteristic
2 marks: Describes a separation method for one component without linking it to a physical characteristic
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about separation methods
markerNotes: Each separation must use a physical difference that one component has and the others lack, such as magnetism for the iron filings or solubility for the salt.
Order matters: the magnet comes first on the dry mixture, and the sand must be filtered out before the salt solution is evaporated.
commonStudentErrors: Proposes filtering the dry mixture first, which cannot separate the sand from the salt because both are solids.
Says the salt is removed by filtration rather than dissolved in water and then recovered by evaporation.
Lists the methods without saying which physical characteristic makes each one work.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dry mixtures of solids are heterogeneous mixtures, so each component can be removed using a physical characteristic it has and the others lack. First, a magnet is passed through the mixture to lift out the iron filings, because iron is magnetic and the sand and salt are not. Next, the remaining solids are stirred into distilled water. The salt dissolves because of its solubility, while the sand does not, so the sand stays as a solid. The sand is removed by filtration, since its particles are too large to pass through the filter paper. Finally, the salt solution is evaporated in the dish until the water is gone, leaving the salt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by applying a physical characteristic to each component and giving a logical order that recovers all three.

sampleAnswers.answer: A magnet removes the iron filings because iron is magnetic. Water is then added to dissolve the salt, and filtration removes the sand from the salt solution.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying suitable methods for at least two components and linking them to a physical characteristic. Explaining how the salt is recovered would move it closer to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A student could separate the mixture using a magnet and some water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with some relevant information about separation methods, but no method is explained or linked to a physical characteristic.

dotPoints.description: Discuss Aboriginal methods of separating mixtures by extracting dyes from plants and using woven baskets for filtration

prompts.question: Describe how a coloured dye can be extracted from plant material with water and then separated from the plant fibres using a woven basket.
prompts.scenario: The syllabus identifies Aboriginal methods of separating mixtures, including extracting dyes from plants and using woven baskets for filtration. These methods are described here in general terms only, and each depends on the physical characteristics of the materials involved.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes soaking plant material in water so the dye dissolves, then straining the liquid through a woven basket to hold back the plant fibres, with reference to solubility
2 marks: Describes one step of the process, such as soaking the plant material in water or straining the liquid
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about extracting dyes or filtration
markerNotes: Credit answers that name water as the solvent and explain that the dye dissolves, while the plant fibres do not.
The woven basket acts as a filter: its gaps hold back the solid plant fibres while the dye solution passes through.
commonStudentErrors: Says the woven basket dissolves the dye out of the plant material.
Describes the extraction without naming a step that removes the plant fibres.
States that water chemically changes the dye rather than dissolving it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Because of its solubility in water, the coloured dye dissolves when the plant material is soaked, which is the first step in extracting dyes from plants. The liquid is then strained through a woven basket. The gaps in the weave hold back the solid plant fibres, while the dye solution passes through. This filtration leaves the dye in the liquid, separate from the plant fibres in the basket.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing both steps and referring to solubility. The description is complete for this question.

sampleAnswers.answer: Plant material is soaked in water, which lets the dye dissolve into the liquid.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one step, the dye dissolving in water. Describing how the plant fibres are separated with the woven basket would meet the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A woven basket can be used for filtration.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about filtration, but the answer does not describe how the dye is extracted or separated.

prompts.question: Discuss why the Aboriginal methods of extracting dyes from plants and using woven baskets for filtration are physical rather than chemical ways of separating mixtures.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a student observes that soaking plant material in water releases a coloured liquid, and that straining the liquid through a woven basket leaves the plant fibres behind. The teacher asks whether a chemical change has taken place.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses both methods as physical separations, explaining that the dye dissolves and the basket filters by particle size, with no new substances formed
4 marks: Discusses both methods as physical separations, with some explanation of the physical characteristics involved
3 marks: Explains one method as a physical separation, with some reference to the physical characteristics involved
2 marks: Identifies a physical characteristic of one method without linking it to the separation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about Aboriginal methods or separating mixtures
markerNotes: Separation by a physical characteristic leaves each substance unchanged, so the extracted dye and the plant fibres are the same substances as before.
Credit answers that assess the processes as separation methods only, and do not add specific cultural details or claims beyond those in the dot point.
commonStudentErrors: Says soaking the plant material causes a chemical reaction that makes the dye.
Claims the woven basket holds back the fibres through a chemical bond with them.
Says the methods are not scientific without discussing the physical characteristics involved.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both Aboriginal methods are physical methods of separating mixtures. When plant material is soaked in water, the coloured dye dissolves because of its solubility, which makes extracting dyes from plants possible without any new substance forming. The dye and water are still the same substances as before, only mixed together. In woven baskets, the gaps are smaller than the solid plant pieces, so the fibres are held back while the liquid passes through. The physical characteristics of the dye and the fibres explain the result, and filtration separates by particle size. No chemical change occurs, which is why both methods are physical rather than chemical.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by discussing both methods as physical separations and explaining the physical characteristics that make each one work.

sampleAnswers.answer: Soaking plant material in water is a physical separation because the coloured dye dissolves into the water and can be collected without any chemical reaction. The solid plant material is left behind, so the method relies on the solubility of the dye.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining one method as a physical separation, using the solubility of the dye. Explaining the woven basket in the same way would move the answer towards the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal methods of separating mixtures include extracting dyes from plants.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the methods, but it does not discuss whether they are physical or chemical processes.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to determine the percentage composition of a mixture by mass

prompts.question: Outline a laboratory experiment that would give the percentage composition by mass of a dry mixture of sand and salt, identifying the measurement taken at each stage.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a student is given a dry mixture of sand and table salt. The student must separate the two solids in the laboratory, then weigh the original mixture and each recovered component.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines a sequence of laboratory steps that separates the components, records a mass at each stage, and explains how these masses give the percentage composition by mass
3 marks: Outlines a sound separation procedure and identifies the masses that need to be measured
2 marks: Identifies a suitable separation method, such as filtration, and mentions weighing
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the laboratory procedure
markerNotes: Weighing the original mixture before separation, and each dried component afterwards, gives the masses needed for the percentage composition by mass.
A strong answer keeps the sequence logical: dissolve the salt, filter off the sand, dry each component, then weigh it.
commonStudentErrors: Weighs only the recovered components and not the original mixture, so there is nothing to compare them against.
Omits drying the sand and the salt before weighing, which leaves water in the recorded masses.
Describes separating the mixture without naming any measurement taken during the experiment.

sampleAnswers.answer: This laboratory experiment begins by weighing a clean, dry evaporating dish and then the dry mixture of sand and salt, so the original mass of the mixture is known. Add distilled water and stir until the salt dissolves. Filter the mixture through pre-weighed filter paper to collect the sand, then wash the sand with a little water. Dry the sand and filter paper, then weigh them. Remove the water from the filtrate by evaporation in the weighed dish, dry the salt fully, and weigh the dish again. Comparing each recovered mass with the original mass of the mixture gives the percentage composition by mass.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining a logical sequence, recording a mass at each stage and linking the masses to the percentage composition by mass.

sampleAnswers.answer: Separate the sand by filtration, then weigh the sand and the salt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a suitable separation method and mentioning weighing. Outlining the measurements at each stage and the order of steps would meet the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mixture is separated in the laboratory.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with some relevant information about the laboratory procedure, but no separation method or measurement is named.

prompts.question: Assess the reliability of this procedure for finding the percentage composition by mass of a mixture, referring to two sources of error and their likely effect on the recovered masses.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a student separates a dry mixture of sand and salt in the laboratory by dissolving the salt in water, filtering off the sand, and then evaporating the filtrate in a weighed dish. The sand and salt are each dried and weighed, and the masses are compared with the mass of the original mixture.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the reliability of the procedure by explaining two specific sources of error and how each would change the measured masses, with a clear overall judgement
5 marks: Assesses the procedure with reference to two sources of error and their effect on the recovered masses
4 marks: Explains one source of error and its likely effect on the measured masses
3 marks: Identifies a source of error in the procedure without explaining its effect on the result
2 marks: Describes some steps of the procedure with limited reference to errors
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the procedure
markerNotes: Water left in a recovered component makes its mass too high, so the percentage composition by mass of that component is overstated.
Material lost during transfer or filtration lowers the recovered mass, so a strong answer states the direction of each error.
commonStudentErrors: Says the procedure is reliable because it uses a balance, without examining any source of error.
Lists sources of error without stating how each one changes the recovered masses.
Claims the sand dissolves in the water and passes through the filter paper.

sampleAnswers.answer: This laboratory experiment is reliable only if every component is recovered completely and weighed when dry. Two sources of error are likely to affect the result. The first is incomplete drying. If the sand or the salt still holds water when weighed, its recorded mass is too high, so the percentage composition by mass of that component is overstated. The second is loss during transfer, such as salt left in the beaker or fine sand passing through a torn filter paper. Lost material lowers the recovered mass, so the percentage composition of that component is understated. The two errors push the measured masses in opposite directions, so they can partly cancel and hide the problem when the recovered total looks close to the original mass of the mixture. Overall, the procedure is reasonably reliable for a quick check, but it can mislead about the percentage composition by mass unless drying is complete and transfers are careful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by explaining two sources of error, their direction of effect on the masses, and an overall judgement on reliability.

sampleAnswers.answer: Incomplete drying is one source of error. If the sand still holds water when it is weighed, its recorded mass is too high, so the percentage composition by mass of the sand is overstated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining one source of error and the direction of its effect. A second source and an overall judgement on reliability would be needed for the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sand is separated by filtration, then the salt is dried and weighed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing steps of the procedure with little reference to errors. Naming a source of error and its effect would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Use the element symbol, atomic number and mass number from the periodic table to construct models of atoms and illustrate the particles present

prompts.question: Describe what the element symbol, atomic number and mass number of an atom each tell you about the particles it contains, using lithium-7 as an example.
prompts.scenario: An atom of lithium-7 is written as ⁷₃Li. Lithium is the element with atomic number 3, and this atom has a mass number of 7.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes what the symbol, atomic number and mass number each tell you about the protons, neutrons and electrons, linking each piece of notation to the particles it identifies
3 marks: Describes the atomic number and mass number and what each tells you about the nucleus
2 marks: Identifies the element from its symbol and describes one of the numbers
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about atomic notation
markerNotes: The atomic number gives the protons, which also equals the electrons in a neutral atom, while the mass number gives the protons and neutrons together.
A strong answer links each piece of notation to the particles it identifies, rather than listing the numbers alone.
commonStudentErrors: Says the mass number gives the number of electrons in the atom.
Confuses the atomic number with the mass number when describing the nucleus.
States that the element symbol gives the number of neutrons in the atom.

sampleAnswers.answer: The element symbol Li identifies the atom as lithium. The atomic number 3 is the number of protons in the nucleus, and it also equals the number of electrons in a neutral atom. The mass number 7 is the total number of protons and neutrons together in the nucleus. Electrons are not counted in the mass number because they have very little mass, and they occupy the space around the nucleus. Together these three pieces of notation give the element, its number of protons and electrons, and the total number of particles in its nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by linking each piece of notation to the particles it identifies.

sampleAnswers.answer: The symbol Li shows that the atom is lithium, and the atomic number 3 tells you how many protons it has.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the element from its symbol and describing the atomic number. Explaining what the mass number tells you about the nucleus would meet the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Lithium has an atomic number of 3.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about atomic notation, but the symbol and mass number are not described.

prompts.question: Construct a written model of this atom that labels the position and charge of each type of particle present, and explain why the atom as a whole has no overall charge.
prompts.scenario: An atom of chlorine-37, written as ³⁷₁₇Cl, contains 17 protons, 20 neutrons and 17 electrons. The element symbol Cl and atomic number 17 identify this atom as chlorine, and the mass number is 37.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Constructs a labelled model that places the protons and neutrons in the nucleus and the electrons outside it, and explains the neutral charge through equal numbers of protons and electrons
4 marks: Constructs a model with the correct location and charge of each particle, with some explanation of the neutral charge
3 marks: Constructs a partly accurate model that labels the nucleus and at least two particle types
2 marks: Identifies some particles in the atom without showing where they are located
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the structure of an atom
markerNotes: The model should show the nucleus holding the protons and neutrons, with the electrons in the space around it, and labelling each particle is enough.
The neutral charge comes from the 17 positive protons balancing the 17 negative electrons, while the 20 neutrons carry no charge.
commonStudentErrors: Places the electrons inside the nucleus alongside the protons and neutrons.
Says the neutrons carry a negative charge, so they balance the protons.
Gives a labelled model without explaining why the charges cancel out.

sampleAnswers.answer: The element symbol Cl and atomic number 17 identify this atom as chlorine, and the mass number 37 shows that the nucleus holds 37 protons and neutrons in total. In the model, the nucleus sits at the centre of the atom and contains the 17 protons and 20 neutrons. Each proton carries a positive charge, while the neutrons carry no charge. The 17 electrons are located outside the nucleus, in shells around it, and each carries a negative charge. The atom has no overall charge because the 17 positive protons are balanced by the 17 negative electrons, while the neutrons add mass without changing the charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row with a labelled model that places each particle correctly and explains the neutral charge.

sampleAnswers.answer: The nucleus is at the centre of the atom and holds the protons and neutrons. The electrons are outside the nucleus and carry a negative charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row with a partly accurate model that labels the nucleus and two particle types. Explaining why the atom has no overall charge would move the answer up to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atoms have a nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving some relevant information about atomic structure, but no particles are identified or located.

dotPoints.description: Describe the distribution of mass and charge in an atom

prompts.question: Describe the distribution of mass and charge between the nucleus and the electrons in a neutral atom of carbon-12.
prompts.scenario: Carbon-12 is a common isotope of carbon. A neutral atom of carbon-12 contains 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons, and its nucleus is very small compared with the whole atom.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes how nearly all of the mass is in the nucleus while the charge is carried by protons and electrons, and explains why the atom is neutral overall
2 marks: Describes where the protons, neutrons and electrons are located, with some reference to mass or charge
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the structure of the atom
markerNotes: Nearly all the mass is in the nucleus, because protons and neutrons are far heavier than electrons, which contribute very little mass.
Charge is carried by protons (positive) and electrons (negative), and equal numbers of each make the neutral atom uncharged.
commonStudentErrors: Says the electrons hold most of the mass of the atom.
States that neutrons carry a positive charge like protons.
Describes the mass distribution without mentioning charge.

sampleAnswers.answer: The distribution of mass and charge in this neutral atom is uneven. Almost all of the mass is in the nucleus, which contains the protons and neutrons, while the electrons have very little mass. Protons carry a positive charge and electrons carry an equal negative charge, so the 6 protons are balanced by the 6 electrons and the atom is neutral overall. The neutrons carry no charge but add to the mass of the nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing where the mass and charge sit and explaining why the atom is neutral overall.

sampleAnswers.answer: The protons and neutrons are in the nucleus, and the electrons are around it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing where the particles are located, but mass and charge are not linked to them. Explaining why nearly all the mass is in the nucleus would move it up the ladder.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atoms have a nucleus at the centre.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with some relevant information about atomic structure, but neither mass nor charge is described.

prompts.question: Analyse the student's claim that electrons make almost no difference to an atom's properties because they have so little mass, using the distribution of mass and charge in an atom.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a student writes that electrons make almost no difference to the properties of an atom, because they have so little mass compared with the rest of the atom. The same notes correctly state that the atom is neutral because its protons and electrons balance.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the claim by separating mass from charge, showing that the electrons' negative charge and number govern bonding, and makes a sound judgement that the claim is wrong
4 marks: Analyses the mass and charge of the nucleus and the electrons, with a clear link to whether the claim holds
3 marks: Explains the distribution of mass and charge in an atom with some reference to the claim
2 marks: Describes the mass or charge of one particle without linking it to the claim
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about electrons or atomic structure
markerNotes: Separate the two halves of the claim: electrons do have very little mass, but their charge and number decide how an atom bonds and reacts.
Credit answers that show the distribution of mass and charge is uneven: mass sits in the nucleus, while the charge is shared between protons and electrons.
commonStudentErrors: Accepts the claim because electrons have negligible mass, without considering their charge.
Says electrons do not affect chemical properties because they sit outside the nucleus.
Argues that neutrons decide the chemical properties of an atom.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is wrong, although its first part is correct. Electrons have very little mass, so almost all of the mass is in the nucleus, which is part of the distribution of mass and charge. Charge is distributed differently: each electron carries a negative charge equal in size to the positive charge on a proton, and the electrons are spread around the nucleus. The number of electrons equals the number of protons in a neutral atom, and this number decides how an atom bonds and reacts. Electrons therefore strongly affect chemical properties, so the student's conclusion does not follow from the evidence about mass.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by separating mass from charge, showing that electron number governs chemical properties, and judging the claim wrong.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons have very little mass, which is correct, and most of the mass is in the nucleus. The electrons still carry a negative charge that balances the positive charge of the protons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the distribution of mass and charge with some reference to the claim. Showing that electron number controls chemical properties, and reaching a judgement on the claim, would meet the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons are negatively charged particles outside the nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about electrons, but no link to the claim is made.

dotPoints.description: Compare the number of protons and neutrons in various isotopes of an element

prompts.question: Compare the number of protons and the number of neutrons in carbon-12 and carbon-14, and explain why both atoms are atoms of the same element.
prompts.scenario: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. Carbon-12 atoms contain 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and carbon-14 atoms contain 6 protons and 8 neutrons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Compares the protons and neutrons of both isotopes, showing that the protons are identical and the neutrons differ, and explains why both are atoms of carbon
3 marks: Compares the numbers of protons and neutrons in both isotopes with a clear statement of the difference
2 marks: States that the protons are the same in both isotopes and that the neutron numbers differ
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about isotopes or carbon atoms
markerNotes: Both atoms have 6 protons, so the number of protons, which sets the element, is the same, while carbon-14 has 2 more neutrons.
A strong answer explains that the element depends on the protons, so the extra neutrons make the isotope heavier without making a different element.
commonStudentErrors: Says carbon-14 has more protons than carbon-12.
States that carbon-14 is a different element because it has more neutrons.
Compares the two isotopes without naming the numbers of protons or neutrons in each.

sampleAnswers.answer: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes of carbon. Both atoms have 6 protons, so the number of protons is the same in each isotope. Carbon-14 has 8 neutrons, which is 2 more than the 6 neutrons in carbon-12, so the number of neutrons is different in the two isotopes. Both atoms are atoms of the same element, carbon, because the number of protons, which is the atomic number, determines the element. The extra neutrons change the mass of the atom, but not its identity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by comparing the protons and neutrons of both isotopes and explaining why both are carbon.

sampleAnswers.answer: The protons are the same in both isotopes, but carbon-14 has more neutrons than carbon-12.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by stating that the protons are the same and the neutron numbers differ. Giving the actual numbers in each isotope would meet the 3-mark row, and explaining why both are carbon would meet the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about isotopes, but it does not compare the two carbon isotopes in the scenario.

prompts.question: Examine the student's statements about the protons and neutrons in isotopes, and correct each statement that is inaccurate.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a student's revision notes state that all atoms of an element have the same number of neutrons, and that isotopes of an element must therefore be atoms of different elements. The notes have not yet been checked against a textbook.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Examines both statements, showing that isotopes of an element differ only in neutron number, and corrects the claim that they must be different elements with a clear reference to protons
4 marks: Examines both statements and corrects at least one, with a sound reference to the protons and neutrons in each isotope
3 marks: Examines one statement and identifies the error in it, with some reference to protons or neutrons
2 marks: Identifies a relevant idea about isotopes without examining the student's statements
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about protons, neutrons or isotopes
markerNotes: The first statement is false because isotopes of one element have different neutron numbers, and the second is false because the element is set by the number of protons.
Credit corrections that keep the right idea, such as isotopes share the same protons but have different neutrons.
commonStudentErrors: Accepts the notes without checking whether isotopes share the same number of protons.
Corrects the first statement but accepts that isotopes are different elements.
Says isotopes have different numbers of protons, so they are different elements.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first statement is incorrect. Atoms of an element all have the same number of protons, but isotopes of an element have different numbers of neutrons, so the neutron count is not the same for all atoms of an element.
