The second statement is also incorrect. Isotopes of an element share the same number of protons, which sets the element, so they are atoms of the same element, not different elements. Isotopes differ in mass because of their extra neutrons, while their chemical behaviour is similar. The corrected statement is that isotopes of an element have the same protons but different neutrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by examining both statements and correcting each with reference to protons and neutrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first statement is wrong because isotopes of an element have different numbers of neutrons. Atoms of an element always have the same number of protons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by examining the first statement and identifying its error with reference to neutrons. The second statement is not examined, so the answer does not reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Isotopes contain neutrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about neutrons in isotopes, but neither statement is examined or corrected.

dotPoints.description: Calculate the relative atomic mass from isotopic composition
Use examples to explain why isotopes have similar chemical properties but different densities

prompts.question: Explain, using chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 as examples, why isotopes of an element have similar chemical properties.
prompts.scenario: Chlorine has two naturally occurring isotopes, chlorine-35 and chlorine-37. Each isotope forms a neutral atom with 17 electrons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains that the electron arrangement is the same in both isotopes and controls bonding, so the chemical properties are similar, and notes that the extra neutrons change only the mass and density
3 marks: Explains that both isotopes have the same electrons and so bond in the same way, with a clear example
2 marks: Describes how chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 react in a similar way without explaining why
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about isotopes or chlorine
markerNotes: Chemical properties depend on the electrons, which are the same in both chlorine isotopes, so the extra neutrons have little effect on bonding.
A strong answer names the extra neutrons in chlorine-37 and says they change the mass and so the density, not how the atom bonds.
commonStudentErrors: Says chlorine-37 reacts differently because it has more neutrons.
States that isotopes have similar properties because they have the same mass.
Explains the similarity without using chlorine as an example.

sampleAnswers.answer: Chemical properties depend mainly on the arrangement of electrons, especially the outer electrons. Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 are two examples of isotopes, and both have 17 electrons, so they have the same electron arrangement and form the same bonds. For example, both react with sodium to form sodium chloride. The extra two neutrons in chlorine-37 do not change its electrons, so its chemical properties match chlorine-35. These extra neutrons do give chlorine-37 a greater mass, so the isotopes have different densities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining the shared electron arrangement and noting that the extra neutrons change only the mass and density.

sampleAnswers.answer: Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 both react with sodium in similar ways.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the similar reactions of both isotopes. Explaining that both have 17 electrons, which controls bonding, would meet the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Chlorine has two isotopes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about isotopes, but no chemical property is described or explained.

prompts.question: Apply the idea of isotopes to explain why heavy water has similar chemical properties to ordinary water but a higher density.
prompts.scenario: Heavy water (D₂O) is water in which the hydrogen atoms are replaced by deuterium, an isotope of hydrogen with one proton and one neutron in its nucleus. Ordinary water (H₂O) contains hydrogen whose nucleus has no neutrons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies the idea of isotopes to explain that deuterium has the same electrons and bonding as hydrogen, so chemical properties are similar, and that the extra neutron increases mass and density
4 marks: Applies the idea of isotopes to explain both the similar chemical properties and the higher density of heavy water
3 marks: Explains that deuterium and hydrogen are isotopes with the same electrons, with some reference to the density difference
2 marks: Identifies that heavy water contains deuterium without linking this to chemical properties or density
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about isotopes or water
markerNotes: Deuterium has one electron like hydrogen, so its oxygen bonds form and break in much the same way, while the extra neutron makes each molecule heavier.
Density depends on mass per unit volume, so the answer should explain why a heavier molecule packed in a similar way gives a higher density.
commonStudentErrors: Says heavy water has different chemical properties because deuterium carries a different charge.
Claims heavy water is denser because it contains more protons.
States that heavy water is denser without linking this to the extra neutron.

sampleAnswers.answer: Deuterium and hydrogen are isotopes, so each atom has one proton and one electron, and their electron arrangement is the same. Because chemical properties depend on the electrons, the oxygen-deuterium bonds in heavy water form and break in much the same way as oxygen-hydrogen bonds, so the chemical properties are similar. The deuterium nucleus contains an extra neutron, which adds mass without changing the electrons. Each heavy water molecule is therefore heavier, so a given volume of heavy water has more mass and a higher density than ordinary water. The two liquids have different densities even though their chemical properties are similar. Heavy water and ordinary water are two examples of this idea.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by applying the idea of isotopes to explain both the similar chemical properties and the higher density.

sampleAnswers.answer: Deuterium and hydrogen are isotopes with the same number of electrons, so they bond in the same way. Deuterium has an extra neutron, so heavy water is slightly denser.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that the isotopes have the same electrons, with some reference to density. The answer does not yet apply this to the chemical properties of the molecule, which the 5-mark row requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heavy water is a type of water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about water, but deuterium and isotopes are not explained.

dotPoints.description: Relate Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country to the presence of radioactive material

prompts.question: Explain why radioactive material can be harmful to people nearby, in the context of Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country.
prompts.scenario: Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country identifies places that people are advised to avoid. Uranium ore is a radioactive material found in the ground in some regions, and it emits radiation as its unstable nuclei decay.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains that unstable nuclei in radioactive material release radiation that can damage cells, and relates this physical hazard to the places identified in sickness Country
3 marks: Explains radioactive decay and the harm caused by its radiation, with some reference to sickness Country
2 marks: Describes radioactive decay or the radiation emitted without explaining why it is harmful
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about radioactive material or Aboriginal Knowledge
markerNotes: Ionising radiation from unstable nuclei damages cells, which is the physical reason radioactive material can be harmful to people nearby.
A strong answer treats Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country as a knowledge system in its own right, and links it to the radiation hazard rather than dismissing it.
commonStudentErrors: Says radioactive material is harmful only when it is touched, without considering the radiation it emits.
Describes sickness Country as superstition, without relating it to any physical feature of the ground.
States that radioactive material is harmful because it is heavy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Radioactive material contains unstable nuclei, which decay by releasing energy as alpha, beta or gamma radiation. This ionising radiation can knock electrons out of atoms in living cells, which damages the cells and makes the material harmful to people nearby. The radiation from this radioactive decay is therefore a physical hazard, not simply a feature of the ground. Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country identifies places that are to be avoided, and the presence of radioactive material in the ground gives a physical reason why such places could be harmful. Relating the two in this way links a cultural understanding of place to a measurable hazard, without reducing either to the other.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining the radiation hazard from unstable nuclei and relating it to the places identified in sickness Country.

sampleAnswers.answer: Radioactive material releases radiation as it decays, and this can be harmful.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the radiation released, but it does not explain why this is harmful or refer to sickness Country.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country is one body of knowledge about places.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with some relevant information about Aboriginal Knowledge, but nothing about radioactive material is explained.

prompts.question: Discuss how Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country can be related to the presence of radioactive material, and the limits of relating the two.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: a geologist surveying a region records raised radiation readings at a site that local Aboriginal knowledge holders identify as sickness Country. The survey measures radiation levels only and does not record the knowledge that identifies the site.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses a sound physical link between the knowledge and radioactive material, such as radiation from unstable nuclei, and makes a judgement about the limits of relating the two
4 marks: Discusses a sound link between the knowledge and radioactive material, with some reference to its limits
3 marks: Explains one way the knowledge could relate to radioactive material
2 marks: Describes radioactive material or the knowledge without linking the two
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about radioactive material or Aboriginal Knowledge
markerNotes: Credit answers that treat Aboriginal Knowledge as a knowledge system in its own right, linking it to radiation hazards without claiming that science replaces it.
A strong answer names a real limit, such as a site being unsafe for reasons other than radiation, or radiation being present in only part of an area.
commonStudentErrors: Dismisses sickness Country as superstition, without discussing how it relates to radioactive material.
Claims that Aboriginal Knowledge proves the presence of radioactive material, without discussing the limits of the comparison.
States that radioactive material is harmful only if it is eaten or touched.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Knowledge of sickness Country identifies places that people are advised to avoid. A physical link to radioactive material is plausible: radioactive material emits ionising radiation from unstable nuclei, which can damage cells in people who spend time nearby. A place with raised radiation could therefore match the knowledge that it is unsafe. The relation is not one of proof, however. Radiation may be present in only part of an area, so a survey may miss the exact site that the knowledge identifies. The knowledge also describes places in terms of safety and relationship to Country, which cannot be reduced to radiation readings, so the comparison has clear limits.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by linking the knowledge to a physical hazard and judging the limits of the comparison.

sampleAnswers.answer: Radioactive material in the ground emits radiation, which can damage cells in people who spend time nearby. This could be one reason why a place is identified as unsafe in sickness Country.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining one way the knowledge could relate to radioactive material. Discussing the limits of this relation would move the answer towards the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal Knowledge is held and passed on by Aboriginal communities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about Aboriginal Knowledge, but no link to radioactive material is made.

dotPoints.description: Identify naturally occurring radioisotopes that undergo nuclear reactions and emit radiation, resulting in background radiation

prompts.question: OUTLINE how carbon-14 is formed in the upper atmosphere by a nuclear reaction, and how its decay contributes to background radiation.
prompts.scenario: Carbon-14 is one of the naturally occurring radioisotopes found in the environment. It is continuously produced in the upper atmosphere and taken up by living things, so its radiation forms part of natural background radiation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the nuclear reaction that forms carbon-14 from neutrons and nitrogen-14, its beta decay, and how this contributes to background radiation
3 marks: Outlines how carbon-14 forms by a nuclear reaction and emits radiation as it decays, without clearly linking this to background radiation
2 marks: Identifies carbon-14 as a naturally occurring radioisotope that emits radiation, with limited reference to how it is formed
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about radioactive isotopes in the environment
markerNotes: Trace the sequence in order: cosmic rays release neutrons, a neutron reacts with nitrogen-14, and the carbon-14 formed emits radiation as it decays.
The link to background radiation lifts an answer to full marks: state that carbon-14 is taken up by living things, so its radiation reaches the body.
Name the reaction and the emission, not just the product, because the question asks how carbon-14 is formed and how it contributes.
commonStudentErrors: Says carbon-14 forms when alpha particles strike nitrogen-14 nuclei, which is not the reaction that produces it.
Describes carbon-14 as radioactive without saying how it forms in the upper atmosphere.
Explains background radiation only in terms of rocks and soil, and leaves out carbon-14 taken up by living things.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cosmic rays, which are high-energy particles from space, strike nuclei in the upper atmosphere and release neutrons. One of these neutrons reacts with a nitrogen-14 nucleus in a nuclear reaction, forming carbon-14 and a proton. Carbon-14 is one of the naturally occurring radioisotopes, and it is unstable, so it decays by beta emission and emits radiation. Living things take up carbon-14 from carbon dioxide and food, so this radiation contributes to background radiation. This is how carbon-14 is continuously replenished in the atmosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by tracing the nuclear reaction that forms carbon-14, its beta decay, and its link to background radiation through uptake by living things.

sampleAnswers.answer: Carbon-14 is a naturally occurring radioisotope that emits radiation as it decays. It is formed in the upper atmosphere.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying carbon-14 as a naturally occurring radioisotope that emits radiation, with limited reference to where it forms. Describing the nuclear reaction that forms it would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Carbon-14 is a radioactive isotope found in the environment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about carbon-14, but it gives no formation, decay or link to background radiation.

prompts.question: ANALYSE why the background radiation in Town A is higher than in Town B, with reference to the naturally occurring radioisotopes in the rock and soil and the radon-222 they produce.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Town A is built on granite, which contains higher concentrations of uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40 than most sedimentary rock. Town B is built on sedimentary rock with much lower concentrations of these radioisotopes. Both towns are at sea level and have similar buildings.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the radioisotopes in the granite and the radon-222 they produce account for the higher background radiation in Town A, with cosmic radiation ruled out as the cause
5 marks: Analyses the link between the radioisotopes in each town's rock and soil and its background radiation, with a sound account of radon-222 but limited reference to cosmic radiation
4 marks: Explains how the radioisotopes in the granite raise the background radiation in Town A, with some reference to radon-222
3 marks: Identifies the radioisotopes in granite and their radiation, with a limited comparison between the two towns
2 marks: Identifies one naturally occurring radioisotope in rock and its contribution to background radiation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about background radiation
markerNotes: Compare the towns directly: the granite in Town A supplies more uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40, and this explains the difference.
Show the radon chain: uranium-238 decays through a series of steps to radon-222, a gas that can escape from rock and collect in buildings.
Rule out the shared factor explicitly: both towns are at sea level, so cosmic radiation is similar and cannot account for the difference.
commonStudentErrors: Says the towns differ because of cosmic radiation, even though both are at sea level.
Names uranium-238 and radon-222 as the same radioisotope, without showing how one decays into the other.
Describes the radioisotopes in granite without linking them to the difference in background radiation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Granite contains higher concentrations of naturally occurring radioisotopes such as uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40 than the sedimentary rock beneath Town B. These radioisotopes emit radiation as they decay, so the rock and soil in Town A deliver more terrestrial background radiation to the people living there. Uranium-238 also forms radon-222 as it passes through a decay series, and radon is a gas that escapes from the granite into the air. Radon-222 collects in enclosed buildings, where it is inhaled, and the alpha emissions of radon and its decay products irradiate the lungs, so the radon in Town A adds to the background radiation. Cosmic radiation cannot explain the difference, because both towns are at sea level and receive similar amounts from space. The higher background radiation in Town A therefore comes from the radioisotopes in its rock and the radon they produce.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing how the granite's radioisotopes and their radon-222 raise background radiation in Town A, and by ruling out cosmic radiation as the cause.

sampleAnswers.answer: Granite in Town A contains more uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40, which emit radiation as they decay, so the background radiation is higher. Uranium-238 also forms radon-222, which can collect in buildings and add to the radiation people receive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the radioisotopes in the granite raise background radiation in Town A, with some reference to radon-222. Cosmic radiation is not addressed, so it stops short of the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Uranium-238 is a naturally occurring radioisotope in rock that adds to background radiation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one naturally occurring radioisotope and its contribution to background radiation, without comparing the towns.

dotPoints.description: Describe the mass and charge properties of alpha (α), beta (β) and gamma (γ) radiations

prompts.question: DESCRIBE the mass and the charge of alpha, beta and gamma radiation.
prompts.scenario: Radiation from unstable nuclei is commonly classified as alpha, beta or gamma radiation. Each type is emitted during radioactive decay, but the particles or waves involved differ in mass and charge.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the mass and the charge of alpha, beta and gamma radiation accurately, identifying the particle or wave for each type
2 marks: Describes the mass or the charge of all three types of radiation, with the other property omitted or misstated
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about radiation from unstable nuclei
markerNotes: Give each type its particle or wave first, then its mass and charge, so the marker can match each description to a type.
State alpha as a helium nucleus with a relative mass of 4 and a charge of +2, and beta as an electron with a negligible mass and a charge of -1.
Gamma radiation has no mass and no charge, so state both properties for it rather than leaving it out.
commonStudentErrors: Says alpha radiation has a negative charge, which reverses the charge of the particle.
Gives beta particles a mass similar to that of an alpha particle.
Describes gamma radiation as having a charge because it is a form of radiation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha radiation consists of helium nuclei, each with a relative mass of 4 and a charge of +2. Beta radiation consists of electrons, which have a negligible mass and a charge of -1. Gamma radiation is a high-energy electromagnetic wave with no mass and no charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the mass and charge of each type and identifying the particle or wave for each.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha radiation has a positive charge, beta radiation has a negative charge and gamma radiation has no charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the charge of all three types, but the mass of each type is omitted. Adding the mass of each type would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha, beta and gamma are types of radiation emitted by unstable nuclei.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by stating relevant information about the radiations, but it describes neither the mass nor the charge.

prompts.question: DISTINGUISH between alpha, beta and gamma radiation by their mass and charge, and by how each is deflected when it passes between two oppositely charged plates.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student directs a narrow beam of each type of radiation from a sealed source into the electric field between two oppositely charged plates. The student then observes how far each beam is deflected.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes the three types of radiation by mass and charge, and explains their deflection in the electric field, with the larger deflection of beta particles justified by their small mass
4 marks: Distinguishes the three types of radiation by mass and charge, and explains the deflection of alpha and beta particles, without justifying why beta particles are deflected more
3 marks: Distinguishes the types of radiation by charge and describes their deflection in the electric field, without explaining the role of mass
2 marks: Identifies the charge of some types of radiation, with limited reference to deflection
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about alpha, beta and gamma radiation
markerNotes: Set each type against both properties in turn, because the question asks for a distinction by mass and by charge, not a list of facts.
Link charge to direction: positive alpha particles bend towards the negative plate and negative beta particles bend towards the positive plate.
Explain the size of the deflection with mass, since a lighter particle of the same charge accelerates more in the same field, and state that gamma is not deflected.
commonStudentErrors: Says alpha and beta particles are deflected towards the same plate, which ignores their opposite charges.
Says beta particles are deflected less than alpha particles because beta particles are heavier.
Omits gamma radiation from the comparison, so no distinction between all three types is made.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha radiation consists of helium nuclei with a relative mass of 4 and a charge of +2, whereas beta radiation consists of electrons with a negligible mass and a charge of -1. Gamma radiation is an electromagnetic wave with no mass and no charge. In the electric field, the positively charged alpha particles are deflected towards the negative plate, and the negatively charged beta particles are deflected towards the positive plate. Beta particles are deflected much more than alpha particles because their mass is so small that the same electric force produces a much larger acceleration. Gamma radiation is not deflected at all, because it carries no charge, so it passes straight through the electric field. This deflection depends on both the charge and the mass of each particle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by distinguishing all three types by mass and charge, and explaining the deflection of each with the larger beta deflection justified by mass.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha particles are positively charged and beta particles are negatively charged, so they are deflected in opposite directions between the plates. Gamma radiation has no charge, so it is not deflected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by distinguishing the types by charge and describing their deflection. Explaining the role of mass in how far beta particles are deflected would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha particles are positively charged, and gamma rays are not charged.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by stating relevant information about charge for two types, with no mention of beta radiation or deflection.

dotPoints.description: Construct balanced nuclear equations for nuclear decay and nuclear fission

prompts.question: OUTLINE the two conservation rules that every balanced nuclear equation must obey, and what each rule means for the particles in a nuclear decay or nuclear fission equation.
prompts.scenario: In a nuclear equation, each nucleus or particle is written with its mass number as a superscript and its atomic number as a subscript. For example, a carbon-14 nucleus decays to a nitrogen-14 nucleus and a beta particle.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the conservation of mass number and atomic number in a balanced nuclear equation, and explains why both must balance for nuclear decay and nuclear fission
3 marks: Outlines both conservation rules, with some explanation of why the particles on each side must balance
2 marks: Outlines the conservation of mass number or atomic number in a nuclear equation, without explaining why it holds
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about nuclear equations
markerNotes: State both rules with their totals: the mass numbers add to the same total on each side, and the atomic numbers add to the same total on each side.
Apply the rules to both decay and fission, since a full answer shows that the rules hold for both processes.
Explain why: nuclear reactions rearrange nucleons and charge but do not create or destroy them.
commonStudentErrors: Says the mass number must balance but not the atomic number, which is only a chemical property.
Lists the rules without saying what they mean for the particles in the equation.
Confuses the mass number with the number of neutrons, so the rule is described incorrectly.

sampleAnswers.answer: A balanced nuclear equation obeys two conservation rules. First, the total mass number is conserved, so the sum of the mass numbers of the reactants equals the sum of the mass numbers of the products. Second, the total atomic number is conserved, so the sum of the atomic numbers on each side is equal. These rules apply to both nuclear decay and nuclear fission because nuclear reactions do not create or destroy nucleons or charge. The conservation of mass number and atomic number therefore means that every particle emitted or absorbed must be included in the equation for it to balance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining both conservation rules and explaining why they must hold for both nuclear decay and nuclear fission.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mass numbers on each side of a nuclear equation must add to the same total.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining one conservation rule for nuclear equations, without explaining why it holds. Adding the atomic number rule and why both must balance would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A nuclear equation shows the particles produced in a decay or fission.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about nuclear equations, but no conservation rule is stated.

prompts.question: CONSTRUCT balanced nuclear equations for the alpha decay of radon-222 and for the nuclear fission of uranium-235 when it absorbs a neutron, and explain how each equation conserves mass number and atomic number.
prompts.scenario: Radon-222 has an atomic number of 86 and undergoes alpha decay to form polonium-218, which has an atomic number of 84. Uranium-235 has an atomic number of 92 and absorbs a neutron to form barium-141 (atomic number 56) and krypton-92 (atomic number 36), releasing three neutrons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs both balanced nuclear equations with correct mass numbers, atomic numbers and particles, and explains that each conserves mass number and atomic number
5 marks: Constructs both nuclear equations with correct particles and one minor notation omission, and explains the conservation of mass number
4 marks: Constructs one balanced nuclear equation correctly, with a partly correct second equation and limited explanation of conservation
3 marks: Constructs one nuclear equation with correct particles, without showing that either equation conserves mass number or atomic number
2 marks: Identifies the particles produced in one of the reactions, with limited notation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about nuclear reactions
markerNotes: Write the superscript as the mass number and the subscript as the atomic number, for every particle including the neutrons and the alpha particle.
Show the conservation for both equations: the mass numbers and the atomic numbers on each side are equal.
Name the alpha particle as a helium-4 nucleus and the neutron as mass number 1, atomic number 0.
commonStudentErrors: Writes the three neutrons released in fission without including them as products.
Leaves out the atomic numbers, so the equation shows the mass numbers but not the charge.
Writes the alpha particle as an electron, which changes the particle emitted.

sampleAnswers.answer: The alpha decay of radon-222 is written ²²²₈₆Rn → ²¹⁸₈₄Po + ⁴₂He, where the alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus. The nuclear fission of uranium-235 is written ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3 ¹₀n, where the neutron has mass number 1 and atomic number 0. In both balanced nuclear equations, the total mass number on the reactant side equals the total mass number on the product side, and the total atomic number is the same on each side, so no nucleons or charge are created or destroyed. In the decay, the alpha particle accounts for the mass number and atomic number that separate radon-222 from polonium-218, so the products balance. In the fission, the three neutrons released must be written as products for the mass number to balance, and every particle is included so that each equation is complete.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing both equations with the correct particles and notation, and explaining that each conserves mass number and atomic number.

sampleAnswers.answer: Radon-222 decays to polonium-218 and an alpha particle, written ²²²₈₆Rn → ²¹⁸₈₄Po + ⁴₂He. For fission, uranium-235 and a neutron form barium-141 and krypton-92 with three neutrons, but the atomic numbers are left out of the equation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing one balanced equation correctly, with the fission equation only partly correct because its atomic numbers are missing. Adding them and explaining the conservation would lift it higher.

sampleAnswers.answer: Uranium-235 splits into barium-141 and krypton-92 when it absorbs a neutron.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the particles produced in the fission, with no balanced equation and limited notation.

dotPoints.description: Explain how the emitted radiation type and half-life determine the use of natural and human-made radioisotopes

prompts.question: EXPLAIN why technetium-99m, which emits gamma radiation and has a half-life of about six hours, is used for medical imaging.
prompts.scenario: Technetium-99m is a radioisotope widely used in medical imaging. It emits gamma radiation, and its half-life is about six hours.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains how the penetrating gamma radiation and the short half-life make technetium-99m suitable for medical imaging, with both properties linked to the imaging process
2 marks: Identifies the penetrating gamma radiation as detectable outside the body, without explaining the role of the half-life
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about technetium-99m
markerNotes: Link each property to the outcome: gamma radiation escapes the body to reach the detector, and the half-life limits how long the patient is exposed.
Use the half-life as a reason, not just a fact: the activity falls within hours, so the dose stays low.
Name the emitted radiation and the half-life, so the marker can see both properties addressed.
commonStudentErrors: Says technetium-99m is used because it is ionising, which would damage tissue rather than make an image.
Says the half-life is the time for the whole sample to decay, rather than the time for half of it to decay.
Says gamma radiation is absorbed by the body, so the image comes from radiation staying in the patient.

sampleAnswers.answer: The emitted radiation is gamma radiation, which is highly penetrating, so it can pass out of the body and be detected by an external detector to form an image. The half-life of about six hours means the activity of this radioisotope falls quickly, so the patient receives only a short exposure and the material does not stay in the body. These properties make technetium-99m suitable for medical imaging.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the penetrating gamma radiation and the short half-life each make technetium-99m suitable for imaging.

sampleAnswers.answer: Gamma radiation can pass out of the body, so it can be detected to form an image.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the penetrating gamma radiation as detectable outside the body. The role of the half-life in limiting exposure is missing, so it does not reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technetium-99m is a radioisotope used in some medical tests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about technetium-99m, without explaining the properties that make it suitable.

prompts.question: ASSESS which of these two radioisotopes is more suitable for medical imaging, with reference to the type of radiation each emits and its half-life.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A hospital must choose a radioisotope to tag a radiopharmaceutical for a diagnostic scan. It is considering technetium-99m, which emits gamma radiation and has a half-life of about six hours, and americium-241, which emits alpha radiation and has a half-life of about 432 years.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses both radioisotopes using their radiation type and half-life, and makes a justified judgement that technetium-99m is the more suitable for medical imaging
5 marks: Assesses both radioisotopes using radiation type and half-life, with a sound judgement of suitability that is only partly justified
4 marks: Explains how the gamma emission and half-life of technetium-99m suit medical imaging, with some comparison to americium-241
3 marks: Identifies the radiation type and half-life of each radioisotope, with a limited comparison of their suitability for imaging
2 marks: Identifies the radiation emitted by one radioisotope, with a limited link to its use in imaging
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about radioisotopes and medical imaging
markerNotes: Judge on two criteria at once, radiation type and half-life, and keep the judgement tied to the purpose: an image needs a radiation that can be detected outside the body and that clears quickly.
Explain why alpha fails for imaging: it is stopped by the skin, so it cannot reach an external detector, and it is strongly ionising inside the body.
Give a clear verdict for technetium-99m and say why americium-241 is less suitable, since assess questions need a conclusion.
commonStudentErrors: Says americium-241 is better because alpha radiation is more penetrating than gamma radiation.
Describes each radioisotope in turn without making a judgement about which is more suitable.
Says a longer half-life makes a radioisotope better for imaging, because it lasts longer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technetium-99m is the more suitable radioisotope. Its gamma radiation is highly penetrating, so it can pass out of the body and be detected by an external detector to form an image. Alpha radiation from americium-241, by contrast, is stopped by the skin or a few centimetres of air, so it cannot reach a detector outside the body. Alpha particles are also strongly ionising, so any alpha emitted inside the patient would damage the surrounding tissue. The half-life of technetium-99m is about six hours, so its activity falls rapidly and the patient receives only a short exposure. The half-life of americium-241 is about 432 years, so it would remain active for centuries, which means a prolonged exposure and a long-term disposal problem. Americium-241 is useful in other applications, such as smoke detectors, but for medical imaging the radiation type and half-life of technetium-99m are both better matched to the purpose.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing both radioisotopes on radiation type and half-life, and giving a justified judgement that technetium-99m is more suitable.

sampleAnswers.answer: Technetium-99m emits gamma radiation, which can be detected outside the body, so it can form an image. Its half-life of about six hours means the patient is exposed for only a short time. Americium-241 emits alpha radiation, which is absorbed by the skin, so it is not suitable for imaging.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining how the gamma emission and half-life of technetium-99m suit imaging, with some comparison to americium-241. The judgement is not developed, so it stops short of the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha radiation is stopped by the skin, so americium-241 cannot be detected outside the body.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the radiation emitted by one radioisotope, with a limited link to its use in imaging.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to justify the use of a selected radioisotope in medicine, industry or environmental monitoring

prompts.question: OUTLINE the steps of a secondary-source investigation that would justify the use of cobalt-60 in industry, and the information you would record at each step.
prompts.scenario: Cobalt-60 is a radioisotope that emits gamma radiation and has a half-life of about 5.3 years. It is used in industrial radiography to inspect steel welds for hidden flaws.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the complete investigation, from a clear question through selecting and recording sources to comparing findings and reaching a justified conclusion
3 marks: Outlines most steps of the investigation, with sources selected and information recorded, but the conclusion only partly justified
2 marks: Outlines one or two steps of the investigation, such as locating secondary sources, with limited detail
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about radioisotopes used in industry
markerNotes: Give the steps in order and make each one specific: state the question, the sources, what is recorded from each, and how the findings are compared.
Check the reliability of sources, not just their existence: a secondary source is only useful if it is current and from an authoritative body.
Tie the recorded data to the use: the penetrating gamma radiation and the half-life support the industrial choice.
commonStudentErrors: Lists sources without saying what information is recorded from each one.
Treats a single website as enough, without checking its date or authority.
Jumps to a conclusion about cobalt-60 without comparing the findings against selection criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: A secondary-source investigation starts with a clear question, such as why cobalt-60 is used in industry. Next, reliable secondary sources are located, such as textbooks, government safety publications and peer-reviewed articles, and each source is checked for its date and authority. Information about the radioisotope is then recorded, including the type of radiation emitted, the penetrating power of the gamma radiation, the half-life and the uses in industrial radiography. Finally, the findings are compared with selection criteria such as cost, safety and the material being tested, to reach a conclusion that justifies the use of cobalt-60 in industry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining each step, from the question through selecting and recording sources to a justified conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Find a textbook or a government safety report on cobalt-60 and note its uses in industry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining one step, locating a secondary source, with limited detail. Recording the information and comparing the findings are missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cobalt-60 is a radioisotope used in industry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the radioisotope, but no investigation steps are outlined.

prompts.question: JUSTIFY the use of iodine-131 in medicine, using the information in the student's secondary-source notes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's secondary-source notes state that the thyroid gland absorbs iodine, that beta particles from iodine-131 travel only a short distance in tissue, and that iodine-131 has a half-life of about eight days and also emits gamma radiation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the use of iodine-131 in medicine by linking its absorption, beta emission, gamma detection and half-life to treatment, and evaluates the reliability of the secondary-source notes
5 marks: Justifies the use of iodine-131 in medicine with a sound link between its radiation types and half-life, but with limited evaluation of the notes
4 marks: Explains how the beta emission and half-life of iodine-131 suit its use in thyroid treatment, with little reference to the notes
3 marks: Identifies the radiation types and half-life of iodine-131, with a limited link to its medical use
2 marks: Identifies one property of iodine-131 that relates to its use in medicine
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about iodine-131 and the thyroid gland
markerNotes: Justify by linking each property of iodine-131 to the treatment: absorption by the thyroid concentrates it, beta emission destroys the tissue, and the half-life limits exposure.
Evaluate the notes as a secondary source: check them against other sources, since a single set of notes may be incomplete or out of date.
Name both beta radiation and gamma radiation, so the marker can see that each emission is addressed.
commonStudentErrors: Says iodine-131 is absorbed by all body tissues equally, which ignores the uptake by the thyroid gland.
Explains that the beta particles travel long distances in tissue, which is the opposite of what the notes state.
Accepts the secondary-source notes without any check against other sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: Iodine-131 is suited to treating thyroid disorders in medicine because the thyroid gland absorbs iodine, so the radioisotope concentrates in the tissue being treated. Its beta radiation has a short range in tissue, so its energy is deposited locally, destroying overactive or cancerous thyroid cells while limiting damage to nearby organs. The gamma radiation it also emits can be detected outside the body, which allows the uptake of the radioisotope to be monitored during treatment. Its half-life of about eight days is long enough for the iodine to be taken up and for the treatment to take effect, but short enough that its activity falls quickly, limiting the patient's long-term exposure and the handling of waste. The secondary-source notes are useful, but they should be checked against other sources before being relied on. Taken together, the notes show that iodine-131 is well matched to its medical use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying the use of iodine-131 through its absorption, emissions and half-life, and by evaluating the secondary-source notes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Iodine-131 emits beta radiation, which has a short range in tissue, so its energy is deposited in the thyroid and damages the overactive cells there. Its half-life of about eight days means its activity falls within weeks, which limits the exposure of the patient.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining how the beta emission and half-life suit thyroid treatment, with little reference to the notes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Iodine-131 is absorbed by the thyroid gland, which is why it is used for thyroid treatment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one property of iodine-131 that relates to its medical use.

dotPoints.description: Explain the contributions of selected scientists to society’s understanding of the atom

prompts.question: EXPLAIN how the gold foil experiment led by Ernest Rutherford changed understanding of the structure of the atom.
prompts.scenario: In 1909, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working under Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at a thin sheet of gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, while a small number were deflected through large angles.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains how the scattering of alpha particles from gold foil showed that the atom has a small, dense, positive nucleus, leading to the nuclear model
2 marks: Identifies the gold foil experiment and its conclusion about the nucleus, without explaining how the scattering results support it
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the structure of the atom
markerNotes: Link the observation to the conclusion: most particles passing through shows empty space, and the few strong deflections show a small, dense, positive centre.
Name the scientists and the experiment accurately, since the question asks about a contribution and the marker expects the link between the experiment and the model.
Explain why the model changed, not just what it is: the earlier plum pudding model could not account for the large deflections.
commonStudentErrors: Says Rutherford discovered the electron, which was the work of J.J. Thomson.
Describes the gold foil experiment without linking the scattering results to the nucleus.
Says most alpha particles were deflected, which reverses the main result of the experiment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geiger and Marsden, working under Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, showing that the atom is mostly empty space, while a few were scattered through large angles. This scattering could only be explained if the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom were concentrated in a small, dense nucleus, which led to the nuclear model of the atom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the scattering results showed a small, dense, positive nucleus and led to the nuclear model.

sampleAnswers.answer: The gold foil experiment led by Ernest Rutherford showed that the atom has a small, dense nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the experiment and its conclusion about the nucleus. It does not explain how the scattering results support that conclusion, so it stops short of the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ernest Rutherford worked on the structure of the atom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the structure of the atom, but no experiment or finding is described.

prompts.question: ASSESS the extent to which the contributions of John Dalton, J.J. Thomson and Ernest Rutherford advanced understanding of the atom, including the limitations of each model.
prompts.scenario: Dalton proposed in the early 1800s that all atoms of an element are identical and that compounds form when atoms combine in fixed ratios. Thomson's discovery of the electron in 1897 led to a model of a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it. Rutherford's gold foil experiment in 1909 led to the nuclear model, with a small, dense, positive nucleus.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses each scientist's contribution against the evidence of its time and its limitations, and makes a justified judgement about which advanced understanding of the atom most
5 marks: Assesses the contributions of all three scientists with a sound judgement of their significance, but with limited reference to the limitations of each model
4 marks: Explains how the work of at least two of the scientists changed the model of the atom, with some assessment of their limitations
3 marks: Describes the main ideas of each scientist's model of the atom, with limited assessment of its contribution
2 marks: Identifies one scientist and the model of the atom they proposed, with limited detail
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about early ideas of the atom
markerNotes: Assess each contribution against the evidence of its time: Dalton's theory fitted chemical combination, the electron fitted Thomson's model, and the scattering data fitted Rutherford's model.
Judge significance with a stated criterion, such as which model explained the most evidence, and then state a clear verdict.
Name a limitation for every scientist, since an assess answer that praises each model without any limit is not balanced.
commonStudentErrors: Describes each scientist's model without judging how far it advanced understanding.
Says Dalton discovered the electron, which was the work of Thomson.
Treats the nuclear model as complete, without noting that it could not explain why electrons do not fall into the nucleus.

sampleAnswers.answer: The atomic theory of Dalton was a foundation for chemistry, because it explained why elements combine in fixed ratios and treated the atoms of each element as identical. Its limitation was that atoms were treated as indivisible, so the theory could not account for electricity, radioactivity or isotopes. The discovery of the electron by Thomson showed that atoms are divisible and contain negative charges, and the plum pudding model placed electrons in a positively charged sphere. This advanced understanding, but the model could not explain the large deflections later observed. The gold foil experiment led by Rutherford showed that the atom has a small, dense, positive nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space, which overturned the plum pudding view. Its limitation was that classical physics predicted electrons would spiral into the nucleus, a problem later addressed by Bohr's model. Each atomic model in this sequence changed understanding, but the nuclear model advanced it most, because it explained the scattering evidence and placed electrons around a central nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing each contribution against its evidence and limitations, with a justified judgement that the nuclear model advanced understanding most.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dalton explained why elements combine in fixed ratios, but treated atoms as indivisible. Thomson discovered the electron, showing that atoms have parts, and Rutherford showed that the atom has a small, dense nucleus. Each scientist changed the model of the atom, although each model had limitations.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining how the work of several scientists changed the model of the atom, with some reference to limitations. A judgement of which contribution advanced understanding most is missing, so it does not reach the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Thomson discovered the electron, so atoms are not indivisible.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one scientist and the model that followed from his work, with limited detail.

dotPoints.description: Compare the energy of electrons in discrete energy levels, sublevels and orbitals

prompts.question: COMPARE the energy of electrons in the 2s and 2p sublevels of a multi-electron atom, and the energy of electrons in two different orbitals within the 2p sublevel.
prompts.scenario: Electrons occupy discrete energy levels, and each energy level contains one or more sublevels, labelled s, p, d and f. Each sublevel contains one or more orbitals, which are regions where an electron is most likely to be found.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Compares the energy of the 2s and 2p sublevels, and states that different orbitals within the same sublevel have equal energy
2 marks: Compares the energy of the 2s and 2p sublevels, without addressing the orbitals within a sublevel
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about energy levels, sublevels and orbitals
markerNotes: Compare the sublevels first, then the orbitals, and keep the two comparisons separate so the marker can credit each one.
Give the reason: sublevels within one energy level differ in energy, with p above s, so the 2p electrons carry more energy.
State that the orbitals within a sublevel are equal in energy, which is the key point for the orbital part of the question.
commonStudentErrors: Says all electrons in the same energy level have exactly the same energy, which ignores the sublevels.
Says the 2s sublevel has more energy than the 2p sublevel because it is filled first.
Compares the orbitals within the 2p sublevel as if each has a different energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a multi-electron atom, electrons in the 2p sublevel have more energy than electrons in the 2s sublevel, because sublevels within the same energy level differ in energy and p sublevels lie above s sublevels. Two different orbitals within the 2p sublevel have the same energy as each other, so an electron in one 2p orbital has the same energy as an electron in the other.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by comparing the 2s and 2p sublevels and showing that orbitals within the same sublevel have equal energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons in the 2p sublevel have more energy than electrons in the 2s sublevel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by comparing the energy of the 2s and 2p sublevels. It does not address the two orbitals within the 2p sublevel, so it stops short of the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons occupy energy levels, sublevels and orbitals in an atom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by stating relevant information about energy levels, sublevels and orbitals, but no comparison of energy is made.

prompts.question: APPLY the idea of discrete energy levels, sublevels and orbitals to explain why the emission spectrum of excited hydrogen atoms consists of a set of separate coloured lines.
prompts.scenario: When hydrogen gas in a discharge tube is energised, its atoms absorb energy and become excited. As electrons fall back to lower energy levels, the atoms emit light, which passed through a prism shows separate coloured lines rather than a continuous rainbow.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies the idea of discrete energy levels, with orbitals of equal energy in the same sublevel, to explain why each transition gives a specific line in the emission spectrum
4 marks: Applies the idea of discrete energy levels to explain why the emission spectrum consists of separate lines, with limited reference to sublevels and orbitals
3 marks: Explains that electrons in fixed energy levels emit light of particular energies, without linking this to the separate lines in the spectrum
2 marks: Identifies that electrons occupy energy levels in an atom, with limited reference to the emission spectrum
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about hydrogen and light
markerNotes: Use the energy difference: each emitted photon has energy equal to the gap between two levels, which fixes its colour and gives a single line.
Address the sublevel and orbital part of the question directly, saying that orbitals in one sublevel share an energy, so moves between them add no new lines.
Make the link to the spectrum explicit, because the question asks why the spectrum is made of separate lines.
commonStudentErrors: Says electrons emit a continuous range of energies as they move between levels.
Says the lines form because electrons move between orbitals of the same sublevel, which have the same energy.
Describes the energy levels without linking them to the emitted light.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons in an atom occupy discrete energy levels, so each electron can have only one of a fixed set of energies. When an electron in an excited hydrogen atom falls from a higher energy level to a lower one, it releases energy equal to the difference between the two levels. This energy is emitted as a photon of light with a specific frequency, so each transition produces one coloured line. Orbitals within the same sublevel have the same energy, so moves between them do not produce a new energy and do not add a line. Because the gaps between the energy levels are fixed, the same transitions always produce the same lines, giving a line emission spectrum rather than a continuous rainbow.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by applying discrete energy levels, with equal-energy orbitals in a sublevel, to explain each specific line in the emission spectrum.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons occupy discrete energy levels, and when they fall to a lower level they emit light with a fixed energy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that electrons in fixed energy levels emit light of particular energies. The link to the separate lines in the spectrum is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hydrogen atoms emit light when their electrons are excited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by providing relevant information about hydrogen and light, with no use of energy levels.

dotPoints.description: Apply spdf notation to describe electron configurations of atoms and ions of various elements up to Z = 36

prompts.question: DEMONSTRATE the spdf notation for a neutral sulfur atom, which has atomic number 16, by writing its full electron configuration in the order the sublevels are filled.
prompts.scenario: Sulfur is a non-metal in Group 16 of the periodic table. A neutral sulfur atom has 16 electrons, the same number as its 16 protons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates the spdf notation for sulfur by writing the full electron configuration in the order of filling, with superscripts that account for all of its electrons
2 marks: Writes the electron configuration of sulfur with some sublevels or superscripts incorrect
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about electron arrangements in atoms
markerNotes: Fill the sublevels in order of increasing energy, 1s then 2s then 2p then 3s then 3p, and check that the configuration accounts for every electron in the neutral atom.
Write the spdf notation with superscripts, not as a list of letters, since the superscript carries the number of electrons.
Use the atomic number as the electron count, which tells you how far to fill the sublevels.
commonStudentErrors: Fills 3p before 3s, so the sublevels are written in the wrong order.
Writes superscripts that do not account for all 16 electrons, such as 3p2 for sulfur.

sampleAnswers.answer: A neutral sulfur atom has 16 electrons, which fill the sublevels in order of increasing energy: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴. This is the spdf notation for the electron configuration, where each letter gives the sublevel and each superscript gives the number of electrons in it. The configuration accounts for every electron of the atom, which matches the atomic number of sulfur.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by writing the full configuration in order of filling, with superscripts that account for all 16 electrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: The electron configuration of sulfur is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p².
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by writing the configuration with the sublevels in the right order, but the 3p superscript is wrong, so the configuration accounts for only 14 electrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sulfur atoms have electrons arranged in sublevels around the nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about electron arrangement, but no configuration or notation is written.

prompts.question: APPLY the rules for filling sublevels to write the spdf notation for chromium (atomic number 24) and for the Fe²⁺ ion of iron (atomic number 26), and explain why the chromium electron configuration does not follow the usual filling order.
prompts.scenario: Chromium and iron are transition metals. Chromium has atomic number 24, iron has atomic number 26, and the Fe²⁺ ion forms when iron loses two electrons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Applies the filling rules to write both configurations correctly, and explains both the chromium exception and why iron loses its 4s electrons first
5 marks: Applies the filling rules to write both configurations correctly, with a sound explanation of the chromium exception but little reasoning for the ion
4 marks: Writes both configurations with some errors, and offers a partial explanation of the chromium exception
3 marks: Writes the chromium configuration with the 3d sublevel, with limited explanation and no reference to the ion
2 marks: Writes one configuration with some correct sublevels, with limited detail
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about electron configurations
markerNotes: Show the exception clearly: write the usual filling order result, then the actual chromium configuration, and say why one 4s electron moves to 3d.
Explain the ion using the outermost electrons: the 4s electrons are lost first, so Fe2+ keeps all six 3d electrons.
Write each configuration with superscripts that total the number of electrons in the neutral atom or ion, so the marker can check them.
commonStudentErrors: Writes chromium as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁴ 4s², which follows the usual order but is not the actual configuration.
Removes the 3d electrons first when forming the Fe²⁺ ion, which leaves the wrong configuration.
Gives the reason for the chromium exception as a rule of the order, without mentioning the stability of a half-filled sublevel.

sampleAnswers.answer: The electron configuration of chromium in spdf notation is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ 4s¹. The usual filling order would give 3d⁴ 4s², but one 4s electron moves into the 3d sublevel, so the 3d sublevel is exactly half full. A half-filled sublevel is more stable because its electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, which lowers the energy of the atom. This is an exception to the usual filling order, so the chromium configuration cannot be predicted by the rules alone. Iron, with atomic number 26, has the neutral configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s² in spdf notation. When it forms the Fe²⁺ ion, it loses its two 4s electrons first, because the 4s electrons are the outermost and highest-energy electrons in the neutral atom, so the ion is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by writing both configurations correctly, explaining the chromium exception, and explaining why the 4s electrons are lost first from iron.

sampleAnswers.answer: Chromium is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ 4s¹ because a half-filled sublevel is more stable. The Fe²⁺ ion is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁴ 4s².
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by writing both configurations with an error in the ion, and giving a partial explanation of the chromium exception. The 4s electrons are lost first in the ion, which this sample does not show.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cr is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁴ 4s².
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by writing one configuration with the sublevels in the usual filling order. That is the pattern the question asks about, so the chromium configuration is wrong.

dotPoints.description: Relate the electron configuration of an element to its position on the periodic table

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how the highest energy level in the electron configuration of chlorine shows the period in which chlorine is placed on the periodic table.

sampleAnswers.answer: The period of an element is set by the highest energy level it occupies in its electron configuration. For chlorine, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵, the highest energy level is 3, which places chlorine in Period 3 of the periodic table. Its valence electrons in the 3s and 3p sublevels, which are the outermost electrons, show where it sits within that period.

sampleAnswers.answer: Chlorine is in Period 3 because its highest energy level is 3.

sampleAnswers.answer: Elements in the same period have the same highest energy level.

prompts.question: DEDUCE the period and the block of each element from its electron configuration, and explain how the sublevel that the last electron enters determines the block.
prompts.scenario: Two elements have the following electron configurations. Element 1 has 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹. Element 2 has 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s².
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Deduces the period and block of both elements correctly, and explains that the period depends on the highest energy level while the block depends on the sublevel that the last electron enters
5 marks: Deduces the period and block of both elements correctly, with a sound explanation of the period but limited explanation of the block
4 marks: Deduces the period of both elements and one correct block, with a partial explanation of how the sublevel sets the block

markerNotes: Read the period from the highest energy level in each configuration, and the block from the sublevel where the last electron enters.
Explain the block with the sublevel, not just the answer: s-block elements end in an s sublevel and d-block elements end in a d sublevel.

commonStudentErrors: Places Element 2 in the s-block because its configuration ends with 4s2.
Gives Element 1 the period 1 because it has a single outer electron.
Says both elements are in the same block because they share a period.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both elements are placed in Period 4 of the periodic table, because the highest energy level in each electron configuration is 4, and the period is set by that level. The block of each element is set by the sublevel that its last electron enters. For Element 1, the last electron enters the 4s sublevel, so the element is in the s-block, in Group 1 of the periodic table. For Element 2, the 3d sublevel is filled after the 4s sublevel, so its last electron enters a 3d sublevel, which places the element in the d-block among the transition metals. The two elements share a period because they have the same highest energy level, but they belong to different blocks because the sublevel being filled differs. This shows that the electron configuration determines both the period and the block of an element.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by deducing the period and block of both elements, and explaining that the sublevel being filled sets the block.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both elements are in Period 4 of the periodic table. Element 2 is in the d-block because it has d electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by deducing the period of both elements and one correct block, with a partial explanation. Element 1 is not placed in its block, and the sublevel reasoning is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Element 1 is in Period 4 because its highest energy level is 4.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to determine the flame colours produced by heated metal ion solutions

prompts.question: Describe a laboratory experiment a student could use to determine the flame colours produced by heated metal ion solutions, including how the nichrome wire is cleaned between tests.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 11 class is given labelled solutions of several metal ion salts and asked to observe the flame colour each one produces. Each student has a Bunsen burner, a nichrome wire loop, concentrated hydrochloric acid and distilled water.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes a sound, controlled procedure for the flame test, including cleaning the nichrome wire between samples so the flame colour is not contaminated
2 marks: Describes the main steps of heating a metal ion solution in a flame and recording the flame colour
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about flame tests
markerNotes: The strongest answers treat cleaning the nichrome wire between samples as the key control, because carry-over from one metal ion would change the flame colour.
A full-mark answer names the hottest part of the blue flame as the place to hold the wire, and records the colour after each test.
commonStudentErrors: Holds the wire in the yellow, luminous part of the flame, which is cooler and gives a weaker colour.
Tests the next solution without cleaning the wire, so traces of the previous metal ion appear in the flame colour.
Records the flame colour without any control, so the colour cannot be linked to the sample alone.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this laboratory experiment, dip a nichrome wire loop in concentrated hydrochloric acid and heat it in the blue flame until no colour appears. Dip the clean loop into the metal ion solution and hold it in the hottest part of the blue flame. Record the flame colour, then rinse the loop with distilled water and repeat the cleaning step before testing the next solution.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing a controlled procedure in which the wire is cleaned before each sample and the flame colour is recorded.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dip a nichrome wire into the metal ion solution and hold it in the flame. Record the colour that appears.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the main steps and recording the colour. The wire is not cleaned between samples, so the next result could be contaminated.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heat the wire in the flame and look at the colour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information, but it does not say how to clean the wire, so the result would be unreliable.

prompts.question: Analyse the result of a flame test on an unknown metal ion solution, explaining why a yellow flame does not confirm that potassium is present and what the student should do next.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student tests an unknown metal ion solution in an open classroom using a nichrome wire and a Bunsen burner. The flame shows a strong yellow colour, and the student concludes that the solution contains potassium, which normally gives a lilac flame.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the flame test result thoroughly, explaining how sodium contamination or masking prevents the yellow flame from confirming potassium, and recommending specific checks
4 marks: Explains why the yellow flame does not confirm potassium and suggests one relevant check
3 marks: Identifies sodium as a likely source of the yellow colour and describes one limitation of the test
2 marks: Describes the yellow flame without linking it to the presence of potassium
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the flame test
markerNotes: Credit the masking effect: sodium's intense yellow emission can hide the weaker lilac colour of potassium, so a yellow flame alone is not valid evidence.
Specific checks, such as a distilled water control or viewing through cobalt blue glass, earn more credit than general advice to repeat the test.
commonStudentErrors: Concludes that potassium is present because the flame is yellow, without considering sodium masking the lilac colour.
Says the wire must be cleaned, but does not explain how contamination would change the flame colour.
States that cobalt blue glass changes the colour of the flame, rather than absorbing the yellow light from sodium.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this laboratory experiment, sodium emits a strong yellow flame, and this yellow light can mask the lilac colour of potassium in a metal ion solution. The flame colour therefore does not confirm that potassium is present, because the yellow colour may come from sodium in the solution or from contamination on the wire, such as dust or skin. The student should run a control with distilled water to check that the wire is clean. The student should then view the flame through cobalt blue glass, which absorbs yellow light and makes any lilac colour from potassium visible. Repeating the test with a fresh sample, a clean wire and a known potassium standard would give more reliable evidence. Without these checks, the student cannot conclude which metal ion caused the colour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the masking effect, explaining the role of contamination and recommending two specific checks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The yellow colour may come from sodium, which masks the lilac colour of potassium, so the flame test does not prove potassium is present.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying sodium as a likely source and noting a limitation. It does not suggest a specific check, which the 4-mark row needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should try the test again.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the flame test, but it does not analyse the yellow flame or name sodium as a likely source.

dotPoints.description: Relate flame tests to emission spectroscopy

prompts.question: Outline the relationship between a flame test and emission spectroscopy, referring to the light emitted by excited electrons.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student sees a crimson flame when a strontium compound is heated. A teacher then shows the line spectrum of strontium from a spectrometer.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines that both techniques rely on excited electrons emitting light of specific wavelengths, and links the flame colour to the line spectrum
2 marks: Outlines a link between flame tests and emission spectroscopy, referring to light emitted by electrons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about flame tests or emission spectroscopy
markerNotes: Strong answers explain the shared mechanism, excited electrons falling to lower energy levels, before comparing what each technique records.
The best answers note that a flame test shows the visible colour, while emission spectroscopy resolves the individual wavelengths.
commonStudentErrors: Says flame tests and emission spectroscopy both measure the mass of the metal ions, rather than the light they emit.
Treats the flame colour as a chemical reaction in the flame, rather than light emitted by excited electrons.
Describes emission spectroscopy as a separate technique with no link to the flame test.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both techniques depend on excited electrons that move to higher energy levels. As these electrons fall back to lower energy levels, they emit light of specific wavelengths that are characteristic of the metal. A flame test shows the visible colour of this light, while emission spectroscopy records the individual wavelengths as a line spectrum.

sampleAnswers.answer: Flame tests show the colour of light from excited electrons, and emission spectroscopy shows the same light in more detail.
