4 marks: Analyses the evidence and modifies the hypothesis so that it is consistent with the results
3 marks: Explains why the original hypothesis is not supported by the evidence, with some modification
2 marks: Identifies that the evidence does not support the hypothesis, with some reference to the secondary source
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the evidence
markerNotes: Test the original hypothesis against the new evidence first, then change only the part of the hypothesis that the evidence contradicts.
Keep the modified question testable by fixing the mass of zinc, so that surface area is the only variable being tested.
commonStudentErrors: Keeps the original hypothesis unchanged and explains the result as a mistake in the experiment.
Changes the hypothesis to fit the new evidence without giving a reason from scientific knowledge.
Rewrites the question so it can no longer be tested, such as asking which zinc is better.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The new evidence does not support the original hypothesis. The student predicted that the granules would react faster, but the powder reacted faster in every trial. This matches the secondary source, which explains that surface area controls how many zinc particles are exposed to the acid, so a powder with a larger surface area has more collisions with acid particles each second. The original hypothesis relied on the mass of the zinc, which is not the factor controlling the rate.

The hypothesis should therefore be modified to state that zinc powder will react faster than granules of the same mass, because its larger surface area gives more collisions. The question should change from why granules react faster to whether a larger surface area increases the rate when the mass of zinc is kept constant. This keeps the question testable and links it to the evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the new evidence against the original hypothesis, then modifying both the hypothesis and the question into testable form consistent with the secondary source. The change is justified by surface area.

sampleAnswers.answer: The evidence does not support the hypothesis, because the powder reacted faster than the granules. The hypothesis should be changed to say that the powder reacts faster because of its larger surface area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining why the original hypothesis is not supported, with a modification. It does not modify the question or use the secondary source in depth.

sampleAnswers.answer: The powder reacted faster than the granules.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the evidence. It does not analyse the hypothesis.

dotPoints.description: Justify the use of independent, dependent and controlled variables, and experimental controls in a valid scientific investigation

prompts.question: Outline the independent, dependent and controlled variables, and one experimental control, for this investigation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student investigates how the temperature of water affects the rate at which an effervescent tablet dissolves and releases carbon dioxide. The student plans to measure the time taken for the fizzing to stop at three water temperatures, using the same tablet and volume of water each time.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the independent, dependent and controlled variables with a clear reason for keeping each controlled, and describes an experimental control that provides a baseline
3 marks: Outlines the independent, dependent and controlled variables, with some reason for each controlled variable
2 marks: Identifies the independent and dependent variables, with one controlled variable
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about variables
markerNotes: State a reason for each controlled variable, since the justification is what separates a valid design from a list of factors.
Describe the control as a baseline trial that the other trials are compared against, not as a second version of the experiment.
commonStudentErrors: Identifies the time of fizzing as the independent variable, reversing the roles of the variables.
Lists the controlled variables without saying why each must stay the same.
Calls the temperature a control, because it is kept at the same value in every trial.

sampleAnswers.answer: The independent variable is the temperature of the water, which the student deliberately changes between three set values. The dependent variable is the time taken for the fizzing to stop, which the student measures for each temperature. The controlled variables are the mass and size of the effervescent tablet, the volume of water and the stirring method. These must stay the same so that temperature is the only factor changing. An experimental control is a trial with the same tablet and volume of water at room temperature, which gives a baseline fizzing time to compare the heated and cooled trials against.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by identifying all three variable types, giving a reason for the controls, and describing a baseline control. The roles of the variables are stated correctly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The temperature of the water is the independent variable, and the time for the fizzing to stop is the dependent variable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the independent and dependent variables. It does not identify the controlled variables in full.

sampleAnswers.answer: The volume of water should be kept the same.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about variables. It does not identify the three variable types.

prompts.question: Justify why this investigation needs controlled variables and an experimental control, referring to the student's design, before a valid conclusion can be drawn about the two brands.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student wants to show that a new brand of effervescent tablet fizzes for longer than an older brand. The student uses a different volume of water for each brand and does not include a control trial, because the student believes the brand is the only difference.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the controlled variables and the experimental control with reference to the design flaw, explaining how each supports a valid comparison of the two brands
5 marks: Justifies the need for controlled variables in a valid investigation, with a sound reference to the student's design
4 marks: Explains that the volume of water must be controlled so that only the brand changes, with some reference to the experimental control
3 marks: Describes controlled variables in the investigation, with some reference to the student's design
2 marks: Identifies the controlled variables or an experimental control, with some reference to validity
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about controlled variables
markerNotes: Name the design flaw in the student's set-up first, then say which variable it introduces, since justification needs a link to the evidence.
Explain what the control does, not just that one is needed: it provides the baseline that the other trials are compared against.
commonStudentErrors: Says the investigation is valid because the student repeated the trial, without controlling the volume of water.
Calls the brand of tablet a control, when the brand is the variable being tested.
Lists the controlled variables without saying why each one must stay constant.

sampleAnswers.answer:
A valid scientific investigation must change only one variable at a time, so that the dependent variable can be attributed to that change. The student's design changes two things at once: the brand of effervescent tablet and the volume of water. Because the volume is not controlled, any difference in fizzing time could come from the water, so the comparison of brands is not valid. The volume of water, the mass of each tablet and the water temperature are controlled variables that must be kept constant, so the only difference between trials is the brand.

An experimental control is needed as a baseline. A control trial, such as repeating the older brand in the same volume of water at the same temperature, shows whether the method gives a consistent result. Without a control, the student cannot tell whether a long fizzing time comes from the brand or from the way the trial was set up. Repeated trials under identical controlled conditions would also show whether differences are reliable. Only when controlled variables are kept constant, and a control is included, can the student draw a valid conclusion about which brand fizzes for longer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying the controlled variables and the experimental control with direct reference to the design flaw. It shows how each supports a valid comparison of the two brands.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student changes the volume of water as well as the brand, so the comparison is not valid. The volume should be controlled, so that the only difference between trials is the brand. A control trial would also show whether the method is consistent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining that the volume of water must be controlled, with some reference to the experimental control. It does not justify each controlled variable.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should keep the volume of water the same. An experimental control would help.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a controlled variable and an experimental control, with some reference to validity. It does not explain why.

dotPoints.description: Explain how reliable primary data is obtained

prompts.question: Describe two steps the student can take to make the primary data from this gas syringe method reliable.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student measures the volume of hydrogen gas produced when magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, using a gas syringe. The student wants the data to be reliable enough to compare with the class results.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two specific steps that make the primary data reliable, such as repeat trials and careful measurement, and explains why each improves consistency
2 marks: Describes one step that makes the primary data reliable, with some reference to consistency
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about primary data
markerNotes: Explain why each step improves reliability, in terms of consistency between repeated readings, rather than only naming the step.
Use the method details from the scenario, such as the gas syringe and the same mass of magnesium, so the steps fit the investigation.
commonStudentErrors: Describes reliability as getting the answer the student expected, rather than repeatable readings.
Names a step such as using a better apparatus without saying how it makes the readings more consistent.
Gives steps for accuracy only, such as calibrating the equipment, and leaves out repeatability.

sampleAnswers.answer: Primary data is more reliable when the student repeats each trial, because repeat results show whether the measurement is consistent and the mean can be used. The student should also check that the gas syringe is clean, gas-tight and read at eye level, so the volume of hydrogen gas is measured consistently. Using the same mass of magnesium and the same concentration of acid for each trial keeps the method repeatable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two specific steps, repeat trials and careful measurement with the gas syringe, and explaining why each improves consistency. The steps fit the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should repeat each trial to check the results are consistent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one step that makes the primary data reliable, with reference to consistency. It does not describe a second step.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should measure the gas carefully.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about primary data. It does not explain reliability.

prompts.question: Examine how the methods of the two students affect the reliability of their primary data, including the steps needed to obtain data that can be trusted.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two students collect primary data on the rate of the same reaction. Student A records one trial and reports a single average. Student B repeats each trial three times, records the readings at set times, and checks that the apparatus is gas-tight before starting.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Examines how repeat trials and an apparatus check affect reliability, explaining how each step reduces random or systematic error, and states the steps needed for reliable primary data
4 marks: Examines the difference between the two methods, with a sound explanation of why repeat trials improve reliability
3 marks: Explains that repeat trials show consistency, with some reference to the apparatus check
2 marks: Identifies that repeating trials makes data more reliable
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about primary data
markerNotes: Link each step to the type of error it reduces: repeat trials address random error, and an apparatus check addresses systematic error.
Describe the method as a set of steps that would let someone else reproduce the data.
commonStudentErrors: Reports one trial as reliable without any repeats, so consistency is never checked.
Says a result is reliable because it matches what the student expected, rather than because the method is repeatable.
Confuses accuracy with reliability by saying the data is reliable because it is close to the textbook value.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Student A's method does not produce reliable data, because a single trial cannot show whether the result is consistent. Reporting one average from one trial gives no measure of spread, so a faulty reading may go unnoticed. Student B's method is more reliable. Repeat trials, each run three times, let the student check the consistency of the readings and identify an outlier. Checking that the apparatus is gas-tight prevents gas leaking away, which would make readings consistently low. This is a systematic error, which repeats alone would not remove.

Reliable primary data is therefore obtained by controlling the method, repeating each measurement, recording values at set times and checking the equipment before starting. A data set obtained this way can be compared with other trials, because the same method has been applied each time and the variability between repeats is known.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by examining how repeat trials and the gas-tight check reduce random and systematic error, and stating the steps needed for reliable primary data. The two methods are compared directly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Repeat trials show whether the readings are consistent, which makes the primary data more reliable. Checking that the apparatus is gas-tight also helps.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that repeat trials show consistency, with some reference to the apparatus check. It does not link the steps to types of error.

sampleAnswers.answer: Primary data is collected by the student.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about primary data. It does not explain reliability.

dotPoints.description: Assess the reliability of secondary data and information when planning

prompts.question: Describe two features of this secondary data source that reduce its reliability when the student plans the investigation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student plans an investigation into the rate of a reaction and finds a value for the rate in an online blog written by an anonymous author. The blog gives no date, no method and no reference to a source.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two features of the blog that reduce reliability, each linked to how the student could check the data before planning
2 marks: Describes one feature of the blog that reduces its reliability, with some reference to checking the data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about secondary data
markerNotes: Link each feature to a check the student can make before planning, such as finding the date or the method, since reliability is judged by what can be verified.
Use the features given in the scenario rather than general comments about online sources.
commonStudentErrors: Says the blog is unreliable because it is online, without naming a feature of this source.
Describes the anonymous author as a problem but does not explain how it limits checking.
Gives a general statement about secondary data without linking it to planning.

sampleAnswers.answer: The anonymous author means the student cannot check the expertise of the writer, or whether the data was collected carefully, which lowers the reliability of this secondary data. The post also has no date, so the student cannot tell whether the value is current, and it gives no method or reference, so the student cannot judge how the value was obtained before planning.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two features, the anonymous author and the missing date and method, and linking each to a check before planning. It names the reference and method.

sampleAnswers.answer: The blog gives no date, so the student cannot tell whether the value is current.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one feature that reduces reliability, with reference to checking the data. It does not describe a second feature.

sampleAnswers.answer: The blog is not a verified source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the source. It does not link the feature to planning.

prompts.question: Assess the reliability of these two sources of secondary data, and how far the student should rely on each when planning the investigation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student plans a rate experiment using secondary data from two sources. Source 1 is a published chemistry textbook that gives the author's name, the method and the year of publication. Source 2 is a commercial website that gives a rate value but no method, and its values are cited from an unnamed origin.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the reliability of both sources with sound reasons based on author, method, date and origin, and judges how far each should be relied on when planning
5 marks: Assesses the reliability of both sources with sound reasons, and makes a judgement about their use when planning
4 marks: Explains why the textbook is more reliable than the website, with reference to the method
3 marks: Describes features of each source that affect reliability, with some reference to planning
2 marks: Identifies that one source is more reliable than the other, with some reason
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about secondary data
markerNotes: Judge each source by its traceability and stated method, not only by how recent or detailed it looks.
Name the check that would change your decision, such as the method or the origin of the values, since that shows the judgement rests on evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Treats both sources as equally reliable because they both give a number.
Judges the website as reliable because it is recent, without checking its origin.
Assumes a textbook is always correct, without checking whether its value can be traced.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The textbook is the more reliable secondary data for planning. Its author is named, the method is given, and the year of publication allows the student to check whether the value is current. Published textbooks are usually checked by editors before publication, which gives their data more credibility. The student can therefore use the textbook's method to plan the investigation, although the value should still be checked against a second published source before it is relied on.

The commercial website is less reliable. It gives a rate value but no method, so the student cannot tell the conditions under which it was measured, such as temperature or concentration, and therefore cannot reproduce it. Its unnamed origin means its values cannot be traced to a verified study. The student should not use the website's value to set the planned conditions, although it may suggest a question to investigate. An assessment of reliability should rest on the method and the origin of the data, not on how recent or attractive the source looks.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing both sources on author, method, date and origin, then judging how far each should be relied on when planning. The judgement is qualified by the need for a second source.

sampleAnswers.answer: The textbook is more reliable because its author and method are given, and its date shows whether the value is current. The website gives a value but no method, so its conditions cannot be checked, and it is less reliable for planning.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining why the textbook is more reliable, with reference to its method. It does not assess the website's origin in detail.

sampleAnswers.answer: The textbook is more reliable than the website because its author is named.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying that one source is more reliable, with a reason. It does not describe the features of each source.

dotPoints.description: Assess potential hazards and their associated risks to develop a risk assessment

prompts.question: Outline two hazards in this plan, and for each one the risk it poses to the student, so the student can later develop a risk assessment.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student plans to add concentrated hydrochloric acid to a piece of magnesium ribbon in a test tube, and to heat a second solution over a Bunsen burner to speed up a reaction. The laboratory has safety goggles, gloves and a fume cupboard, but the student has not yet checked the hazards on the safety data sheets.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines two hazards with the specific risk each poses to the student, and links the risks to protective measures or to where the reaction should be done
3 marks: Outlines two hazards and their risks to the student, with some reference to protection
2 marks: Identifies one hazard and its risk to the student
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about laboratory hazards
markerNotes: Name the substance or piece of equipment that is the hazard, then state the risk it creates for a named person, since the two are different.
Link each risk to a protective measure or a change to the plan, which is what the risk assessment is for.
commonStudentErrors: Lists hazards such as chemicals or fire without naming the substance or the risk it creates.
Describes the magnesium as the hazard without explaining the hydrogen gas it produces.
Recommends a fume cupboard for every risk, including burns that the cupboard does not prevent.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first hazard is the concentrated hydrochloric acid, which is corrosive. The risk is that a splash or spray could burn the student's skin or eyes, so goggles and gloves must be worn and the acid handled with care. The second hazard is the Bunsen burner used to heat the solution, with the risk of burns or ignition of flammable material nearby. The magnesium reacting with the acid also releases hydrogen gas, which is flammable, so the flame must be kept away from the reaction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining two hazards, each with a specific risk to the student, and linking the risks to protective measures. The hydrogen gas hazard is identified from the reaction.

sampleAnswers.answer: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is an irritant that can splash onto skin, creating a risk of burns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one hazard and its risk to the student. It does not outline a second hazard.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Bunsen burner is a fire hazard.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about a laboratory hazard. It does not state the risk to the student.

prompts.question: Construct a risk assessment for this experiment, identifying at least three hazards, the risk each poses, and a control measure that reduces each risk.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class plans to investigate the rate of reaction between magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid in a school laboratory. The teacher asks each student to prepare a risk assessment for the experiment, showing each hazard, the risk it poses and the control measures.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a risk assessment that names at least three specific hazards, the risk each poses, and a control measure matched to each risk, ranked by likelihood and consequence
5 marks: Constructs a risk assessment with three hazards, each with its risk and a suitable control measure
4 marks: Constructs a risk assessment with at least two hazards, each with a risk and a control measure
3 marks: Identifies hazards and their risks, with one control measure given
2 marks: Identifies one hazard and its risk to the student
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about laboratory safety
markerNotes: Structure each hazard as a chain: the hazard, the risk it creates for a named person, then the control that lowers that risk.
Rank the hazards by likelihood and consequence, because a risk assessment is judged on priorities as well as on the list.
commonStudentErrors: Lists hazards such as chemicals or glass without naming the substance or the risk it creates.
Gives a control measure that does not match the hazard, such as recommending a fume cupboard for a splash risk.
Confuses a hazard with a risk, describing hydrochloric acid as the risk rather than the hazard that creates one.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Hazard 1 is the hydrogen gas produced by the reaction. Its risk is ignition if it meets a flame or spark, which could cause burns. The control measure is to keep all naked flames away from the reaction, use small quantities of magnesium, and work in a well-ventilated area.

Hazard 2 is the dilute hydrochloric acid, an irritant that can damage skin and eyes. The risk is a splash while measuring or pouring. The control measure is to wear safety goggles and gloves, measure the acid over the bench, and keep sodium hydrogencarbonate ready for spills.

Hazard 3 is the magnesium ribbon, which has sharp edges and reacts vigorously with acid. The risk is cuts while handling the ribbon and splashes from a vigorous reaction. The control measure is to cut the ribbon on a tray, add it with tongs, and keep a tray under the test tube. This risk assessment ranks the acid splash as the highest risk, because it is the most likely and has the most serious consequence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing a risk assessment with three specific hazards, each with its risk and matched control, and ranking the risks. The chain of hazard, risk and control is clear in each case.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hazard 1 is hydrogen gas, which can ignite and cause burns, so flames should be kept away and the room ventilated. Hazard 2 is dilute hydrochloric acid, which can cause skin burns on splashing, so goggles and gloves should be worn.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by constructing a risk assessment with two hazards, each with a risk and a control measure. It does not include a third hazard.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hydrochloric acid is an irritant that can splash onto skin, creating a risk of burns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one hazard and its risk. It gives no control measure or ranking.

dotPoints.description: Select appropriate materials and technologies to design a scientific investigation

prompts.question: Outline the materials and technologies the student should select to measure the volume of gas produced accurately in this investigation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student wants to measure the volume of hydrogen gas produced when a fixed mass of magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, and to compare results across five trials at different acid concentrations.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines suitable materials and technologies for each measurement, with a reason each is precise and appropriate for the investigation
3 marks: Outlines the apparatus for the gas volume and for the mass or acid, with some reason for the choice
2 marks: Identifies one suitable material or technology for the investigation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about apparatus
markerNotes: Match each piece of equipment to the measurement it makes, and say why it is precise enough for comparing five concentrations.
Use the scenario details, such as a fixed mass of magnesium and a set acid concentration, to justify the choice of materials.
commonStudentErrors: Lists equipment without linking any item to the measurement it makes.
Chooses a measuring cylinder for the gas volume without considering its precision.
Selects apparatus that is not needed for the investigation, such as a thermometer, without a reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: The materials and technologies the student should select include a gas syringe, because it measures the volume of gas directly against a fine scale and gives readings that are precise enough to compare five concentrations. A top-pan balance is needed to measure the mass of magnesium accurately, and the dilute hydrochloric acid should be measured with a pipette, so that each trial uses the same volume and concentration. A delivery tube connects the reaction flask to the gas syringe so that all the gas produced is measured.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by selecting apparatus for each measurement with a reason each is precise. The choices fit the scenario of five trials at different concentrations.

sampleAnswers.answer: A gas syringe is suitable because it measures the volume of hydrogen gas directly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one suitable technology for the investigation. It does not cover the mass or the acid.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student needs a balance and a flask.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about apparatus. It does not give reasons for the selection.

prompts.question: Justify the choice of a gas syringe over an upturned measuring cylinder for this scientific investigation, using the need for precise data and the design of the experiment.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a choice between a gas syringe and an upturned measuring cylinder filled with water to measure the volume of hydrogen gas produced in the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid. The student has access to both, and needs data that is precise enough to compare five acid concentrations.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the gas syringe as the appropriate technology by comparing its precision and sealed design with the measuring cylinder, and explains how these materials and technologies support a valid comparison across concentrations
5 marks: Justifies the choice of gas syringe with a sound comparison of precision and the design requirements of the investigation
4 marks: Explains that the gas syringe gives more precise readings than the measuring cylinder, with some reference to water vapour or the design
3 marks: Describes an advantage of the gas syringe in the investigation, with some reference to measurement
2 marks: Identifies the gas syringe as suitable for measuring gas volume
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about apparatus
markerNotes: Justify by comparing both options against the same criterion, here precision, rather than listing features of one option only.
Name the error each option introduces, since a justification shows why the choice reduces that error.
commonStudentErrors: Says the gas syringe is better because it looks more modern, without linking it to precision.
Overlooks the water vapour correction needed when a gas is collected over water.
Describes the features of the gas syringe without comparing them with the measuring cylinder.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The gas syringe is the more appropriate technology for this scientific investigation because its scale is fine and it reads the volume of gas directly, so the student obtains data precise enough to compare five acid concentrations. The upturned measuring cylinder collects gas by displacing water, and its readings depend on the water level against a coarser scale. This makes the readings less precise for small differences between trials, and the student would need to correct for water vapour, which adds error.

The gas syringe also has a sealed connection to the reaction flask through a delivery tube, so the gas produced goes directly into the syringe. The plunger moves to keep the gas at atmospheric pressure, so the reading is the volume produced. For a design that compares several concentrations, the materials and technologies must give repeatable readings under the same conditions, which the gas syringe does. The student should therefore choose the gas syringe, and record the room temperature and any delays so that the data can be checked.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by comparing the gas syringe and the measuring cylinder on precision and sealed design, then explaining how the choice supports a valid comparison across concentrations. The water vapour correction is named as a source of error.

sampleAnswers.answer: A gas syringe gives more precise readings than a measuring cylinder, because its scale is finer and the volume is read directly. Collecting gas over water would also require a correction for water vapour, which adds error to the data.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining that the gas syringe is more precise, with reference to water vapour. It does not address the design requirements in full.

sampleAnswers.answer: A gas syringe is suitable because it measures the volume of gas directly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the gas syringe as suitable for measuring gas volume. It does not compare it with the alternative.

dotPoints.description: Discuss ethical issues in the development and use of scientific knowledge

prompts.question: Describe one ethical issue that could arise in the development of this pesticide, and one that could arise in its use.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A chemical company develops a new pesticide that kills insects in crops. The company's research includes laboratory trials, and a regulator must approve the pesticide before it can be sold.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes an ethical issue in the development and an ethical issue in the use of the pesticide, each linked to the scientific knowledge available
2 marks: Describes one ethical issue in the development or use of the pesticide
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about ethics in science
markerNotes: Name one issue for development and one for use, since the question asks for both.
Link each issue to what is known or unknown about the chemical's effects, which is where scientific knowledge matters.
commonStudentErrors: Lists ethical issues without saying who is affected or why.
Describes only the company's profit as the ethical issue, without considering people or wildlife.
Treats the pesticide's safety as known, without considering the limits of the trials.

sampleAnswers.answer: In development, one of the ethical issues is the welfare of any animals used in laboratory trials, which research must minimise and justify. In use, an ethical issue is the effect of the pesticide on bees and other non-target species, and on people who handle it or eat treated crops. Both issues depend on how complete the scientific knowledge of its effects is, which is why the regulator must weigh the evidence before approving sale.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing an ethical issue in development and one in use, each linked to the scientific knowledge available. The regulator's role is identified.

sampleAnswers.answer: Animals used in laboratory trials may suffer harm, which raises an ethical concern in development.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one ethical issue in development. It does not describe an issue in use.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethics matters when companies develop chemicals.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about ethics. It does not name a specific issue.

prompts.question: Discuss the ethical issues that arise in the development and use of this compound, including how the team should handle its results and the effects on the environment.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A research team develops a new chemical compound that could reduce water pollution, but early trials show it may persist in the environment and accumulate in fish. A company wants to sell the compound quickly, and the team's results are not yet published.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses the ethical issues in both the development and use of the compound, weighing the duty to report results against commercial pressure and environmental risk, and reaches a supported position
4 marks: Discusses the duty to report the results honestly and at least one ethical issue in the use of the compound, with sound reasoning
3 marks: Describes an ethical issue in the development or use of the compound, with some reference to scientific knowledge
2 marks: Identifies an ethical concern about the environment or about reporting the results
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about ethics in science
markerNotes: Weigh the competing interests explicitly, such as the company's commercial interest against public and environmental risk, rather than only naming them.
Use evidence from the scenario, such as accumulation in fish, to show what a decision would mean for people and wildlife.
commonStudentErrors: Says the ethical issue is only whether the company makes a profit, without considering environmental or public risk.
Treats the scientific knowledge as settled, so there seems no need to report uncertain early results.
Lists ethical issues without deciding what the team should do with its results.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The development of the compound raises ethical issues about the results. The research team has a duty to report its early trials honestly, including the finding that the compound may persist in the environment and accumulate in fish. Commercial pressure to sell quickly should not lead to findings being withheld or presented selectively, because the scientific knowledge a community relies on must be complete and unbiased. Results that are published, and open to independent review, allow other scientists to check them before the compound is used.

The use of the compound also raises ethical issues. Releasing a substance that accumulates in fish could harm wildlife and people who eat the fish, and those who bear this harm may not be those who benefit from sales. A responsible decision would weigh the benefit of reduced water pollution against the risk to the environment, and would require further testing and regulation before wide use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by discussing ethical issues in both development and use, and weighing the duty to report against commercial pressure and environmental risk. The position taken is supported by the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Research results should be reported honestly, even when they are unfavourable, because the scientific knowledge used by others must be complete.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing an ethical issue in development with reference to scientific knowledge. It does not discuss use or the environment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Companies should be careful about environmental damage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about ethics. It does not discuss the scenario's issues in depth.

dotPoints.description: Apply safe work practices and manage risks while conducting a scientific investigation

prompts.question: Justify a suitable precaution when using phosgene.
markerNotes: A precaution must be named and justified by the hazard in the stimulus, which is that phosgene is a highly toxic gas.
The justification should tie the precaution to a property of phosgene, such as its gas phase or toxicity, rather than to general safety.
commonStudentErrors: Names a precaution without any reason, which reaches only the 1-mark row.
Justifies a precaution with a reason that does not relate to phosgene’s properties.
Names a precaution that protects the product rather than the people and environment exposed to the gas.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Justifies a named precaution
1 mark: Provides any relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: Phosgene is dangerous to the environment because it is toxic. Therefore, it is important to ensure it does not leak from the reaction vessel, which requires constant monitoring.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by naming a precaution, keeping the phosgene from leaking, and justifying it by the toxicity of the gas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Wear protective equipment when handling phosgene.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by naming a relevant precaution, but gives no reason for it. Linking it to phosgene’s toxicity would meet the 2-mark row.

prompts.scenario: Phosgene is used in industry as a starting material to synthesise useful polymers. Phosgene (Cl₂CO) is a gas at room temperature and is highly toxic.
prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–37. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Construct and manipulate identified materials and technologies to perform scientific investigations

prompts.question: Outline how the student should construct the apparatus from these materials and technologies, and manipulate it so that the investigation can be performed safely.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student plans to investigate how the concentration of hydrogen peroxide affects the rate of oxygen production. The available materials are a conical flask, a bung with a delivery tube, a gas syringe and a manganese(IV) oxide catalyst.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines how to assemble and manipulate the apparatus with a sealed connection, a zeroed gas syringe and a controlled addition of the catalyst, so the investigation can be performed safely
3 marks: Outlines the assembly of the apparatus from the materials and technologies, with a sealed connection
2 marks: Identifies the materials and technologies needed to set up the investigation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the apparatus
markerNotes: Describe the order of the set-up steps, since the sequence is part of constructing a valid investigation.
Name the control steps, such as zeroing the gas syringe and sealing the flask, because they make the method repeatable.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the materials without showing how they are connected or used in the method.
Adds the catalyst before the bung is in place, so gas escapes and the volume readings are too low.
Reads the gas syringe only once, at the end, so the rate of gas production cannot be found.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should construct the apparatus by connecting the conical flask to the gas syringe with the delivery tube, using the bung to seal the flask so that no oxygen escapes. The gas syringe should be checked for free movement of the plunger and set to zero before the reaction starts. Using these materials and technologies, the student measures the hydrogen peroxide into the flask and adds the manganese(IV) oxide catalyst quickly, inserting the bung at once so that the oxygen produced is collected in the syringe rather than escaping. The apparatus should sit on a stable bench, and the seal should be checked before the investigation begins.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining how the apparatus is assembled with a sealed connection and a zeroed syringe, and how the catalyst is added in a controlled way. The steps are ordered and specific to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student connects the flask to the gas syringe with the delivery tube and a bung.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the materials and technologies used in the set-up. It does not describe the order of steps or the controls.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student needs a conical flask and a gas syringe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the apparatus. It does not describe how the apparatus is constructed.

prompts.question: Construct a method for this investigation using only these materials and technologies, showing how the student would manipulate the apparatus to record a series of volume readings against time.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student plans to measure the rate of the reaction between hydrogen peroxide and manganese(IV) oxide. The teacher allows only a limited set of materials and technologies: a gas syringe, a conical flask, a bung and delivery tube, a stopwatch and a 100 mL measuring cylinder.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Constructs a complete method from the given materials and technologies, showing how the apparatus is manipulated to record volume against time, with controls for repeatability
4 marks: Constructs a method that uses the materials and technologies to record volume readings, with a sound sequence of set-up steps
3 marks: Describes the set-up and readings from the materials and technologies, with some sequence
2 marks: Identifies some materials and technologies that would be used in the investigation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the apparatus
markerNotes: Show the order of the steps, since the sequence of set-up is part of constructing a valid scientific investigation.
Name the control steps, such as resetting the syringe between runs, because they make the method repeatable.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the materials without showing how they are connected or used in the method.
Reads the gas syringe only once, at the end, so the rate of gas production cannot be found.
Omits repeat runs, so the reliability of the readings cannot be checked.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using only the available materials and technologies, the student should assemble the conical flask, bung and delivery tube, connecting them to the gas syringe so that all the gas produced goes into the syringe. The hydrogen peroxide is measured into the flask with the measuring cylinder, the manganese(IV) oxide is added, the bung is inserted at once and the stopwatch is started. The student should manipulate the apparatus by reading the gas syringe at fixed intervals, such as every 15 seconds, and recording each volume against time. Between runs, the flask should be rinsed and dried and the syringe reset to zero, so each run starts from the same conditions. This scientific investigation should be repeated at least twice with the same volume of hydrogen peroxide, so that the readings can be compared reliably.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by constructing a complete method from the given materials and technologies, with a clear sequence and controls between runs. The apparatus is manipulated to record volume against time.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student connects the flask to the gas syringe, adds the catalyst, and reads the volume at set times.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the set-up and readings with some sequence. It does not include controls for repeatability.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student uses a gas syringe and a stopwatch.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the apparatus. It does not describe a method.

dotPoints.description: Use equipment appropriately and systematically to collect and record data, information, evidence and findings

prompts.question: Outline how the student should use each piece of equipment appropriately and record the readings systematically, so that the data can be used as evidence.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses a thermometer, a measuring cylinder and a stopwatch to record the temperature of a solution as it cools, taking readings every minute for ten minutes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines how each piece of equipment is used appropriately, with systematic readings at set intervals recorded with units to produce usable evidence
3 marks: Outlines the use of the thermometer and stopwatch with systematic timed readings, with some recording
2 marks: Identifies the equipment and a recording step for the investigation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the equipment
markerNotes: Describe how each instrument is read, not just which instrument is used, since using equipment appropriately is about the reading.
Show how the timing and recording link each reading to a time, so that the record can be used as evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the equipment without saying how each piece is read or used.
Records the readings without the time or units, so the record cannot show a trend.
Takes readings at uneven times, which makes the data unsystematic.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should use the thermometer appropriately by placing it in the centre of the solution, away from the sides of the beaker, and reading it at eye level once the reading has stabilised. The measuring cylinder should be used to measure the volume of solution before cooling, with the bottom of the meniscus read at eye level, so that the equipment gives accurate values. The stopwatch should be started at the first reading and read every minute for ten minutes, so that the readings are taken systematically. Each temperature and time should be recorded in a table as it is taken, with units and the starting volume noted, so that the record is clear and forms reliable evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by outlining how each piece of equipment is used appropriately, with systematic timed readings recorded with units. The record is linked to evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student uses a thermometer to read the temperature and writes each reading in a table.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the equipment and a recording step. It does not describe the timing or the reading method.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student uses a stopwatch to time the readings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the equipment. It does not describe appropriate use or recording.

prompts.question: Assess how these errors in using the equipment and recording the data affect the evidence collected, and how the method should change so that the findings can be trusted.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student records the volume of gas from a gas syringe but reads the scale at a slant, does not wait for the reaction to finish before taking the final reading, and writes each reading on a loose sheet without the time.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses how each error affects the evidence, explaining the direction and size of the effect, and sets out a changed method that makes the findings trustworthy
5 marks: Assesses the effect of the errors on the evidence, with a sound method change for at least two errors
4 marks: Explains how the parallax and early reading errors affect the evidence, with some change to the method
3 marks: Describes the effect of one error on the readings, with some reference to recording
2 marks: Identifies one error in the use of the equipment or the recording
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about recording data
markerNotes: Say what each error does to the evidence: the direction and approximate size of the effect matter more than a list of mistakes.
Give the changed method as specific actions, such as reading at eye level, rather than general advice to be more careful.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the errors but does not say how each one changes the readings.
Says repeating the trial is enough, without changing the method that produced the error.
Treats a volume read before the reaction ends as the final result, without checking that the volume has stopped changing.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Reading the gas syringe at a slant introduces parallax error, so each reading is shifted by a small but consistent amount, and the recorded volumes do not represent the gas actually produced. Using the equipment appropriately means reading the syringe at eye level against its scale. Taking the final reading before the reaction finishes means the final volume is underestimated, and the rate shown by the early readings is distorted, so the evidence about how far the reaction progressed is incomplete. Recording each reading on a loose sheet without the time removes the link between volume and time, so the record cannot show the rate at all, and readings are easily lost or confused.

The student should change the method in three ways. First, read the gas syringe at eye level with the plunger aligned to the scale. Second, wait until the volume stops changing before taking the final reading, and record that value as evidence that the reaction has finished. Third, record each volume with its time in a table as it is taken, with units, so the data can be checked and the findings traced. Repeating the trial with this corrected method would show whether the findings are consistent, giving evidence that can be trusted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing how the parallax, early-reading and recording errors affect the evidence, with the direction of each effect. The changed method is specific and makes the findings trustworthy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Reading the syringe at a slant gives inaccurate volumes, and reading before the reaction finishes gives a volume that is too low. The student should read at eye level and wait until the volume stops changing before recording.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining how the parallax and early-reading errors affect the evidence, with a change to the method. It does not address the recording error.

sampleAnswers.answer: Recording readings without times is an error, since time is needed to show the change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one error in recording. It does not explain the effect on the evidence.

dotPoints.description: Gather data and information from a range of secondary sources

prompts.question: Describe two features of these secondary sources that the student should check before gathering data from them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student needs data on the energy released by the combustion of several alcohols for a report. The student can access a chemistry data book, a government database of chemical properties and a video that shows the combustion of ethanol.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two features of the secondary sources to check, such as authorship, date or method, and explains why each helps the student use the data
2 marks: Describes one feature of the secondary sources to check before gathering data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about secondary sources
markerNotes: Explain why each feature matters for using the data, such as being able to trace a value to its method.
Use the sources named in the scenario, so the features apply to the data book, database and video specifically.
commonStudentErrors: Says the sources should be checked for being on the internet, without naming a feature such as authorship or date.
Lists features of the sources without saying why they affect the use of the data.
Assumes a government database is correct without checking how it is maintained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each of these secondary sources should be checked for who produced it, such as whether the data book names its authors and editors and whether the database states who maintains it. The student should also check the date of publication and whether each source gives its data, information or method, so that the data can be traced. The video can supply information about the combustion process, but its figures should be checked against a published source before use.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing authorship and date or method as features to check, and explaining why each helps the student trace the data. The video is treated appropriately as a source of information.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should check the date of publication of each source.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one feature to check before gathering data. It does not describe a second feature.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should read the sources carefully.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the sources. It does not name a feature to check.

prompts.question: Assess the data and information from these three secondary sources, and how well each supports the energy values needed for the report on biofuels.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student gathers the energy released per mole for ethanol from a data book, from a database and from an online forum. The three values differ, and the forum does not state where its value came from. The student must decide which data to use in a report about biofuels.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the reliability of the data and information in all three sources with sound reasons based on authorship, method, date and origin, and judges which should be used in the report on biofuels
5 marks: Assesses the data and information in the sources with sound reasons, and makes a judgement about which to use for biofuels
4 marks: Explains why the data book and database are more reliable than the forum, with reference to their origin
3 marks: Describes features of each source that affect its data and information, with some reference to biofuels
2 marks: Identifies that one source is less reliable than the others, with some reason
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about secondary sources
markerNotes: Judge each source by its traceability and stated conditions, not only by how recent or detailed it looks.
Name the check that would change your decision, such as the units or the conditions of measurement, since that shows the judgement rests on evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Treats all three sources as equally reliable because each gives a number.
Judges the forum as reliable because it is recent, without checking its origin.
Uses the values from different sources without checking that they use the same units or conditions.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The data book is the most reliable of the three secondary sources. Its values are compiled by authors and checked by editors, it gives the date of publication, and it states the conditions under which the energy value was measured. These features let the student trace the data and judge its relevance to the report on biofuels. The student should still note that the data book's value is itself a secondary value, and cross-check it against a second source where possible.

The database is also reliable, because it is maintained by a named body and its data can be traced to original studies. However, the student must check whether the database reports the energy value per mole or per gram, since the two are not interchangeable, and whether it gives the conditions of measurement. The online forum is the least reliable. Its value has no stated origin and its contributors cannot be checked, so the information cannot be traced to a verified study. The student should not use the forum's value in the report, although it could suggest a question for further investigation. Overall, the data book and database provide the data for the report, and the forum provides only a prompt for investigation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing the data and information in all three secondary sources on origin, conditions and date, then judging which should be used for biofuels. The checks that would change the decision are named.

sampleAnswers.answer: The data book and database are more reliable than the forum, because their values can be traced to named authors and stated conditions. The forum gives a value with no stated origin, so it cannot be checked and should not be used in the report.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining why the data book and database are more reliable, with reference to origin. It does not assess the units or the conditions in depth.

sampleAnswers.answer: The forum is less reliable than the data book because it does not say where its value came from.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying that one source is less reliable, with a reason. It does not describe the features of each source.

dotPoints.description: Select qualitative and quantitative information from texts, diagrams, flow charts, tables, databases, graphs and multimedia resources

prompts.question: Outline the qualitative and quantitative information the student should select from the table and the graph to answer the research question.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is researching the effect of temperature on enzyme activity. The student has a text describing the optimum temperature, a table of measured rates, a graph of enzyme activity against temperature and a short video of an experiment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the qualitative and quantitative information to select from the table and graph, and explains how each is checked against the other sources
3 marks: Outlines the quantitative information in the table and the qualitative information in the graph
2 marks: Identifies a table or graph as a source of information for the investigation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the sources
markerNotes: Name the specific information each source gives, such as the rate at each temperature, rather than the source type alone.
Check the qualitative claims against the quantitative data before using them, since the selection should be supported by evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Selects the video's impression of the experiment as evidence, without checking it against the table.
Lists the table and graph without saying which information each provides.
Treats the text's optimum temperature as measured data, without checking it against the graph.

sampleAnswers.answer: From the table, the student should select the quantitative information, which gives the measured rate of enzyme activity at each temperature, and use these values to identify the temperature with the highest rate. From the graph, the student should select the qualitative information about the shape of the curve, which shows that enzyme activity rises to a peak and then falls. The text gives a qualitative claim about the optimum temperature, which the student should check against the graph before using it. The student should not take the video's impression of the experiment as evidence unless the table or graph confirms it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by selecting quantitative information from the table and qualitative information from the graph, and checking the text against the graph. The selection is specific to enzyme activity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The table and the graph are both sources of information for the investigation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the table and graph as sources. It does not say what information to select from each.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should use the video and the text.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the sources. It does not select information.

prompts.question: Analyse the flow chart, table, multimedia resource and database to select the qualitative and quantitative information the student needs, and identify where the sources conflict.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is given a flow chart of a process for producing a salt, a multimedia presentation with a voiceover that states a yield, a table of masses from the laboratory and a database entry that gives the same yield in a different unit.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the flow chart, table, multimedia resource and database to select qualitative and quantitative information, identifying the conflict between sources and how it should be resolved
4 marks: Analyses the sources and selects relevant quantitative information, with some identification of a conflict between sources
3 marks: Explains which information comes from each source, with some reference to quantitative information
2 marks: Identifies the flow chart or table as a source of information
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the sources
markerNotes: Compare the same value across sources before selecting it, since a conflict is found by checking units and method together.
Name which source is the primary quantitative source and why, so the selection is justified rather than assumed.
commonStudentErrors: Selects the multimedia voiceover's yield without checking it against the table or database.
Treats two values in different units as contradictory without checking whether they describe the same quantity.
Describes each source without selecting the information the student needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should select the qualitative information from the flow chart, which shows the order of the steps in the process, and check that these steps match the process described in the multimedia presentation. The table provides the quantitative information needed for the analysis, such as the masses of the reactants and product recorded in the laboratory. The multimedia voiceover states a yield, but the database entry gives the same yield in a different unit, so the student should identify this as a conflict to be resolved by checking the units and the method before the two values are compared. The table should be the primary quantitative source, and the multimedia voiceover should be treated as a secondary check, because the presentation does not show how the yield was calculated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by selecting qualitative information from the flow chart and quantitative information from the table, and identifying the conflict between the multimedia and database values with a method for resolving it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The table gives the quantitative information the student needs, so it should be the primary source. The multimedia yield and the database value appear to conflict, so the student should check them before using either one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by selecting quantitative information and identifying a conflict between sources. It does not explain the qualitative information from the flow chart.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flow chart and the table are both sources of information for the report.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the flow chart and table as sources. It does not select information or identify a conflict.

dotPoints.description: Apply quantitative processes to data, including unit conversions

prompts.question: DESCRIBE the steps a student should take to make data recorded in mixed units, such as millilitres and litres, consistent before applying any quantitative process to it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student records the volume of carbon dioxide collected in three trials as 45 mL, 52 mL and 0.048 L. The student plans to find the mean of the three trials and compare it with a published value given in litres.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes a sequence that checks every unit, converts the mixed volumes to one unit, checks the converted values, and only then applies the quantitative process
3 marks: Describes converting the mixed units to one unit before a quantitative process is applied, with a reason
2 marks: Identifies that the millilitre and litre values must be put into the same unit
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the units in the data
markerNotes: Check the unit of every value, including the published value, before converting anything, because the conflict can sit in a value that looks similar to the others.
Convert all values to one unit before any quantitative process, because averaging millilitres with litres gives a meaningless mean.
commonStudentErrors: Averages the values as recorded, so the 0.048 L trial is treated as 0.048 mL.
Converts only some of the values, so the mean still mixes units.
Compares the mean with the published value before checking the unit of each value.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should first check the unit of every value, including the three trials and the published value, so that the units are known before anything is changed. The volumes recorded in millilitres should be converted to litres, or the value in litres converted to millilitres, so that all the data uses one unit. Each unit conversion should be checked by estimating whether the new value is sensible for the size of the volume. Only when the data is in consistent units should the student apply quantitative processes, such as finding the mean of the trials, and compare it with the published value.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing a sequence that checks each unit, converts the volumes to one unit and checks the result before the quantitative process is applied.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should convert the millilitre and litre volumes to one unit before finding the mean.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying that the millilitre and litre values must be put into the same unit, but gives no check on the converted values.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should check the units of the trials.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the units, but no conversion or method is described.

prompts.question: DISCUSS whether a mean of the three trials, taken only after the units are made consistent, is a valid basis for comparing the results with the published value, and what else the student should check before drawing a conclusion.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's three trials, recorded as 45 mL, 52 mL and 0.048 L, are to be compared with a published value of 0.05 L for the same reaction. The student has not yet checked the method used in the published source.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses why the mean is valid only after conversion to one unit, what the mean does not show about the spread of the trials, and the checks on the published value needed before a conclusion is drawn
4 marks: Discusses the need for consistent units before the mean, with some reference to a further check on the published value or the spread of the trials
3 marks: Explains that mixed units must be made consistent before the mean is found, with a reason
2 marks: Identifies that the trials are recorded in different units
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the trials or the published value
markerNotes: Separate the validity of the mean from the validity of the comparison: the mean needs one unit, and the comparison also needs the published method to match.
A single mean hides the spread of the trials, so name a second check, such as the range of the three values.
commonStudentErrors: Treats the mean of mixed units as a valid result and draws a conclusion from it.
Assumes that a mean close to the published value confirms the result, without checking the method or the spread.
Discusses unit conversion but does not say what the mean shows or fails to show.

sampleAnswers.answer: A mean of the three trials is valid only after every trial has been converted to the same unit. The 45 mL and 52 mL results must be expressed in litres, or the 0.048 L result expressed in millilitres, before any quantitative processes are applied, because a mean of mixed units has no meaning. Once the units are consistent, the mean summarises the trials, but it does not show how much they vary, so the student should also check the spread of the three values. The student should also check that the published value was measured with the same method, under the same conditions and in the same units, since a difference in method can explain a difference in results. Only after these checks can the student draw a conclusion about whether the trials agree with the published value.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses why the mean is valid only after conversion, what it does not show about spread, and the checks on the published value needed before a conclusion. Meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should convert all the values to one unit before finding the mean, because averaging millilitres with litres gives a meaningless result.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that the mixed units must be made consistent before the mean is found, with a reason, but the spread and the published method are not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should check the units of the three trials.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the trials, but no reason is given.

dotPoints.description: Select and use a range of representations to organise data and information, including graphs, keys, models, diagrams, tables and spreadsheets

prompts.question: DESCRIBE two representations a student could select to organise the temperature readings from a cooling investigation, and state what each one shows about the data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has measured the temperature of a cooling liquid every minute for 10 minutes in three trials, and has recorded the equipment settings and the sample used for each trial.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes two suitable representations and states what each shows about the cooling data, with each linked to the trials
2 marks: Identifies two representations, or describes one representation of the cooling data
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the data or the representations
markerNotes: Name the feature each representation shows, such as the trend in a graph or the exact readings in a table, rather than listing the forms.
Choose representations that suit the data: a graph shows a trend over time, while a table keeps every reading and its trial.
commonStudentErrors: Lists several representations without saying what any of them shows.
Chooses a diagram for the temperature readings, which does not organise numerical data over time.
Describes the cooling liquid rather than the representation of the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two useful representations are a graph and a table. The graph shows how the temperature of the cooling liquid falls with time for each trial, so the shape of the cooling curve is visible. The table can organise the same data as minute-by-minute readings, with one column for each trial, so the values can be checked against the graph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing two suitable representations and stating what each shows about the cooling data for each trial.

sampleAnswers.answer: A graph of temperature against time shows how the liquid cools in each trial.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one representation of the cooling data, but no second representation is given.

sampleAnswers.answer: A table lists the temperature readings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the data, but does not say what the table shows.

prompts.question: DISCUSS the strengths and limitations of a graph, a table and a spreadsheet for organising the cooling data, and why a student should use more than one representation in a report.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has entered the temperature readings for two cooling liquids, with three trials for each liquid, into a spreadsheet and plans to present the results in a report for a class.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses the strengths and limitations of a graph, a table and a spreadsheet for these data, and justifies using more than one representation in a report
4 marks: Discusses the strengths of at least two representations, with a limitation, and links them to the report
3 marks: Explains what a graph shows about the cooling data, with a reference to the need for a table
2 marks: Identifies a graph, a table or a spreadsheet as a way to organise the readings
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the data or the representations
markerNotes: Match each representation to what it does well and what it hides, rather than describing each form in turn.
A report needs more than one representation because the graph shows the trend and the table keeps the exact readings.
commonStudentErrors: Says a graph is always better than a table without naming what the graph hides.
Describes what a spreadsheet can do without relating it to the cooling data.
Recommends a single representation without giving a reason for using only one.

sampleAnswers.answer: A graph is the strongest of these representations for showing how the temperature changes with time, because the shape of each cooling curve and any difference between the two liquids is visible at a glance. Its limitation is that it does not show the exact readings, so a reader cannot check each value. A table keeps every reading, with the trial and the time in each row, which makes the data easy to check, but a table alone does not reveal a trend. A spreadsheet can store the full data set, find averages and draw the graph, but it does not explain the method to a reader who has not seen the investigation. For a report, the student should use a graph to show the trend, a table to show the readings, and should state which representation supports each conclusion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the strengths and limitations of each representation for these data and justifies using more than one in the report. Meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A graph shows the trend in the temperature readings clearly, so it suits the cooling data. A table is still needed, because the graph does not show the exact readings for each trial.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining what a graph shows and referring to the need for a table, but the spreadsheet and the limitations are not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: A spreadsheet can store the temperature readings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the representations, but no discussion of strengths or limitations.

dotPoints.description: Extract data and information from a wide range of sources and acknowledge these sources using an accepted referencing style

prompts.question: OUTLINE the information a student must record from a website so that a value taken from it can be acknowledged in an accepted referencing style.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student takes the solubility of a salt at 20 °C from a government website and wants to use the value in a laboratory report.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the author, date, title and web address to record, with the date of access where the style requires it, and links these details to acknowledging the source in an accepted referencing style
2 marks: Identifies some of the details needed to reference a website, such as the author or the web address
