dotPoints.description: Explain why alkanes, alkenes and alkynes belong to different homologous series

prompts.question: Explain why ethane, ethene and ethyne belong to different homologous series, referring to the bonding between their carbon atoms.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student notes that ethane, ethene and ethyne all contain only carbon and hydrogen atoms, and asks why they are not classed in one homologous series.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that a homologous series shares a general formula and a type of bonding, and that ethane, ethene and ethyne differ in carbon–carbon bonding, so they belong to different series
2 marks: Identifies the three compounds and their bonding, with limited explanation of the homologous series
1 mark: Identifies that the three compounds have different carbon–carbon bonds
markerNotes: A strong answer ties the series to a shared general formula and bonding type, not only to a list of names.
Marks depend on explaining that the change in bonds changes the hydrogen count, so the compounds cannot share a series.
commonStudentErrors: Says the compounds are in one series because they all contain only carbon and hydrogen.
Says ethene and ethyne are in the same series because both are unsaturated.
Describes ethane as an alkene because it is a gas.

sampleAnswers.answer: A homologous series is a family of compounds that share the same general formula and the same type of bonding, and each member differs from the next by a CH₂ unit. Ethane, ethene and ethyne differ in their carbon–carbon bonds: ethane has a single bond, ethene has a double bond and ethyne has a triple bond. Because the type of bonding differs, each compound has a different general formula and they belong to separate series: alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the shared features of a homologous series and how the carbon–carbon bonding places each compound in a different series.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethane has single bonds, ethene has a double bond and ethyne has a triple bond. These are different types of hydrocarbon.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the bonding in each compound. The homologous series and general formula are not explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethene has a carbon–carbon double bond.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the bonding of one compound. The other compounds and the series are not given.

prompts.question: Differentiate between alkanes, alkenes and alkynes in terms of their carbon–carbon bonding, and explain why an alkene decolourises bromine water while an alkane does not.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student adds bromine water to a sample of hexane and to a sample of hex-1-ene, and records a different result for each.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Differentiates the three series by their carbon–carbon bonding, and explains that the pi bond of a double or triple bond allows addition with bromine water while the saturated alkane does not react
5 marks: Differentiates the series by bonding with a sound explanation of the pi bond and addition, but limited reference to saturation
4 marks: Describes the bonding in each series and states that alkenes react with bromine water, with some explanation of why alkanes do not
3 marks: Identifies the bonding in each series, with limited explanation of the reactions with bromine water
2 marks: Identifies that alkenes have a double bond and alkanes have only single bonds, without explaining the reaction
1 mark: Identifies that alkynes contain a triple bond
markerNotes: Strong answers explain the reactivity through the pi bond, not just state that alkenes are more reactive.
Marks depend on distinguishing the three series by bonding and saturation before explaining the reaction with bromine water.
commonStudentErrors: Says alkanes react with bromine water because all hydrocarbons are reactive.
Says the double bond in an alkene is stronger than a single bond, so it reacts more easily.
Says a triple bond is the same as a double bond, so alkynes and alkenes are in the same series.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alkanes, alkenes and alkynes differ in their carbon–carbon bonding. Alkanes contain only single carbon–carbon bonds and are saturated with hydrogen, with each carbon bonded to four other atoms. Alkenes contain at least one carbon–carbon double bond, and alkynes contain a carbon–carbon triple bond. Alkenes and alkynes are unsaturated, because they have fewer hydrogen atoms per carbon than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms. The double bond contains a pi bond, a region of electron density above and below the bond axis that is more exposed and easier to attack than the sigma bond. Bromine water is attacked by this electron-rich region, so the bromine adds across the double bond in an addition reaction and the orange colour disappears. Alkanes have only sigma bonds and no such region, so they do not decolourise bromine water in the absence of light. The triple bond of an alkyne also provides electrons for addition, so alkynes react with bromine water too.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by differentiating the three series by bonding and saturation, then explaining the pi bond and addition with bromine water.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alkanes have only single carbon–carbon bonds and are saturated, so they do not react with bromine water. Alkenes have a pi bond that bromine can attack, so the bromine adds across the double bond and the orange colour disappears.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the bonding and the reaction of alkenes, with a reason why alkanes do not react. The pi bond's role is only briefly explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alkenes have a carbon–carbon double bond, while alkanes have only single bonds.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the bonding in alkenes and alkanes. The reaction with bromine water is not explained.

dotPoints.description: Construct and model the position isomers and geometric isomers of alkenes and alkynes C1–C8 and explore their molecular shapes

prompts.question: Describe the difference between position isomers and geometric isomers, using but-1-ene and but-2-ene as examples.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student modelling the isomers of C₄H₈ alkenes finds two arrangements for the double bond, one with the double bond at the end of the chain and one in the middle.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Distinguishes position isomers by the location of the double bond, and geometric isomers by the arrangement of groups around it, using but-1-ene and but-2-ene
2 marks: Describes position or geometric isomers in general terms, with one example identified
1 mark: Identifies but-2-ene as an alkene with four carbon atoms
markerNotes: A strong answer contrasts the two types directly, rather than defining each one separately.
Marks depend on identifying that the cis and trans forms are geometric isomers of but-2-ene, not position isomers.
commonStudentErrors: Says cis and trans but-2-ene are position isomers of each other.
Says but-1-ene and but-2-ene are the same compound because they have the same formula.
Says geometric isomers have different molecular formulas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Position isomers have the same molecular formula and the same functional group, but the double bond is in a different position along the carbon chain. But-1-ene has the double bond at the end of the chain, while but-2-ene has it in the middle. Geometric isomers have the same bonding order, but the groups are arranged differently around the double bond, giving the cis and trans forms of but-2-ene.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by distinguishing the two types of isomer by the double bond position and the arrangement of groups, using both named alkenes.

sampleAnswers.answer: Position isomers have the double bond in different places. Geometric isomers have different arrangements of groups around the double bond.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing both types in general terms. The examples are not used.

sampleAnswers.answer: But-2-ene is an alkene with four carbon atoms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the alkene. The isomer types are not described.

prompts.question: Analyse why but-2-ene can exist as cis and trans geometric isomers while but-1-ene cannot, referring to the rotation about the double bond and the shape of each molecule.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student builds models of but-1-ene and but-2-ene and tries to twist one end of each molecule about the double bond to see whether a different arrangement results.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the restricted rotation of the double bond and the groups on each carbon, explaining why but-2-ene has cis and trans forms while but-1-ene has no geometric isomers
5 marks: Analyses the restricted rotation and the groups on each carbon, with a sound explanation of the but-2-ene isomers but limited reference to but-1-ene
4 marks: Describes the restricted rotation and the cis and trans forms of but-2-ene, with some reference to why but-1-ene differs
3 marks: Identifies that the double bond restricts rotation, with limited explanation of the cis and trans arrangements
2 marks: Identifies the cis and trans forms of but-2-ene, without explaining the rotation
1 mark: Identifies that a double bond does not rotate freely
markerNotes: Strong answers explain the restricted rotation first, then the arrangement of groups, and only then the number of isomers.
Marks depend on explaining that but-1-ene has two identical hydrogen atoms on one carbon of the double bond.
commonStudentErrors: Says rotation about the double bond is free, so cis and trans forms can interconvert.
Says but-1-ene has cis and trans forms because it has a double bond.
Says the cis and trans forms have different molecular formulas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rotation about a carbon–carbon double bond is restricted, because the pi bond must be broken for the two carbon atoms to rotate relative to each other. Each carbon of the double bond is attached to two groups that lie in a fixed plane. In but-2-ene, each end of the double bond carries a methyl group and a hydrogen atom, so the groups can be placed on the same side (cis) or on opposite sides (trans), and neither arrangement can change into the other without breaking the pi bond. In but-1-ene, the terminal carbon of the double bond carries two identical hydrogen atoms, so there is no second arrangement of groups, and cis and trans forms cannot exist. The twisting of the models therefore cannot produce a new arrangement for but-1-ene. For but-2-ene, the cis and trans forms are geometric isomers that differ only in the spatial arrangement of the same atoms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing the restricted rotation, the groups on each carbon, and why but-1-ene has no geometric isomers.

sampleAnswers.answer: The double bond stops the molecule rotating freely, so the groups on each carbon stay fixed. But-2-ene has a methyl group and a hydrogen on each carbon, so cis and trans forms exist. But-1-ene has two hydrogens on one carbon of the double bond, so it has no second arrangement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing the restricted rotation and the cis and trans forms, with a reason why but-1-ene differs. The role of the pi bond is not developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: But-2-ene has cis and trans forms, which are geometric isomers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the cis and trans forms of but-2-ene. Rotation is not explained.

dotPoints.description: Assess the health and safety risks when handling and disposing of gaseous and liquid hydrocarbons

prompts.question: Outline two health risks and two safety risks of handling gaseous hydrocarbons such as methane or ethene in a school laboratory.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A teacher prepares a demonstration of ethene and methane in a laboratory with the windows closed, and asks students to identify the risks before the lesson starts.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines two health risks, such as oxygen displacement and dizziness, and two safety risks, such as flammability and gas leaks, for methane or ethene
2 marks: Outlines one health risk and one safety risk accurately, without explaining how they arise
1 mark: Identifies that gaseous hydrocarbons are flammable
markerNotes: A strong answer gives two different risks of each type and says what causes each one.
Marks depend on linking each risk to the gas, such as oxygen displacement or ignition, rather than general lab hazards.
commonStudentErrors: Says methane is toxic in small amounts, which overstates its hazard.
Says the gas is safe to breathe because it is a hydrocarbon.
Lists general lab hazards, such as broken glassware, rather than hazards of the gases.

sampleAnswers.answer: Flammability is the main safety risk of gaseous hydrocarbons such as methane and ethene: a leak can form an explosive mixture with air, so there must be no naked flames or sparks. High concentrations displace the oxygen in the air, so inhaling them in a poorly ventilated room is a health risk that can cause dizziness or loss of consciousness. Methane is odourless, so a leak may go unnoticed. Cylinders must be secured, and the room ventilated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining two health risks and two safety risks, each linked to a cause for methane or ethene.

sampleAnswers.answer: Methane and ethene are flammable, so they must be kept away from flames. Breathing high concentrations can cause dizziness.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining one safety risk and one health risk accurately. The causes are not explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethene is flammable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying one risk. No health risk is given.

prompts.question: Assess the risks of disposing of liquid hydrocarbons down a laboratory sink compared with collecting them in a labelled container for hazardous waste collection, referring to flammability, environmental harm and ventilation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has finished an experiment with hexane and proposes pouring the leftover liquid down the sink with plenty of water, arguing that the water will dilute it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses both disposal methods against flammability, environmental harm and ventilation, judging that the sink is unsafe and that labelled collection is appropriate, with a supported conclusion
5 marks: Assesses both methods with a sound comparison of flammability and environmental harm, and a conclusion, but limited reference to ventilation
4 marks: Compares the two disposal methods in terms of at least one risk, with some reference to the other risks
3 marks: Describes one hazard of pouring the liquid down the sink, with limited comparison
2 marks: Identifies that hydrocarbons are flammable and harmful to the environment, without comparing disposal methods
1 mark: Identifies that hydrocarbons should not be poured down a sink
markerNotes: Strong answers judge each method against the risks, and state what the labelled container prevents rather than only listing hazards.
Marks depend on explaining that hydrocarbons float and do not dilute, so water does not reduce the environmental harm.
commonStudentErrors: Says the water dilutes the hydrocarbon, so the sink is safe.
Says hydrocarbons dissolve in water, so they wash away harmlessly.
Says ventilation is not relevant because the liquid is not a gas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pouring liquid hydrocarbons such as hexane down a sink carries several risks. The flammability of hexane vapour means it can build up in the drainage system, where a spark could ignite it, and the vapour can also be inhaled in a poorly ventilated room. Hydrocarbons are not miscible with water, so the liquid floats on the surface and forms a film that is not diluted by the water. This film can enter waterways through the sewer system, causing environmental harm to aquatic life, and it can disrupt treatment processes. Collecting the liquid in a labelled, sealed container for hazardous waste collection avoids these risks, because trained personnel handle the waste and send it for appropriate treatment. The container must still be stored safely away from ignition sources, with good ventilation, but collection keeps the hydrocarbon out of the drainage system. The sink option is therefore unsafe, and the labelled container is the appropriate method of disposal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing both methods against flammability, environmental harm and ventilation, and reaching a supported conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flammability of hexane means its vapour can build up in the pipes, so the sink method is unsafe. The labelled container for hazardous waste collection keeps the hydrocarbon out of the drains and limits the risk of fire.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by comparing the methods on flammability and environmental harm, with a brief conclusion. Ventilation and why the film persists are not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hydrocarbons are flammable and can harm the environment if poured away.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying flammability and environmental harm. The two disposal methods are not compared.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a laboratory experiment to compare the chemical properties of alkanes and alkenes

prompts.question: Describe the observations expected when hexane and hex-1-ene are each shaken with bromine water in separate test tubes kept out of direct sunlight, and what each observation shows about the bonding.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student shakes equal volumes of hexane and hex-1-ene separately with orange bromine water in two test tubes placed in a dark cupboard.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the orange bromine water remaining in hexane and the decolourisation in hex-1-ene, and explains that only the alkene reacts through its double bond
2 marks: Describes the observation for each compound, without explaining why the alkene reacts
1 mark: Identifies that bromine water is decolourised by one of the compounds
markerNotes: A strong answer gives the observation for both tubes and links the colour change to the double bond.
Marks depend on reporting the unchanged colour in the alkane tube, as well as the change in the alkene tube.
commonStudentErrors: Says both tubes decolourise, so hexane and hex-1-ene are equally reactive.
Says hexane decolourises bromine water because all hydrocarbons are reactive.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the test tube with hexane, the orange bromine water stays orange, because hexane is an alkane and does not react with bromine under these conditions. In the test tube with hex-1-ene, the orange colour fades and the liquid becomes colourless, because the alkene undergoes an addition reaction across its double bond. The decolourisation shows that the double bond of the alkene is reactive, whereas the single bonds of the alkane are not.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing both observations and explaining that only the alkene reacts through its double bond.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hexane leaves the bromine water orange. Hex-1-ene turns the bromine water colourless.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the observation for each compound. The reason the alkene reacts is not explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hex-1-ene decolourises bromine water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the decolourisation in the alkene tube. The hexane observation is not described.

prompts.question: Justify why the test tubes must be kept out of direct sunlight when comparing the reactions of hexane and hex-1-ene with bromine water, and what other conditions a fair test requires.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student proposes doing the bromine water test on a sunny bench, arguing that the light will make the reaction faster and show the difference more clearly.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the dark conditions by explaining that light can cause substitution of the alkane, and justifies other conditions of a fair test, including equal volumes and a control, to isolate the effect of the double bond
5 marks: Justifies the dark conditions with a sound explanation of the light-driven reaction, and identifies several conditions of a fair test
4 marks: Explains that light could cause a reaction of hexane, with some reference to the conditions of a fair test
3 marks: Identifies that light could affect the result, with limited explanation of the reaction
2 marks: Identifies one condition of a fair test, without justifying the dark conditions
1 mark: Identifies that the test tubes should be kept in the dark
markerNotes: Strong answers explain that sunlight can drive a substitution reaction in the alkane, which would hide the difference the test is meant to show.
Marks depend on naming the conditions of a fair test, such as equal volumes and a control, not only the dark.
commonStudentErrors: Says sunlight speeds up the addition reaction, so the tubes should be left in the sun.
Says a control tube is unnecessary because bromine water is always orange.
Says the volumes of the two hydrocarbons do not need to be equal for a fair test.

sampleAnswers.answer: Direct sunlight contains ultraviolet light, which can start a free radical substitution reaction between an alkane and bromine, so the test tube with hexane could change colour and give a false positive for an alkene. The sunny bench would therefore make the alkane appear reactive, and the result would not show a difference caused by the double bond. Keeping the tubes in the dark ensures that any reaction with bromine water is an addition to the double bond, rather than a light-driven substitution. A fair test also requires equal volumes of hexane and hex-1-ene, the same volume and concentration of bromine water in each tube, and the same shaking. A control tube containing only bromine water, kept under the same conditions, shows the starting colour and confirms that bromine water alone does not change. The same temperature and mixing time should be used, so that only the type of hydrocarbon is changed. Recording the observations in the same way for each tube allows a valid comparison of the two hydrocarbons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying the dark conditions through the light-driven reaction, and setting out the conditions of a fair test including a control.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sunlight can start a substitution reaction between hexane and bromine, which would change the colour of the alkane tube. The tubes should therefore be kept in the dark, with equal volumes of each hydrocarbon and bromine water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the light-driven reaction and naming conditions of a fair test. The control tube and the validity of the comparison are not developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Equal volumes of each liquid make the test fair.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one condition of a fair test. The dark conditions are not justified.

prompts.question: Describe a chemical test that could be done in a school laboratory to confirm that Q is an alkene. Include expected observations in your answer.

dotPoints.description: Relate intermolecular forces to the shapes, bonding and polarity of molecules

prompts.question: Explain why methane has only London dispersion forces between its molecules, referring to its shape and polarity.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student lists the intermolecular forces present in liquid methane and notes that no hydrogen is bonded directly to a highly electronegative atom.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the symmetrical tetrahedral shape makes methane nonpolar, so London dispersion forces are the only intermolecular forces
2 marks: Identifies that methane is nonpolar or tetrahedral, with limited explanation of the intermolecular forces
1 mark: Identifies London dispersion forces as the forces in methane
markerNotes: A strong answer uses the shape to explain why the bond dipoles cancel, then names the force that remains.
Marks depend on stating that the C–H bonds are only slightly polar, so the molecule is nonpolar overall.
commonStudentErrors: Says methane has hydrogen bonding because it contains hydrogen.
Says the C–H bonds are polar, so methane must have dipole-dipole forces.
Says the molecule is polar because it has four bonds.

sampleAnswers.answer: Methane has a tetrahedral shape with four identical C–H bonds, so its bond dipoles cancel and the molecule has no overall polarity, even though each C–H bond is slightly polar. Nonpolar molecules have no permanent dipole, so the only intermolecular forces between methane molecules are London dispersion forces, which arise from temporary, fluctuating electron distributions. Because there are no hydrogen bonds or permanent dipole-dipole forces, the intermolecular forces in methane are weak.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that the tetrahedral shape makes methane nonpolar, so London dispersion forces are the only intermolecular forces.

sampleAnswers.answer: Methane is tetrahedral and nonpolar, so its molecules have weak forces between them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the shape and polarity. The London dispersion forces are not named or explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Methane has London dispersion forces.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by naming the force. The shape and polarity are not explained.

prompts.question: Discuss how the shape and polarity of ethanol and ethane lead to different intermolecular forces, and explain how these forces account for the large difference in their boiling points.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares ethanol and ethane, which are small molecules of similar size, and finds that ethanol boils at a much higher temperature.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how polarity and shape give ethanol hydrogen bonding and dipole-dipole forces, but ethane only dispersion forces, and explains that these stronger forces account for the much higher boiling point
5 marks: Discusses the forces in both molecules with a sound explanation of hydrogen bonding, but limited link to the boiling point
4 marks: Describes the intermolecular forces in ethanol and ethane, with some explanation of why ethanol boils at a higher temperature
3 marks: Identifies that ethanol is polar and ethane is nonpolar, with limited explanation of the forces
2 marks: Identifies a difference in boiling points without naming the intermolecular forces
1 mark: Identifies that ethanol contains an O–H group
markerNotes: Strong answers link polarity and bonding to specific forces, then to the energy needed to separate molecules when they boil.
Marks depend on naming hydrogen bonding in ethanol, not just polar forces in general.
commonStudentErrors: Says ethanol boils higher because it has a larger molar mass than ethane, ignoring its polarity.
Says ethane has hydrogen bonds because it contains hydrogen atoms.
Says ethanol has covalent bonds between its molecules, which is why it boils higher.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethane is a nonpolar molecule. Its C–C and C–H bonds are only slightly polar and the molecule is symmetrical, so its only intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces. Ethanol contains a polar O–H group, and the oxygen atom is strongly electronegative, so the polarity of ethanol molecules is much greater. The O–H bonds allow hydrogen bonding between ethanol molecules, which is a much stronger intermolecular force than London dispersion forces. The polar –OH group at one end of the molecule also gives dipole-dipole forces between neighbouring molecules. Although the two molecules are small and of similar size, the hydrogen bonds and dipole-dipole forces in ethanol require much more energy to overcome. This explains why ethanol has a much higher boiling point than ethane, whose weaker dispersion forces are easily overcome.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by discussing the polarity, shape and forces of both molecules, and linking the stronger hydrogen bonding to the much higher boiling point.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethanol is polar and can form hydrogen bonding between molecules, while ethane is nonpolar and has only London dispersion forces. The stronger hydrogen bonds in ethanol need more energy to break, so it has a higher boiling point.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the forces in both molecules and explaining the higher boiling point. The role of shape is not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethanol has a higher boiling point than ethane.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the difference in boiling points. The intermolecular forces responsible are not named.

prompts.question: Explain the trend shown in the graph.
markerNotes: The top band links the rising boiling point to increasing molar mass, names dispersion forces and explains that more electrons make them stronger.
The explanation must connect stronger forces to more energy needed to separate molecules, so a description of the trend alone reaches only the 1-mark row.
Dispersion forces, which grow with the number of electrons, are the main intermolecular force to name for this trend.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the trend as the graph going up without giving any reason.
Names hydrogen bonding as the reason for the trend, although 1-chloroalkanes cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other.
Says the boiling point rises because the molecules become heavier, without referring to the forces between molecules.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Provides a thorough explanation of the trend with reference to dispersion forces
2 marks: Provides some explanation of the trend
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: As molar mass increases, the boiling point increases. As molar mass increases, the number of electrons increases which increases the strength of the dispersion forces between molecules. Stronger intermolecular forces require more energy to break and therefore a higher boiling point.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: links the increase in molar mass to more electrons, stronger dispersion forces and a higher boiling point.

sampleAnswers.answer: As molar mass increases, the boiling point increases. Larger molecules have more electrons, which makes the attractions between molecules stronger, so more energy is needed to separate them, which raises the boiling point.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: gives a sound explanation linking more electrons to stronger attractions and a higher boiling point. It does not name dispersion forces, which the 3-mark row requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The boiling point increases as the molar mass increases.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse the relationship between boiling point and chain length of straight chain hydrocarbons C1–C8

prompts.question: Describe the trend in boiling point as the chain length of straight-chain hydrocarbons increases from methane to octane.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's secondary-source table lists boiling points for the straight-chain alkanes from methane to octane, and the student is asked to describe the pattern shown.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the trend of increasing boiling point with chain length, and explains it through stronger London dispersion forces from larger molecules
2 marks: Describes the trend in general terms, without explaining the intermolecular forces
1 mark: Identifies that boiling point increases with chain length
markerNotes: A strong answer describes the trend in direction and links it to the intermolecular forces, not just the data.

commonStudentErrors: Says boiling point decreases as chain length increases, reversing the trend.
Says the trend is caused by hydrogen bonding between the alkane molecules.
Says longer chains have stronger covalent bonds that must be broken to boil.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point increases steadily as the chain length of the straight-chain hydrocarbons increases from methane to octane. Longer molecules have more electrons and a larger surface area, so the London dispersion forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. The trend is therefore a rise in boiling point with each additional carbon atom, which the table would show clearly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the trend and explaining it through stronger London dispersion forces from larger molecules.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point rises as the carbon chain gets longer. This is because the molecules attract each other more strongly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the trend in general terms. The London dispersion forces are not named.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point increases with chain length.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the trend. No reason is given.

prompts.question: Analyse the relationship between boiling point and chain length for straight-chain hydrocarbons from methane to octane, explaining how the increase in London dispersion forces accounts for why the early members are gases at room temperature and the longer members are liquids.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A secondary-source graph plots boiling point against the number of carbon atoms for straight-chain hydrocarbons from methane to octane. A student is asked to explain what the graph shows about the physical state of each hydrocarbon at room temperature.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the relationship, explaining that increasing dispersion forces with chain length raise the boiling point, and uses this to explain why the early members are gases and the longer members are liquids at room temperature
5 marks: Analyses the trend with a sound explanation of dispersion forces, and relates the boiling points to physical state, with limited reference to the cause
4 marks: Describes the relationship between boiling point and chain length, with some explanation of the physical states at room temperature
3 marks: Identifies that boiling point increases with chain length, with limited explanation of the physical state
2 marks: Identifies that some hydrocarbons are gases at room temperature, without linking this to boiling point
1 mark: Identifies that methane is a gas at room temperature
markerNotes: Strong answers connect the trend to the increase in London dispersion forces, then use boiling points to predict the physical state.
Marks depend on comparing boiling points with room temperature to identify gases and liquids, not just stating the states.
commonStudentErrors: Says pentane is a gas at room temperature because it has a low boiling point.
Says the carbon–carbon bonds become weaker as the chain gets longer, so the boiling point rises.
Says the physical state depends only on molar mass, ignoring the strength of intermolecular forces.

sampleAnswers.answer: For the straight-chain hydrocarbons, the graph shows that boiling point rises steadily as chain length increases from methane to octane. The molecules are all nonpolar, so the only intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces. Each additional carbon atom adds electrons and increases the surface area of the molecule, so the London dispersion forces between neighbouring molecules become stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling point rises. At room temperature, methane, ethane, propane and butane boil below room temperature and are therefore gases, while pentane to octane boil above it and are liquids. The physical state of each hydrocarbon at room temperature is therefore set by its boiling point. The trend does not involve any change in the strength of the carbon–carbon or carbon–hydrogen bonds, because these bonds are essentially the same along the series.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing the rise in dispersion forces, and using the boiling points to explain the physical states at room temperature.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point rises with chain length because London dispersion forces get stronger. Butane boils below room temperature, so it is a gas, while pentane boils above it, so it is a liquid.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the trend and linking boiling points to physical states. The link between surface area and dispersion forces is not developed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Methane and ethane are gases at room temperature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying gases at room temperature. The link to boiling point is not made.

dotPoints.description: Use IUPAC nomenclature to name and construct representations of haloalkanes C1–C8

prompts.question: Outline the steps for naming the haloalkane 2-chlorobutane using IUPAC nomenclature, including the position and name of the halogen.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is given the structure of a four-carbon haloalkane with a chlorine atom attached to the second carbon of the chain and must write its IUPAC name.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the steps in order: the longest chain as parent, numbering to give the halogen the lowest locant, and naming the halogen as a chloro prefix before the parent
2 marks: Outlines the main steps, but omits the numbering rule or the halogen prefix
1 mark: Identifies that haloalkanes are named with a halogen prefix
markerNotes: A strong answer applies the chain rule first, then the lowest locant rule for the halogen, and writes the prefix with its locant.
Marks depend on using the prefix chloro, bromo or fluoro, not the element name alone.
commonStudentErrors: Writes the prefix as chlorine, giving chlorinebutane.
Numbers the chain from the end that gives the halogen a higher locant.
Names the molecule butane-2-chloride, using the wrong order.

sampleAnswers.answer: Following IUPAC nomenclature, first identify the longest carbon chain, which has four carbon atoms, so the parent alkane is butane. Number the chain from the end that gives the halogen the lowest locant, which here puts the chlorine on carbon 2. Name the halogen, chlorine, as the prefix chloro with its locant, then the parent, giving 2-chlorobutane. This is a haloalkane, a hydrocarbon in which a halogen replaces a hydrogen atom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the steps in order: longest chain, lowest locant for the halogen, then the chloro prefix before the parent.

sampleAnswers.answer: The longest chain has four carbon atoms, so the parent is butane. Add chloro as a prefix to give chlorobutane.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the parent chain and the halogen prefix. The position of the chlorine is not given, so the name is incomplete.

sampleAnswers.answer: Haloalkanes use a halogen prefix in the name.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the halogen prefix. No steps for the name are given.

prompts.question: Construct the condensed structural formula of 1-bromo-2-chloropropane, and explain how the lowest locants and alphabetical order determine its name.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is given a skeletal structure of a three-carbon chain with a bromine atom on one end carbon and a chlorine atom on the middle carbon, and must write its condensed structural formula and IUPAC name.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs the condensed formula and applies the lowest locant and alphabetical order rules to give 1-bromo-2-chloropropane, with a clear justification of the numbering
5 marks: Constructs the formula and applies the locant rules correctly, with a sound explanation of the alphabetical order but limited justification of the numbering
4 marks: Constructs the correct condensed formula and gives the name with some reference to the locant or alphabetical rules
3 marks: Identifies the positions of the halogens and gives a name with one error, with limited explanation
2 marks: Identifies the halogens and their positions in the structure, without writing the name or formula
1 mark: Identifies bromine and chlorine as halogen substituents
markerNotes: Strong answers apply the lowest locant rule to the whole set of positions before ordering the prefixes alphabetically.
Marks depend on explaining why the numbering starts at the bromine end, not just stating the name.
commonStudentErrors: Orders the prefixes by number, giving 2-chloro-1-bromopropane.
Gives the name 3-bromo-2-chloropropane by numbering from the wrong end.
Writes the condensed formula with bromine on the middle carbon.

sampleAnswers.answer: The condensed structural formula is BrCH₂CHClCH₃, which places the bromine on carbon 1 and the chlorine on carbon 2 of the three-carbon propane chain. This compound is a haloalkane, a hydrocarbon in which halogen atoms replace hydrogen atoms, so the halogens are named as prefixes on the parent alkane, propane. Applying IUPAC nomenclature, the chain is numbered from both ends, and the end that gives the halogen positions the lowest locants is chosen. Numbering from the bromine end gives locants 1 and 2, while numbering from the other end gives 2 and 3, so the lowest locants are 1 and 2. The prefixes are then written in alphabetical order, with bromo before chloro, because the name lists the substituents alphabetically rather than by number. The name is therefore 1-bromo-2-chloropropane. Bromine is named by the prefix bromo and chlorine by the prefix chloro, with the locant of each written before its prefix.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing the condensed formula and applying the lowest locant and alphabetical order rules with a clear justification.

sampleAnswers.answer: An alkene has a carbon–carbon double bond containing a pi bond, which is electron-rich and easily attacked by reagents such as bromine. The alkene therefore undergoes an addition reaction, in which the pi bond breaks and atoms add across the double bond. An alkane has only single bonds and no pi bond, so its reactivity is limited, and it reacts only by substitution reactions, usually needing ultraviolet light.

prompts.question: Analyse why propene and hydrogen bromide give an addition product, while propane and bromine in ultraviolet light give a substitution product, referring to the bonding in each reactant and the conditions needed.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student plans two reactions in a laboratory: propene with hydrogen bromide, and propane with bromine under ultraviolet light, and must predict the type of product each will form.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the pi bond of propene as the site for addition with hydrogen bromide, and the absence of a pi bond in propane, which reacts only by free radical substitution under ultraviolet light
5 marks: Analyses both reactions with a sound explanation of the pi bond and free radical substitution, but limited reference to the conditions
4 marks: Describes the addition reaction of propene and the substitution reaction of propane, with some explanation of why the bonding differs
3 marks: Identifies the type of reaction for each compound, with limited explanation of the bonding
2 marks: Identifies that propene has a double bond and propane does not, without the reaction type
1 mark: Identifies that propane undergoes substitution with bromine under ultraviolet light
markerNotes: Strong answers attribute each reaction to the bonding in the reactant, and to the conditions needed to start it.
Marks depend on explaining why the pi bond provides a site for addition and why the alkane needs ultraviolet light.
commonStudentErrors: Says propane undergoes addition with bromine in the dark because it is a hydrocarbon.
Says hydrogen bromide replaces a hydrogen atom in propene, giving a substitution product.
Says ultraviolet light is needed for propene to add hydrogen bromide.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propene is an alkene, a hydrocarbon with a carbon–carbon double bond containing a pi bond. The pi bond is electron-rich and is attacked by the electrophilic hydrogen of hydrogen bromide, so the double bond opens and the hydrogen and bromine each add to a carbon of the double bond. This addition reaction proceeds without light because the pi bond is weaker than the sigma bond and reacts readily. Propane contains only single bonds and no pi bond, so there is no electron-rich site for hydrogen bromide to attack, and no addition is possible. Propane does react with bromine, but only when ultraviolet light supplies the energy to split the bromine molecule into free radicals. These radicals abstract hydrogen atoms from propane, so a hydrogen is replaced by a bromine atom in a substitution reaction. The two reactions therefore differ in reactivity: the alkene has a reactive pi bond for addition, while the alkane has only strong sigma bonds that bromine radicals attack under ultraviolet light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing the pi bond of propene as the site for addition, and the free radical substitution of propane under ultraviolet light.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propene has a pi bond that hydrogen bromide can attack, so an addition reaction occurs. Propane has only single bonds, so it does not add reagents, but bromine can substitute a hydrogen atom under ultraviolet light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the addition of propene and the substitution of propane, with a reason for the bonding difference. The free radical mechanism is only named.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propene has a double bond and propane does not.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethene is a gas and a hydrocarbon whose carbon–carbon double bond gives it chemical reactivity, which underpins most of its uses. Its chemical properties mean that ethene readily undergoes addition reactions. In the production of polyethene, many ethene molecules join through addition polymerisation, in which the double bonds open and link into long chains, giving a solid with useful properties. Ethene is also hydrated by adding water across the double bond to form ethanol, an addition reaction used industrially to make a solvent and a fuel. As a plant hormone, ethene is used to ripen fruit in storage, where its small size and gaseous state let it diffuse through the air around the produce. These uses all rely on the reactivity of the double bond, but they also raise safety concerns, because ethene is flammable and forms explosive mixtures with air, so it must be stored and handled under controlled conditions.

sampleAnswers.answer: Within an alcohol molecule, the O–H bond is polar because oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so electrons are drawn towards the oxygen and the hydrogen carries a partial positive charge. This is intramolecular bonding, within the molecule itself. The partly positive hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule, and this hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular force that links alcohol molecules together.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares two isomers with the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O, butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol, and records that one boils at a noticeably lower temperature and mixes with water more readily.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how hydrogen bonding and the branched, compact shape of 2-methylpropan-2-ol explain its lower boiling point and greater water solubility than butan-1-ol, using intermolecular bonding throughout
5 marks: Analyses the boiling point difference with a sound explanation of hydrogen bonding and shape, but limited reasoning about water solubility
4 marks: Describes hydrogen bonding in both alcohols and the effect of shape on boiling point, with some explanation of solubility

Marks depend on separating intramolecular bonding within the O–H group from the intermolecular hydrogen bonding between molecules.
commonStudentErrors: Says the O–H bond breaks when the alcohol boils, which is why the boiling point is high.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butan-1-ol is a primary alcohol with an unbranched four-carbon chain, so its molecules can lie close together and have a large surface area for London dispersion forces. Its –OH group is on a terminal carbon and is exposed, so hydrogen bonding occurs between neighbouring molecules through their O–H groups, an intermolecular bonding force that raises the boiling point. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol with a compact, branched shape, so its molecules have a smaller surface area and weaker dispersion forces. Its –OH group is shielded by the three methyl groups around it, so fewer hydrogen bonds can form between molecules. Less energy is therefore needed to separate them, and the boiling point of 2-methylpropan-2-ol is lower than that of butan-1-ol. Water solubility depends on the balance between the polar –OH group and the nonpolar hydrocarbon part. In 2-methylpropan-2-ol, the compact shape leaves the polar –OH group more accessible, so its hydrogen bonding with water is less hindered, and the alcohol dissolves more readily than butan-1-ol.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by analysing how hydrogen bonding and the compact shape explain the boiling point and solubility of the two isomers.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butan-1-ol has a larger surface area and forms hydrogen bonding between molecules, so its boiling point is higher. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is compact, so its boiling point is lower and it dissolves more readily in water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing hydrogen bonding in both and the effect of shape on boiling point. The solubility is stated without explaining the exposed –OH group.

prompts.question: Explain the patterns of the boiling points shown in the graph.
markerNotes: The top response explains the rising trend with dispersion forces and the alcohol-thiol gap with hydrogen bonding.
It also explains why the gap narrows as the chain lengthens, because hydrogen bonding is a smaller share of the total intermolecular forces.
commonStudentErrors: Says alcohols have higher boiling points only because they have more carbon atoms, ignoring hydrogen bonding.
Says thiols form hydrogen bonds as strongly as alcohols because both contain a hydrogen attached to oxygen or sulfur, which is not the case.
Explains the boiling points by bond strength within the molecules, such as C–C or S–H bonds, instead of intermolecular forces.

4 marks: Explains patterns in the boiling points
3 marks: Explains most of the patterns in the boiling points
2 marks: Describes the patterns in the boiling point OR Explains a pattern in the boiling points

sampleAnswers.answer:
Boiling points for both series increase with increasing number of carbon atoms. This is due to dispersion forces increasing with increasing chain length.
The boiling point of the alcohol is always higher than the analogous thiol. This is due to hydrogen bonding between alcohols being stronger than the dispersion forces between thiols.
The difference between the boiling points of analogous alcohols and thiols decreases with increasing chain length. This is due to the hydrogen bonding having a smaller and smaller contribution to total intermolecular forces as chain length increases.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4 row: explains the rising trend with dispersion forces, the alcohol–thiol gap with hydrogen bonding, and why the gap narrows.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling points increase for both alcohols and thiols as the number of carbon atoms increases. The alcohols generally have higher boiling points than the thiols with the same number of carbons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2 row: describes two patterns in the graph but does not explain them with intermolecular forces. Explaining the rise or the alcohol–thiol gap would meet the 3 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Thiols are the sulfur analogues of alcohols, with sulfur replacing oxygen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: restates the stimulus without describing a pattern in the graph. Describing the rising boiling points would lift it to the 2 row.

prompts.question: Explain the relationship between the trend shown in the graph and the relevant intermolecular forces.
markerNotes: The top band names both forces: hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl group and water, which dominates short chains, and dispersion forces between the alkyl chains, which grow and reduce solubility in longer chains.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the molar mass increases, the chain length increases. As the chain length increases, the solubility of alkan-1-ols in water decreases. Shorter chain alcohols dissolve in water due to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the hydroxyl group of the alcohol and water molecules. However, as the chain length increases, the dispersion forces between the alkyl groups become more significant which decreases the solubility of alkan-1-ols in water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: links the falling solubility to dispersion forces between longer alkyl chains and the hydrogen bonding that makes short alkan-1-ols soluble.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the chain length increases, the solubility of alkan-1-ols in water decreases. Short alkan-1-ols dissolve because hydrogen bonds form between the hydroxyl group and water molecules, so these alcohols are soluble.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the trend and explains short-chain solubility through hydrogen bonding. It does not explain the falling solubility of longer chains with dispersion forces, which the 3-mark row needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The solubility of alkan-1-ols falls as the molar mass rises.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse the relationship between chain length, boiling point and solubility in water in straight chain primary alcohols C1–C8

prompts.question: Describe how the boiling point and the solubility in water change as chain length increases across the straight chain primary alcohols from methanol to octan-1-ol, and identify the intermolecular force that changes the boiling point.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is reviewing secondary-source data for the straight chain primary alcohols from methanol to octan-1-ol, including their boiling points and their solubilities in water.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the rise in boiling point and the fall in solubility in water as chain length increases, and identifies London dispersion forces as the force that grows with chain length
2 marks: Describes the change in boiling point or solubility in water with chain length, without identifying the intermolecular force
1 mark: Identifies that boiling point increases as chain length increases
markerNotes: A strong answer describes both trends in direction and names London dispersion forces as the cause of the boiling point rise.
Solubility falls because the non-polar hydrocarbon chain grows while the single hydroxyl group stays the same.
commonStudentErrors: Says boiling point falls as chain length increases, reversing the trend.
Says the boiling point rise is caused by stronger covalent bonds within the molecules.
Says solubility increases with chain length because larger molecules have more hydrogen bonding.

sampleAnswers.answer: Across the straight chain primary alcohols, boiling point increases steadily from methanol to octan-1-ol, because longer molecules have stronger London dispersion forces between them. Solubility in water falls as chain length increases, because the hydrocarbon part grows while the single hydroxyl group stays the same. Methanol and ethanol mix completely with water, whereas octan-1-ol is only sparingly soluble.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing both trends and naming London dispersion forces as the force that grows with chain length.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point increases as chain length increases, because the molecules attract each other more strongly. Solubility in water decreases as the chain gets longer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing both trends without naming the intermolecular force.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point increases with chain length.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the rise in boiling point. No solubility trend or cause is given.

prompts.question: Analyse the relationship between chain length, boiling point and solubility in water for the straight chain primary alcohols from methanol to octan-1-ol, showing how both trends arise from the same change in molecular structure.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class is compiling a secondary-source table of properties for the straight chain primary alcohols from methanol to octan-1-ol, including boiling points and solubilities in water. The teacher asks students to use the table to draw conclusions about molecular structure.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the relationship between chain length, boiling point and solubility in water, linking both trends to the growing hydrocarbon chain and the constant hydroxyl group, with precise reference to London dispersion forces and hydrogen bonding
5 marks: Analyses both trends and links them to the increasing size of the hydrocarbon chain, with relevant reference to intermolecular forces
4 marks: Describes both trends accurately and gives a partial explanation that refers to the forces involved
3 marks: Describes one trend accurately, with a reason for it
2 marks: Identifies the trends in boiling point or solubility without explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about alcohols
markerNotes: A strong answer connects both trends to one structural change, the growing hydrocarbon chain, rather than treating them as separate facts.
The explanation must name the forces, since saying the molecules are bigger does not explain why the properties change.
commonStudentErrors: Says solubility increases with chain length because the molecules are larger.
Explains the boiling point trend by covalent bonds breaking, instead of intermolecular forces.
Says the hydroxyl group becomes more strongly hydrogen bonded as the chain grows, when it is the same in every alcohol.

sampleAnswers.answer: The straight chain primary alcohols form a series in which each member adds one CH2 unit. As chain length increases, boiling point rises steadily. Longer molecules have a larger surface area and more electrons, so the London dispersion forces between them are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them. Hydrogen bonding between the -OH groups is present in every member, so it does not explain the difference along the series. Solubility in water falls in the same direction. The hydroxyl group can hydrogen bond with water in every member, but the hydrocarbon chain is non-polar and grows with each CH2 unit, so the balance shifts towards insolubility. Both trends therefore come from the same change in molecular structure, a longer hydrocarbon chain with an unchanged hydroxyl group. The secondary-source data for methanol to octan-1-ol show this pattern consistently.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by linking both trends to the growing hydrocarbon chain and the constant hydroxyl group, with the forces named.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point rises along the series because the molecules get bigger and London dispersion forces get stronger. Solubility in water falls as the chain gets longer, because the hydrocarbon part is non-polar. Both trends are linked to chain length.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing both trends with a partial explanation of the forces. Hydrogen bonding and the constant hydroxyl group are not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Boiling point increases with chain length. Solubility in water decreases as chain length increases.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying both trends without any explanation.

dotPoints.description: Use IUPAC nomenclature to name and construct representations of position isomers of alcohols C1–C8

prompts.question: Demonstrate that butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are position isomers by writing the condensed structural formula of each and naming each using IUPAC nomenclature.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is preparing a revision card for a Year 12 class that shows the structure and IUPAC name of each butanol isomer.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates that both compounds share a four carbon chain and differ only in the position of the hydroxyl group, with correct condensed structural formulas and IUPAC names for each
2 marks: Gives correct condensed structural formulas and names for both compounds, without linking them as position isomers
1 mark: Identifies that the two compounds differ in the position of the hydroxyl group
markerNotes: The strongest answers show the carbon chain is the same and that only the position of the -OH group changes, then name each compound from the longest chain.
Numbering starts at the end nearest the hydroxyl group, so the hydroxyl group receives the lowest possible number.
commonStudentErrors: Names butan-2-ol as butan-3-ol by numbering the chain from the wrong end.
Says the two compounds are functional group isomers, which is a different class of isomer.
Gives the same name to both compounds, which hides the change in position.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using IUPAC nomenclature, the condensed structural formula of butan-1-ol is CH3CH2CH2CH2OH, with the hydroxyl group on the first carbon of a four carbon chain. The condensed structural formula of butan-2-ol is CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3, with the hydroxyl group on the second carbon. Both are alcohols with the molecular formula C4H10O and the same carbon chain, so they are position isomers that differ only in where the hydroxyl group sits.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by showing the shared carbon chain, the different hydroxyl position, and correct names and formulas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butan-1-ol is CH3CH2CH2CH2OH and butan-2-ol is CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3, both of which are alcohols.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row with correct formulas and names. The link between the two compounds as position isomers is not made.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two compounds differ in where the -OH group is.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the difference in hydroxyl position. No formulas or names are given.

prompts.question: Construct the condensed structural formula and IUPAC name of each straight chain position isomer of pentanol, and state whether each isomer is a primary or secondary alcohol.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A teacher asks a Year 12 class to prepare a reference table of the straight chain alcohols with five carbon atoms, showing every position isomer.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs correct condensed structural formulas and IUPAC names for all three straight chain position isomers of pentanol, and correctly classifies each as primary or secondary from the carbon bonded to the hydroxyl group
5 marks: Constructs correct formulas and names for all three isomers, with the classification correct for two of them
4 marks: Constructs correct formulas and names for two isomers, with some classification given
3 marks: Constructs a correct formula and name for one isomer, with its classification given
2 marks: Names one isomer correctly, without its classification
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about pentanol isomers
markerNotes: Check that each isomer keeps a five carbon chain and that the hydroxyl group sits on a different carbon in each case.
A secondary alcohol has its hydroxyl carbon bonded to two other carbon atoms, so classify from the structure, not from the name.
commonStudentErrors: Gives pentan-3-ol the name pentan-2-ol by numbering from the wrong end.
Says pentan-2-ol is primary because its hydroxyl group is not on an end carbon.
Omits pentan-3-ol and lists only the isomers with the hydroxyl group on an end or second carbon.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using IUPAC nomenclature, the condensed structural formulas of the three straight chain position isomers of pentanol are as follows. Pentan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH, has the hydroxyl group on the first carbon, which is bonded to one other carbon, so it is a primary alcohol. Pentan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH3, has the hydroxyl group on the second carbon, which is bonded to two other carbons, so it is a secondary alcohol. Pentan-3-ol, CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2CH3, has the hydroxyl group on the middle carbon, which is also bonded to two other carbons, so it is a secondary alcohol. All three share the same five carbon chain and differ only in the position of the hydroxyl group. The chain is numbered from the end nearest the hydroxyl group, which gives the carbon carrying the -OH group the lowest possible number.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing and naming all three isomers and classifying each one correctly from its structure.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pentan-1-ol is CH3CH2CH2CH2CH2OH and is a primary alcohol. Pentan-2-ol is CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2CH3 and is a secondary alcohol.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing correct formulas and names for two isomers, with their classification given.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pentan-1-ol is one isomer, with the hydroxyl group on the first carbon.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by naming one isomer correctly. Its formula and classification are missing.

dotPoints.description: Compare the reactants, products and experimental conditions of complete and incomplete combustion reactions

prompts.question: Compare the reactants, products and experimental conditions of the complete combustion and the incomplete combustion of ethanol in the two burners.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student lights ethanol in two spirit burners. In the first burner the air vents are fully open, and in the second burner the air vents are partly blocked.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Compares the reactants, products and experimental conditions of both reactions with accurate, specific detail, showing how the oxygen supply determines the products and the flame
3 marks: Compares the reactants, products and conditions of both reactions, with accurate detail for most of them
2 marks: Identifies some differences in the reactants, products or conditions of the two reactions
1 mark: Identifies that the two reactions differ in the amount of oxygen available
markerNotes: A strong answer compares all three features for both reactions, rather than describing each reaction separately.
The key contrast is the oxygen supply: complete combustion uses excess oxygen, while incomplete combustion uses a restricted supply.
commonStudentErrors: Says incomplete combustion produces only carbon dioxide and water, the same as complete combustion.
Lists carbon monoxide as a product of complete combustion.
Says complete combustion needs a catalyst, which is not a condition of combustion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both reactions use ethanol and oxygen as reactants. Complete combustion has a plentiful supply of oxygen from open air and gives carbon dioxide and water as its only products, with a clean pale blue flame. Incomplete combustion has a restricted oxygen supply because the vents are blocked, and gives carbon monoxide, water and some carbon soot, with a yellow, smoky flame. The reactants are the same, but the experimental conditions control the products.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by comparing reactants, products and conditions for both reactions, with the oxygen supply as the key difference.

sampleAnswers.answer: Complete combustion uses plenty of oxygen and gives carbon dioxide and water. Incomplete combustion uses less oxygen and gives carbon monoxide.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying differences in the oxygen supply and products. The experimental conditions are not compared.

sampleAnswers.answer: Incomplete combustion has less oxygen than complete combustion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the difference in oxygen supply only.

prompts.question: Apply your understanding of complete and incomplete combustion to explain why the blocked stove produces a yellow, sooty flame, referring to the reactants, products and experimental conditions.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A camping stove burns ethanol. When its air holes are partly blocked, the flame turns yellow and leaves black soot on a cold metal pan held above it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Applies knowledge of both combustion types to explain the yellow, sooty flame, with accurate reference to the reactants, products and experimental conditions, and why the carbon is not fully oxidised
5 marks: Explains the yellow, sooty flame by linking the restricted oxygen supply to incomplete combustion, with accurate reference to the products
4 marks: Explains the link between restricted oxygen and incomplete combustion, with some reference to the products or conditions
3 marks: Identifies incomplete combustion as the cause of the sooty flame, with limited explanation
2 marks: Identifies that less oxygen is available when the air holes are blocked
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about combustion
markerNotes: Strong answers treat the blocked stove as a change in one condition, the oxygen supply, and trace that change through the products.
Soot and carbon monoxide are the products to name, since they show the carbon has not been fully oxidised.
commonStudentErrors: Says the blocked stove produces carbon dioxide and water only, the same as the open stove.
Says the yellow colour comes from the ethanol changing its structure rather than from the carbon particles.
Says more oxygen is needed when the vents are blocked.

sampleAnswers.answer: The stove burns ethanol, which is the reactant in both cases, with oxygen from the air as the second reactant. When the air holes are open, the experimental conditions give a plentiful supply of oxygen, so the reaction is complete combustion. Carbon dioxide and water are the only products, and the flame is pale blue. When the air holes are blocked, the oxygen supply is restricted, so the reaction becomes incomplete combustion. The products now include carbon monoxide and carbon particles, and the particles glow yellow in the flame. The soot that deposits on the cold pan shows that the carbon has not been fully oxidised. The blocked stove therefore shows that the oxygen supply controls both the products and the appearance of the flame. Clearing the air holes restores the plentiful supply of oxygen, so the reaction returns to complete combustion with a clean blue flame.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by explaining the yellow, sooty flame through restricted oxygen, with the reactants, products and conditions all addressed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The blocked stove has less oxygen, so the fuel undergoes incomplete combustion. This gives carbon monoxide and soot, which make the flame yellow.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the link between restricted oxygen and incomplete combustion, with some reference to products. The conditions are not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The stove is not getting enough oxygen, so it burns incompletely.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the restricted oxygen supply. No products or reasons are given.

prompts.question: Explain why biodiesel (C₁₄H₃₀O₂) produces less soot than diesel (C₁₈H₃₈) when combusted under the same conditions. Support your answer with balanced chemical equations.
markerNotes: The top response explains that diesel needs more oxygen for complete combustion, so incomplete combustion and soot are more likely, and supports this with balanced equations.
NESA’s sample equations are not balanced as printed; balanced forms are 2C₁₈H₃₈ + 55O₂ → 36CO₂ + 38H₂O, 2C₁₄H₃₀O₂ + 41O₂ → 28CO₂ + 30H₂O and 2C₁₈H₃₈ + 41O₂ → 20CO₂ + 4CO + 12C + 38H₂O.
A student who writes the equations without balancing them cannot show the oxygen difference, so balancing is the key check.
commonStudentErrors: Gives an equation for diesel with the wrong oxygen coefficient, so the oxygen requirement cannot be compared.
Says biodiesel produces less soot because it contains oxygen, without comparing the oxygen needed for combustion.
Writes an equation for complete combustion only and does not explain the soot from incomplete combustion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains why biodiesel produces less soot than diesel; Supports answer with relevant and correctly balanced chemical equations (states NOT required)
2 marks: Makes use of at lease one substantially correct balanced equation to provide an explanation OR Provides two correctly balanced equations
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
C₁₈H₃₈ + O₂ → 18 CO₂ + 19H₂O
C₁₄H₃₀O₂ + O₂ → 14 CO₂ + 15H₂O
More supplied oxygen is required for the complete combustion of diesel compared to biodiesel. Therefore it is more likely that diesel will combust incompletely, producing soot.
Eg C₁₈H₃₈ + O₂ → 10 CO₂ + 2CO + 6 C + 19H₂O
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3 row: explains the difference in oxygen demand and supports it with correctly balanced equations for complete and incomplete combustion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Diesel (C₁₈H₃₈) needs more oxygen for complete combustion than biodiesel (C₁₄H₃₀O₂) does: C₁₈H₃₈ + 27½O₂ → 18CO₂ + 19H₂O. When oxygen is limited, the combustion becomes incomplete, so diesel is more likely to form soot.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2 row: uses one substantially correct balanced equation to explain why diesel forms more soot. Adding a second balanced equation for the incomplete combustion pathway would meet the 3 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Diesel produces more soot because it has more carbon atoms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: gives a relevant point about carbon content without an equation or a combustion explanation. Explaining the oxygen requirement would lift it to the 2 row.

prompts.question: Predict the products of the complete combustion of methanol, and state the conditions needed for the reaction to occur.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A methanol-fuelled heater is being tested in a well-ventilated shed, and the technician wants to know what the burning fuel releases.

3 marks: Predicts carbon dioxide and water as the products, and states that excess oxygen and an ignition source are needed for complete combustion
2 marks: Predicts both products correctly, without stating the conditions
1 mark: Identifies carbon dioxide or water as a product
markerNotes: Name both products, since complete combustion of any alcohol gives carbon dioxide and water only.
The conditions are an excess of oxygen and a source of ignition to start the reaction, so state both.
commonStudentErrors: Predicts carbon monoxide as the main product, which comes from incomplete combustion.
Forgets the water and gives only carbon dioxide.
Omits the oxygen condition, giving heat alone as the condition.

sampleAnswers.answer: The complete combustion of this alcohol gives carbon dioxide and water as the only products. The conditions needed are excess oxygen, which means burning in plenty of air, and an ignition source such as a flame or spark to start the reaction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by predicting both products and stating excess oxygen and an ignition source as conditions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The products are carbon dioxide and water, and the reaction needs oxygen.

sampleAnswers.answer: Carbon dioxide is formed.
