prompts.question: Construct the balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of octan-1-ol, and explain why carbon dioxide and water are the only products that can form from the atoms of the alcohol and the oxygen.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A chemistry teacher is preparing a model answer for a Year 12 class on the combustion of an alcohol with eight carbon atoms, to show how atoms are conserved.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a correct balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of octan-1-ol, and explains that carbon dioxide and water are the only products because all the carbon and hydrogen atoms are oxidised and atoms are conserved
5 marks: Constructs a correct balanced symbol equation with a clear explanation of the products, but omits one part of the reasoning about conservation
4 marks: Constructs a correct balanced symbol equation, with some explanation of the products
3 marks: Constructs a symbol equation with the correct products but an error in balancing
2 marks: Identifies carbon dioxide and water as the products, without a symbol equation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the combustion of alcohols
markerNotes: Balance carbon first, then hydrogen, and check oxygen last, since oxygen appears in both the alcohol and the oxygen reactant.
The explanation should refer to the conservation of atoms, not just list the products.
commonStudentErrors: Writes CO instead of CO2 for complete combustion, which is the product of incomplete combustion.
Forgets the oxygen atom in the hydroxyl group when counting oxygen atoms.
Writes water as H2 instead of H2O.

sampleAnswers.answer: The balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of octan-1-ol is C8H17OH + 12O2 → 8CO2 + 9H2O. In this alcohol, each carbon atom is oxidised to carbon dioxide, which gives eight molecules of carbon dioxide. The eighteen hydrogen atoms form nine molecules of water. Because of the conservation of atoms, no other products can form from the carbon, hydrogen and oxygen supplied. The oxygen atoms balance as well, with 25 on each side: the alcohol and the twelve oxygen molecules supply 25 atoms, and the products contain 16 in carbon dioxide and 9 in water. Excess oxygen is present for the complete reaction, and carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are all accounted for in the products. Each carbon atom of the alcohol forms one molecule of carbon dioxide, so the equation is balanced by counting carbon first, then hydrogen, and oxygen last.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing the balanced equation and explaining that the products follow from conservation of atoms.

sampleAnswers.answer: The balanced symbol equation is C8H17OH + 12O2 → 8CO2 + 9H2O. The products are carbon dioxide and water because the alcohol burns completely.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing a correct balanced equation, with some explanation of the products.

sampleAnswers.answer: The products are carbon dioxide and water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying both products without a symbol equation.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the relationship between enthalpy of combustion and chain length of alcohols

prompts.question: Predict whether one mole of octan-1-ol releases more or less energy on complete combustion than one mole of methanol, and explain why.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares two alcohols that are both used as fuels, methanol with one carbon atom and octan-1-ol with eight carbon atoms, each burned completely in excess oxygen.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Predicts that octan-1-ol releases more energy per mole, and explains that its longer chain has more carbon-hydrogen and carbon-carbon bonds to break and form, so the enthalpy of combustion is more negative
2 marks: Predicts that octan-1-ol releases more energy per mole, without a valid explanation
1 mark: Identifies that the energy released depends on which alcohol burns
markerNotes: Compare the energy per mole, because the enthalpy of combustion is quoted per mole of fuel.
A strong answer links the larger energy release to more bonds broken and formed, not to the hydroxyl group, which is the same in both alcohols.
commonStudentErrors: Says methanol releases more energy because it burns more easily.
Says the enthalpy of combustion becomes less negative as chain length increases.
Says the energy released depends on the mass of fuel rather than the number of moles.

sampleAnswers.answer: Octan-1-ol releases more energy per mole than methanol. Because of its longer chain length, this alcohol has more carbon-hydrogen and carbon-carbon bonds to break and form, so its enthalpy of combustion is more exothermic. Each extra CH2 group adds a similar amount of energy release per mole.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by predicting the direction and explaining it through the extra bonds in the longer chain.

sampleAnswers.answer: Octan-1-ol releases more energy per mole because it is bigger.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by predicting the direction. The explanation does not refer to bonds.

sampleAnswers.answer: The energy released depends on which alcohol burns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that the alcohol affects the energy. No prediction is made.

prompts.question: Analyse the relationship between the enthalpy of combustion and chain length for the alcohols from methanol to octan-1-ol, using the bonds broken and formed during complete combustion.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A teacher shows a Year 12 class a table of enthalpies of combustion, all measured per mole, for the alcohols from methanol to octan-1-ol. Students use the pattern in the table to draw a conclusion about molecular structure.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the relationship, showing that the enthalpy of combustion becomes more negative with each added CH2 group, and links this to the greater number of bonds broken and formed during complete combustion, with the energy compared per mole
5 marks: Analyses the trend in enthalpy of combustion with chain length, linking it to the bonds broken and formed during complete combustion
4 marks: Describes the trend in enthalpy of combustion with chain length, with some reference to bonds
3 marks: Describes the trend in enthalpy of combustion accurately, without reference to bonds
2 marks: Identifies that the enthalpy of combustion changes with chain length

markerNotes: Enthalpy of combustion is negative, so a more negative value means more energy released per mole.

sampleAnswers.answer: The enthalpy of combustion becomes more negative as chain length increases across the alcohols from methanol to octan-1-ol. A more negative value means more energy is released per mole during complete combustion, so the relationship is one of increasing energy release with chain length. Each extra CH2 group adds carbon-hydrogen and carbon-carbon bonds to the molecule. During complete combustion, more bonds are broken and more bonds form in the carbon dioxide and water, so the overall reaction releases more energy. The hydroxyl group is the same in every alcohol, so it does not cause the trend. The data show a steady, regular increase with each added CH2 group, which means chain length is the variable that controls the enthalpy of combustion. This means the energy released per mole rises steadily along the series, so the trend is a useful guide when choosing an alcohol as a fuel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by linking the more negative enthalpy to the extra bonds in each added CH2 group, with the energy compared per mole.

sampleAnswers.answer: Enthalpy of combustion becomes more negative as the chain gets longer, so more energy is released. Longer molecules have more bonds that are broken and formed when they burn.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the trend with some reference to bonds. The hydroxyl group and the data are not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The enthalpy of combustion changes as chain length increases.

prompts.question: Describe the measurements you would record to determine the enthalpy of combustion of ethanol in a school laboratory, using a spirit burner and a metal can of water.

2 marks: Describes a mass or temperature measurement, without the full set of measurements

The volume of water, the can and the distance from the flame must be kept the same, so that the readings can be compared fairly.
commonStudentErrors: Measures the volume of alcohol used instead of the mass lost from the burner.
Records only the final temperature of the water, without a starting temperature.

sampleAnswers.answer: Weigh the spirit burner containing ethanol before lighting it, then weigh it again after burning for a set time, to find the mass of alcohol burned. Measure a fixed volume of water in the metal can, record its starting temperature, and record the final temperature after heating. Keep the water volume and the distance from the flame constant, and shield the can to reduce heat loss. These readings give the enthalpy of combustion of the ethanol.

prompts.question: Assess the spirit burner method for measuring the enthalpy of combustion of alcohols in a school laboratory, including its main source of error and how that error could be reduced.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's spirit burner results give an enthalpy of combustion for ethanol that is well below the value in a data book. The student wants to evaluate the method before repeating the experiment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the spirit burner method with sustained judgement, identifying heat loss to the surroundings as the main source of error and proposing specific improvements such as a draught shield and a lid on the can
5 marks: Assesses the method and identifies heat loss as the main source of error, with a relevant improvement suggested
4 marks: Identifies heat loss as an error and outlines one relevant way to reduce it
3 marks: Identifies one limitation of the method, without explaining its effect on the result
2 marks: Identifies a measurement that could be inaccurate
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the method
markerNotes: A strong answer explains the effect of heat loss, namely that less heat reaches the water, so the enthalpy value is underestimated.
Improvements must target the named error, so a draught shield or lid is better than a general call to repeat the experiment.
commonStudentErrors: Says the method is accurate because the burner was weighed before and after burning.
Blames the error on the balance without linking it to heat loss.
Suggests a hotter flame as the improvement, which does not reduce heat loss.

sampleAnswers.answer: The spirit burner method is simple and inexpensive, and it gives a useful measure of the enthalpy of combustion of an alcohol. However, its main source of error is heat loss. Much of the heat from the flame escapes to the air and the surroundings rather than heating the water in the can, so the temperature rise is smaller than it should be. Because less heat is absorbed, the enthalpy of combustion is underestimated, which may explain the low value the student obtained. Heat loss can be reduced with a draught shield around the can, a lid with a small hole for the thermometer, and a fixed distance between flame and can. The method is therefore useful for comparing alcohols in a school setting, but it is not accurate enough to match a data book value.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by identifying heat loss as the main error, suggesting specific improvements and giving a judgement of the method.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heat loss to the surroundings is the main error, because less heat reaches the water. A draught shield would reduce this heat loss.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying heat loss and outlining one way to reduce it. The judgement of the method is limited.

prompts.question: Predict the organic product and the other product formed when propan-1-ol is heated with concentrated sulfuric acid, and state the conditions required.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is preparing propene in a school laboratory by dehydrating an alcohol, and the teacher asks the student to predict the products before starting.

3 marks: Predicts propene and water as the products, and states that concentrated sulfuric acid and heat are required
2 marks: Predicts both products correctly, without stating the conditions
1 mark: Identifies that the alcohol forms an alkene
markerNotes: Name the organic product, propene, and the second product, water, since dehydration removes water from the alcohol.
State both the acid and the heat, because the dehydration needs both.
commonStudentErrors: Predicts an alkane as the product, rather than an alkene.
Predicts propene and hydrogen gas, forgetting the water.
Omits the heat from the conditions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The organic product is propene, CH3CH=CH2, which is an alkene. The other product is water, removed from the alcohol when the hydroxyl group leaves with a hydrogen atom from the neighbouring carbon. The conditions are heating propan-1-ol with concentrated sulfuric acid, which acts as a catalyst in this dehydration reaction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by predicting both products and stating the acid and heat as conditions.

sampleAnswers.answer: The products are propene and water.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propene is formed.

prompts.question: Construct the balanced symbol equation for the dehydration of butan-1-ol, state the conditions, and explain why butan-1-ol can form only one alkene.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class is comparing the dehydration of primary alcohols, and the teacher asks students to write the reaction for butan-1-ol with full reasoning.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a correct balanced symbol equation for the dehydration of butan-1-ol, states the conditions, names water as the second product, and explains that only one alkene forms because only one neighbouring carbon has hydrogen atoms available for removal
5 marks: Constructs a correct balanced symbol equation and states the conditions, with a valid explanation of why only but-1-ene forms
4 marks: Constructs a correct balanced symbol equation with the conditions stated, without a full explanation of the single alkene
3 marks: Constructs a symbol equation with one error, with the conditions and products described in general terms
2 marks: Identifies but-1-ene as the organic product, without a balanced equation
1 mark: Identifies that the alcohol is converted to an alkene
markerNotes: Check the balance: butan-1-ol is C4H10O, so the alkene is C4H8 and the second product is H2O.
The explanation depends on the carbon atoms next to the carbon that carries the -OH group, so count their hydrogen atoms.
commonStudentErrors: Gives but-2-ene as the product, without recognising that butan-1-ol can form only one alkene.
Leaves water out of the equation, so the atoms are not conserved.
States that heat alone is needed, without the concentrated sulfuric acid.

sampleAnswers.answer: The balanced symbol equation for the dehydration of butan-1-ol is C4H9OH → C4H8 + H2O, forming the alkene but-1-ene and water. The conditions are heating the alcohol with concentrated sulfuric acid. Butan-1-ol has its hydroxyl group on carbon 1. Dehydration removes the -OH group and a hydrogen atom from the neighbouring carbon, carbon 2. Carbon 2 is the only neighbour of carbon 1 that carries hydrogen atoms available for removal, so the double bond can only form between carbons 1 and 2, giving but-1-ene. The atoms are conserved, because the hydroxyl group and a hydrogen atom together form the water. Ethanol gives only ethene by the same reasoning, while propan-1-ol gives only propene. The dehydration is an elimination reaction because a small molecule, water, is removed from the alcohol, leaving a carbon-carbon double bond behind.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by giving the balanced equation, the conditions and a valid reason why only one alkene forms.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butan-1-ol forms but-1-ene and water when heated with concentrated sulfuric acid. The balanced symbol equation is C4H9OH → C4H8 + H2O.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing a correct balanced equation with the conditions stated. The reason for the single alkene is not given.

sampleAnswers.answer: The organic product is but-1-ene.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the alkene without a balanced equation.

prompts.question: Describe the organic product formed when propan-2-ol is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate, and state the colour change of the oxidising agent.

markerNotes: Propan-2-ol is secondary, so its oxidation gives a ketone, propanone, rather than an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid.
The orange to green colour change shows that the dichromate has been reduced while the alcohol is oxidised.
commonStudentErrors: Names the product as propanal, which would need a primary alcohol.
Says the product is a carboxylic acid, which needs a primary alcohol.
Reports the colour change as green to orange, which reverses the reaction.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, so its oxidation gives a ketone, propanone (CH3COCH3), rather than an aldehyde. The acidified potassium dichromate is reduced, and the colour change is from orange to green. This colour change is a standard observation that confirms oxidation of the alcohol.

prompts.question: Analyse why primary alcohols can form aldehyde or carboxylic acid products on oxidation, while secondary alcohols form only ketones and tertiary alcohols are not oxidised, giving reasons based on the hydrogen atoms on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class oxidises three alcohols with acidified potassium dichromate, one primary, one secondary and one tertiary, and must explain the products or the lack of them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the oxidation of each alcohol type, linking the aldehyde or carboxylic acid from a primary alcohol to the two hydrogen atoms on its hydroxyl carbon, the ketone from a secondary alcohol to one hydrogen atom, and the lack of oxidation of a tertiary alcohol to the absence of any such hydrogen
5 marks: Analyses the products of all three alcohol types, with the link to the hydrogen atoms given for two of them
4 marks: Describes the products of primary and secondary alcohols accurately, with some reason for the difference
3 marks: Describes the product of one alcohol type accurately, without a reason
2 marks: Identifies that some alcohols are oxidised and others are not
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about alcohol oxidation
markerNotes: The deciding feature is whether the carbon bearing the -OH group has a hydrogen atom: primary alcohols have two, secondary alcohols have one and tertiary alcohols have none.
An aldehyde can be oxidised further to a carboxylic acid when the oxidant is in excess and the aldehyde stays in the mixture, so the product depends on the conditions.
commonStudentErrors: Says tertiary alcohols are oxidised to ketones because they have a carbon bearing an -OH group.
Says ketones are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids under the same conditions.
Says primary alcohols form ketones because they have more carbon atoms.

sampleAnswers.answer: Oxidation depends on the hydrogen atoms on the carbon that carries the hydroxyl group. A primary alcohol has two hydrogen atoms on that carbon, so it is oxidised first to an aldehyde. The aldehyde can be oxidised further to a carboxylic acid if the oxidant is in excess and the aldehyde stays in the reaction mixture under reflux, so the product is an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol has one hydrogen atom on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group, so its oxidation gives a ketone. The carbon in a ketone has no hydrogen left to remove, so the ketone cannot be oxidised further under these conditions. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen atom on the carbon with the hydroxyl group, so it resists oxidation and the dichromate does not change colour. The three cases give different products because the hydrogen atoms on the hydroxyl carbon control the outcome of the oxidation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by linking each alcohol type to the hydrogen atoms on its hydroxyl carbon, with the products analysed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Primary alcohols give an aldehyde, which can be oxidised further, because the carbon bearing the -OH group has two hydrogen atoms. Secondary alcohols give a ketone because that carbon has one hydrogen atom. Tertiary alcohols do not react.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the products of primary and secondary alcohols with a reason for the difference. The tertiary case has no reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised, but tertiary alcohols are not.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying that some alcohols are oxidised and others are not.

prompts.question: Each isomer produces a different product when oxidised. Write equations to represent the oxidation reactions of the two isomers. Include reaction conditions.
markerNotes: The top band gives two balanced equations, one for each isomer, with the correct product and the reaction conditions for each.

commonStudentErrors: Gives propanoic acid as the product of propan-1-ol without stating that the conditions must be controlled to stop at the aldehyde.
Writes the product of propan-2-ol as an aldehyde, such as propanal, rather than a ketone.
Omits the reaction conditions, such as acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and heat, which the question requires.
prompts.markingCriteria:

2 marks: Writes ONE correct equation, with correct product and correct reaction conditions OR Writes TWO equations with correct product and does not include or includes incorrect reaction conditions

sampleAnswers.answer: Propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol, and its oxidation with acidified potassium dichromate(VI) under reflux gives the ketone propanone, which cannot be oxidised further: 3CH₃CH(OH)CH₃(l) + Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) → 3CH₃COCH₃(l) + 2Cr³⁺(aq) + 7H₂O(l). Propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol. Warming it with the same acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and distilling the product off as it forms gives the aldehyde propanal: 3CH₃CH₂CH₂OH(l) + Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) → 3CH₃CH₂CHO(l) + 2Cr³⁺(aq) + 7H₂O(l).
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: writes two balanced equations with the correct products, and states the reaction conditions for each oxidation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propan-2-ol is oxidised to propanone: 3CH₃CH(OH)CH₃(l) + Cr₂O₇²⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) → 3CH₃COCH₃(l) + 2Cr³⁺(aq) + 7H₂O(l). The conditions are acidified potassium dichromate and heat, but the equation for propan-1-ol is missing. This is a secondary alcohol, so the product is a ketone that cannot be oxidised further.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: writes one correct equation with its product and conditions. Adding a balanced equation for propan-1-ol, with the aldehyde product and its conditions, would meet the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propan-2-ol is oxidised to a ketone, which is propanone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the product of one isomer, with no equation or conditions. An equation with the reaction conditions would lift it to the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The balanced symbol equation for ethanol is C2H5OH + HBr → C2H5Br + H2O. The product is bromoethane, a haloalkane, and water is the by-product. prompts.question: Describe the observations expected when a primary, a secondary and a tertiary alcohol are each warmed with acidified potassium dichromate solution in separate test tubes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class receives three unlabelled alcohols, one primary, one secondary and one tertiary, and must test each with acidified potassium dichromate solution.

3 marks: Describes the orange solution turning green for the primary and secondary alcohols, and no colour change for the tertiary alcohol, with each test warmed under the same conditions
2 marks: Describes a colour change for the primary and secondary alcohols, without describing the tertiary alcohol
1 mark: Identifies that the tertiary alcohol gives a different result from the other two
markerNotes: Record the colour change for each tube, because the test depends on the orange dichromate turning green when it is reduced.
A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the -OH group, so the solution stays orange.
commonStudentErrors: Says the tertiary alcohol turns the solution green as well, which contradicts its resistance to oxidation.
Says the solution turns from green to orange, reversing the colour change.
Describes the result only as the alcohols reacting, without giving an observation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The primary alcohol and the secondary alcohol both undergo oxidation, so the orange acidified potassium dichromate solution turns green in each tube when warmed. This colour change shows oxidation of the alcohol. The tertiary alcohol does not oxidise, so its solution stays orange and shows no colour change. The result demonstrates the reactivity of the three alcohol types with the oxidising agent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the green colour change for two alcohols and no change for the tertiary alcohol.

sampleAnswers.answer: The primary and secondary alcohols change the solution from orange to green.

sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the different result for the tertiary alcohol. No observations are given for the other two.

prompts.question: Assess how well the acidified potassium dichromate test distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, and identify one limitation of the test.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student proposes using only the acidified potassium dichromate test to identify an unlabelled alcohol as primary, secondary or tertiary, and presents the result to the class.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the test with sustained judgement, showing that it separates tertiary from primary and secondary alcohols through the oxidation result, identifies that it cannot tell primary from secondary alcohols, and suggests a further test that could separate them
5 marks: Assesses the test, showing that it separates tertiary from the other two, and identifies that it cannot separate primary and secondary alcohols
4 marks: Describes how the test distinguishes the tertiary alcohol, with a limitation identified
3 marks: Describes the test result for at least two alcohol types, without a judgement of its usefulness
2 marks: Identifies that the test produces a colour change for some alcohols
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the test
markerNotes: A strong answer identifies that the test works for tertiary alcohols but cannot separate primary from secondary alcohols.
A suggested improvement must target the limitation, for example a test that identifies the aldehyde or ketone product.
commonStudentErrors: Says the test proves an alcohol is primary when the solution turns green.
Says the test can separate all three alcohol types, which it cannot do.
Says the test is reliable because the colour change is easy to see, without naming a limitation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The acidified potassium dichromate test is useful for separating tertiary alcohols from the other two types. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on the carbon that carries the hydroxyl group, so it is not oxidised and the orange solution stays orange. Primary and secondary alcohols are oxidised, so the solution turns green, and a positive result shows that the alcohol is primary or secondary. A limitation of the test is that it cannot separate primary from secondary alcohols, because both give the same colour change. A primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde and then possibly to a carboxylic acid, while a secondary alcohol gives a ketone, but the colour change does not reveal which product forms. The test therefore shows the reactivity of tertiary alcohols clearly, and a further test that identifies the aldehyde or ketone product is needed to separate primary from secondary alcohols.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing the test, identifying its limitation and suggesting a further test.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fermentation converts plant sugars, such as glucose, into ethanol and carbon dioxide, using yeast enzymes in an anaerobic environment at a mild temperature. Crude oil is cracked to produce ethene, which is hydrated with steam at high temperature and pressure over an acid catalyst to give alcohol. The alcohol from crude oil therefore comes from ethene, not from plant material.

prompts.question: Evaluate the fermentation of plant sugars and the production of ethanol from crude oil as processes for producing alcohol, referring to their sustainability, the purity of the product and their cost.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A fuel company must choose one process to supply ethanol for a blended petrol. It is considering fermentation of plant sugars or hydration of ethene from crude oil.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Evaluates both processes with sustained judgement, weighing the renewability of the feedstock, the purity and concentration of the product, the energy used in separation and the cost, and reaches a justified conclusion about which process better suits the fuel company
7 marks: Evaluates both processes against renewability and purity, reaching a supported conclusion
5-6 marks: Compares the processes against renewability and purity, reaching a conclusion that is only partly supported
3-4 marks: Describes features of both processes, with one relevant point of comparison
2 marks: Describes one process, with no comparison to the other
1 mark: Identifies that the two processes use different starting materials
markerNotes: A strong evaluation weighs both processes against the same criteria, such as renewability, purity and energy, and then judges which is better for the stated purpose.
Fermentation gives a dilute solution that needs distillation, while hydration gives a purer product from a non-renewable feedstock, and the answer should weigh both.
commonStudentErrors: Says fermentation is better because it uses sugar, without weighing the energy needed to separate the dilute product.
Says both processes produce pure ethanol at the same concentration.
Lists advantages and disadvantages of each process without reaching a judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fermentation of plant sugars is a renewable route to alcohol production, because the feedstock is grown again each season. It uses mild conditions, with yeast in a simple, low-energy process. Its main weakness is purity. The fermentation mixture contains only a dilute ethanol solution, because high concentrations of ethanol kill the yeast, so the product must be separated by distillation, which uses substantial energy. Hydration of ethene from crude oil is a continuous process that gives a high-purity ethanol product in large quantities. However, it depends on a non-renewable feedstock and needs high temperature, high pressure and an acid catalyst, so its sustainability is lower. The cost of purification is lower for hydration, because less separation is needed. For a fuel company blending petrol, the purity advantage of hydration matters less than the renewable source and the sustainability of the supply. Fermentation therefore suits a blended fuel that aims at sustainability, although hydration remains the better choice where high purity and large volumes are the main priorities. A full comparison also needs the energy and cost of distillation, so the company should compare the full cost of distillation with the cost of the crude oil feedstock before deciding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-8 mark row by weighing renewability, purity, energy and cost, and reaching a justified conclusion for the fuel company.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fermentation uses plant sugars and yeast, so its feedstock is renewable. However, the product is dilute and must be purified, while hydration of ethene from crude oil gives a purer product from a non-renewable source. Fermentation is the better choice for a renewable fuel, although hydration gives a purer product.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by comparing both processes on renewability and purity, with a conclusion that is only partly supported.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fermentation turns plant sugars into ethanol using yeast.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one process. No comparison or judgement is made.

prompts.question: Explain TWO advantages and TWO disadvantages of using bioethanol (ethanol produced from biomass) as an alternative to a fossil fuel.
markerNotes: The top response gives two advantages and two disadvantages and explains each, linking them to renewable production, carbon neutrality, food supply and fertiliser runoff.
A carbon-neutral claim needs the condition that the energy used to grow and distil the ethanol is not from fossil fuels, which separates the top band.
commonStudentErrors: Lists advantages and disadvantages without explaining why each one is an advantage or a disadvantage.
Says bioethanol is carbon neutral in every case, without noting that fossil fuels used in production add carbon.

prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains TWO advantages and TWO disadvantages of using bioethanol as an alternative to a fossil fuel
3 marks: Outlines TWO advantages and TWO disadvantages of using bioethanol as an alternative to a fossil fuel; Explains at least TWO of them

sampleAnswers.answer: Bioethanol is produced from renewable resources while petrol is produced from non-renewable crude oil reserves. Thus, ethanol is a sustainable fuel, which may be continually produced while petrol is unsustainable. Combustion of petrol increases greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere. If green energy is used to produce bioethanol, the carbon dioxide released during the combustion may be removed by plants during photosynthesis, resulting in a carbon neutral process. Increased demand for ethanol to replace petrol may cause crops to be grown for fuel rather than food. Food shortages or increased food prices may result. As more crops are grown to produce biofuels, more fertiliser is used. The excess use of fertilisers can result in soil erosion and can lead to land and water pollution.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4 row: explains two advantages and two disadvantages, linking each to renewability, carbon neutrality, food supply and water or soil pollution.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bioethanol is made from renewable crops, so it does not use up the limited crude oil reserves. However, growing crops for fuel can raise food prices and compete with food production, and the fertiliser used can pollute water.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2 row: explains one advantage and one disadvantage of bioethanol. Adding a second of each, with explanations, would meet the 4 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Bioethanol can be made from renewable resources, unlike petrol.

prompts.question: Demonstrate how the molecular formula and the condensed structural formula of propanoic acid each show its carboxyl group, by writing both representations.

sampleAnswers.answer: The molecular formula of propanoic acid is C3H6O2, and its condensed structural formula is CH3CH2COOH, in which COOH is the carboxyl group. The expanded structural formula shows every bond, including the C=O and the -OH of the carboxyl carbon. In the skeletal structure, the group is drawn as a C=O and an OH at the end of a three carbon zigzag, so it appears the same way in every representation of this organic acid.

prompts.question: Construct the molecular formula, condensed structural formula and expanded structural formula of the unbranched organic acid with molecular formula C4H8O2, and describe its skeletal structure.

6 marks: Constructs the correct molecular formula, condensed structural formula and expanded structural formula of butanoic acid, and describes the skeletal structure with the carboxyl group at one end of an unbranched four carbon chain

sampleAnswers.answer: The molecular formula is C4H8O2. The condensed structural formula is CH3CH2CH2COOH, which shows an unbranched four carbon chain ending in the carboxyl group, -COOH. The expanded structural formula shows every bond: four carbon atoms, each bonded to its hydrogen atoms, with the terminal carbon double bonded to one oxygen atom and single bonded to a hydroxyl group, -OH. This is butanoic acid, an organic acid with the carboxyl group at one end. In the skeletal structure, the chain is drawn as a zigzag of lines, with a C=O and an OH group at the end and no branches along the chain, so the carbon skeleton is unbranched. The same four carbon skeleton is present in every representation, so each form describes the same molecule. Checking the expanded structure against the molecular formula confirms four carbon atoms, eight hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms.

prompts.question: Construct the condensed structural formula and IUPAC name for each of the four carboxylic acid isomers with molecular formula C5H10O2.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A teacher asks a Year 12 class to list every carboxylic acid with the molecular formula C5H10O2, using IUPAC names for a revision handout.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs correct condensed structural formulas and IUPAC names for all four carboxylic acid isomers, and explains that each is an organic acid with the same molecular formula but a different carbon skeleton
5 marks: Constructs correct formulas and IUPAC names for all four isomers, without explaining the isomer relationship

3 marks: Constructs correct formulas and names for two of the four isomers
2 marks: Constructs a correct formula and name for one isomer
1 mark: Identifies that the acids share the same molecular formula
markerNotes: The parent chain must be the longest chain that includes the carboxyl carbon, so 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid uses a three carbon parent chain.
Check each structure by counting carbons: five in total, including the carboxyl carbon and any methyl substituents.
commonStudentErrors: Names 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid as 2-methylbutanoic acid, which is a different structure.
Leaves out 3-methylbutanoic acid because it is branched, assuming only straight chains are isomers.
Numbers the chain from the wrong end, so the substituent position is wrong.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Using IUPAC nomenclature, the four carboxylic acid isomers with molecular formula C5H10O2 have these condensed structural formulas:
CH3CH2CH2CH2COOH, pentanoic acid.
CH3CH2CH(CH3)COOH, 2-methylbutanoic acid.
(CH3)2CHCH2COOH, 3-methylbutanoic acid.
(CH3)3CCOOH, 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid.
Each is an organic acid with the same molecular formula, C5H10O2, but a different carbon skeleton. Each contains the carboxyl group, -COOH, at the end of its parent chain, so they are isomers of one another. The names follow the rules of IUPAC nomenclature: the longest chain including the carboxyl carbon gives the parent name, and any methyl groups are numbered from the carboxyl carbon as carbon 1. For example, the 2,2-dimethyl isomer has two methyl groups on carbon 2, so its parent chain is only three carbons long. Each name identifies the chain length and the position of every methyl group, so the four names are distinct, and 2-methylbutanoic acid and 3-methylbutanoic acid differ only in where the methyl group sits.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing and naming all four isomers and explaining their shared molecular formula and carbon skeletons.

prompts.question: Explain why the solubility in water of unbranched carboxylic acids falls as chain length increases, while their boiling points rise.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has collected secondary-source data for the unbranched carboxylic acids from methanoic acid to octanoic acid and is checking how their properties change along the series.

3 marks: Explains that the carboxyl group hydrogen bonds with water while the growing hydrocarbon chain reduces solubility in water, and that longer chains have stronger London dispersion forces, which raise the boiling point
2 marks: Explains one of the trends with a reason, without linking the boiling point trend to intermolecular forces

commonStudentErrors: Says solubility in water increases with chain length because the acid molecules are bigger.

sampleAnswers.answer: Unbranched carboxylic acids all share the same carboxyl group, which forms hydrogen bonding with water. As chain length increases, the non-polar hydrocarbon chain grows too, so the solubility in water falls because the molecule mixes less readily with water. Boiling point rises for a different reason: longer chains have stronger London dispersion forces between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them.

prompts.question: Assess the validity of concluding from secondary-source data that solubility in water falls as chain length increases in unbranched carboxylic acids, considering whether the data can be used to explain the cause.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class report uses secondary-source tables from several textbooks to claim that solubility in water falls steadily as chain length increases for unbranched carboxylic acids. The teacher asks students to test that claim.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity of the conclusion, explaining that the trend is supported by the non-polar chain argument, and evaluates the secondary sources for consistency, measurement conditions and any missing data points
5 marks: Assesses the conclusion with reasoned judgement about the trend and the reliability of the sources
4 marks: Analyses the solubility trend with a reason, and comments briefly on the reliability of the data
3 marks: Describes the solubility trend accurately, with some comment on the data sources
2 marks: Identifies the solubility trend without a judgement of its validity
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about carboxylic acids
markerNotes: A strong answer tests the claim against the data: does solubility fall steadily, and do the sources use the same temperature and units?
Secondary sources can differ in units and temperature, such as grams per 100 mL, so check these before comparing values from different textbooks.
commonStudentErrors: Says the conclusion is valid because the textbooks agree, without checking the data.
Says the data prove the trend because it is shown in a table.
Says methanoic acid is insoluble in water, which contradicts the starting point of the trend.

sampleAnswers.answer: The validity of the conclusion is partial. The trend is supported by chemical reasoning: the carboxyl group forms hydrogen bonds with water in every acid, so solubility in water depends mainly on the size of the hydrocarbon chain, which is non-polar and grows with each CH2 unit. However, the claim that solubility falls steadily needs checking against the data. The first few unbranched carboxylic acids, such as methanoic, ethanoic and propanoic acid, are fully miscible with water, so no fall is seen across that part of the series. Secondary sources may also report results at different temperatures or in different units, such as grams per 100 mL, so values from different textbooks cannot be compared without checking. A valid conclusion should state that solubility falls only once chain length is large enough for the acid to be sparingly soluble, and that the trend comes from the hydrocarbon chain rather than the carboxyl group, which is the same in every acid.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by assessing the validity of the claim, using the non-polar chain argument and the reliability of the sources.

sampleAnswers.answer: Solubility in water falls as the hydrocarbon chain grows, which is a reasonable explanation. However, the data sources may use different temperatures, so the trend should be checked.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by analysing the trend with a reason and commenting briefly on the reliability of the data.

sampleAnswers.answer: Solubility in water falls as chain length increases in the table.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the trend without a judgement of its validity.

prompts.question: Describe the reagent, conditions and intermediate product needed to convert ethanol into ethanoic acid by oxidation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is writing a short answer for a Year 12 class on how a primary alcohol can be converted into a carboxylic acid in a school laboratory.
prompts.markingCriteria:

2 marks: Describes the oxidising agent and the conditions, without naming the intermediate

markerNotes: Name the intermediate as ethanal, an aldehyde, which is oxidised again to the carboxylic acid when the oxidant is in excess.
Reflux with excess oxidant produces the acid, while distilling the aldehyde off as it forms stops the reaction at the aldehyde stage.
commonStudentErrors: Says the alcohol is reduced to the acid, which reverses the oxidation.
Says the product is a ketone, which can only be made from a secondary alcohol.
Omits the conditions and says only that the mixture is stirred at room temperature.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethanol is a primary alcohol, and its oxidation is carried out with acidified potassium dichromate as the oxidising agent. The mixture is heated under reflux with excess oxidant. The intermediate is ethanal, an aldehyde, which is oxidised further to ethanoic acid, the carboxylic acid product.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by naming the oxidant, the reflux conditions with excess oxidant, and the aldehyde intermediate.

prompts.question: Construct the two equations, using [O] for the oxidising agent, for the oxidation of propan-1-ol to propanal and then to propanoic acid, and explain why excess oxidant under reflux gives the acid rather than the aldehyde.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class is writing a reaction pathway for converting propan-1-ol into a carboxylic acid, and the teacher asks students to show the intermediate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs both equations correctly, naming propanal as the intermediate and propanoic acid as the product, and explains that excess oxidant under reflux drives the aldehyde on to the acid, whereas distilling it off would stop at the aldehyde
5 marks: Constructs both equations correctly and explains the role of excess oxidant under reflux
4 marks: Constructs both equations correctly, without explaining the role of excess oxidant or reflux
3 marks: Constructs one equation correctly and identifies the aldehyde intermediate
2 marks: Identifies propanoic acid as the product of the oxidation of propan-1-ol
1 mark: Identifies that a primary alcohol is oxidised in the process
markerNotes: Both steps must appear, the alcohol to propanal and then propanal to propanoic acid, because the aldehyde is the intermediate.
Distilling off the aldehyde as it forms prevents further oxidation, which is how the aldehyde itself is made.
commonStudentErrors: Writes the first step as producing propanone, which is a ketone from a secondary alcohol.
Writes the equations with the acid as the first product, skipping the aldehyde step.
Says heating with a limited amount of oxidant gives the acid.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first step is CH3CH2CH2OH + [O] → CH3CH2CHO + H2O, in which propan-1-ol, a primary alcohol, is oxidised to the aldehyde propanal. The second step is CH3CH2CHO + [O] → CH3CH2COOH, in which the aldehyde is oxidised further to propanoic acid, the carboxylic acid. The oxidation to the acid needs excess oxidant and is carried out by heating the mixture under reflux, so the propanal formed stays in contact with the oxidant and is oxidised again. If the aldehyde were distilled off as it formed, the reaction would stop at the propanal stage instead. The acid therefore forms because the oxidant is in excess and the aldehyde is not removed from the reaction mixture, so the propanal has time to react further with the oxidant.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing both equations and explaining the role of excess oxidant under reflux.

sampleAnswers.answer: CH3CH2CH2OH + [O] → CH3CH2CHO + H2O, then CH3CH2CHO + [O] → CH3CH2COOH. The mixture is heated under reflux.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing both equations correctly, without explaining the role of excess oxidant or reflux.

sampleAnswers.answer: Propan-1-ol is oxidised to propanoic acid.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying propanoic acid as the product. No equations or intermediate are given.

2 marks: Describes effervescence and identifies carbon dioxide, without the limewater test
1 mark: Identifies that effervescence occurs when an acid reacts with a carbonate
markerNotes: Link the fizzing to carbon dioxide, and use the limewater test to confirm that the gas is carbon dioxide.
Describe the observation first, fizzing or bubbling, and then state the inference, which is carbon dioxide.
commonStudentErrors: Says a precipitate forms in the sodium hydrogencarbonate solution as the test result.
Says the gas is hydrogen, which comes from a metal reacting with acid rather than a carbonate.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, producing effervescence and bubbles of gas. The gas is carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky when it is bubbled through. This fizzing shows that a carboxylic acid is present, because the acid reacts with the carbonate to release carbon dioxide.

prompts.question: Justify whether a positive sodium hydrogencarbonate test on its own is sufficient to confirm that an unknown liquid is a carboxylic acid, and describe one further test that would strengthen the conclusion.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student adds an unknown liquid to sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, which fizzes vigorously, and concludes that the liquid is a carboxylic acid.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies that the test shows an acid but not specifically a carboxylic acid, because other acids also release carbon dioxide, and describes a further test, such as esterification, that strengthens the conclusion
5 marks: Justifies the limits of the test with reference to other acids, and identifies a suitable further test
4 marks: Explains that effervescence shows an acid, and notes one limit of the test
3 marks: Describes the effervescence and the carbon dioxide, with a limited comment on what this shows
2 marks: Identifies that the liquid is acidic from the fizzing
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the test
markerNotes: The test shows a stronger acid than carbonic acid, not specifically a carboxylic acid, so the conclusion needs a second piece of evidence.
Phenols are weakly acidic but do not fizz with sodium hydrogencarbonate, which is why the test separates them from carboxylic acids.
commonStudentErrors: Says any fizzing with a carbonate proves that the liquid is a carboxylic acid.
Says phenols also fizz with sodium hydrogencarbonate, which is incorrect.
Recommends a second bicarbonate test, which repeats the same evidence rather than adding new evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: A positive test is not sufficient on its own. Sodium hydrogencarbonate reacts with any acid stronger than carbonic acid, so strong mineral acids such as hydrochloric acid also release carbon dioxide from a carbonate. The effervescence therefore shows that the unknown is an acid, but not that it is a carboxylic acid. Phenols do not fizz with sodium hydrogencarbonate, so the test does separate carboxylic acids from phenols, which makes it useful as a first check. A further test would strengthen the conclusion. For example, warming the unknown with an alcohol and a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid should produce an ester with a sweet smell, which is a characteristic reaction of carboxylic acids. Together, the two observations make a carboxylic acid far more likely, but the conclusion remains a judgement based on evidence rather than proof.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying the limit of the test and describing a further test that strengthens the conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Effervescence shows that an acid is present, but a strong mineral acid would also fizz, so the test cannot confirm a carboxylic acid alone. Phenols do not react, so the test does separate them.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the effect of intermolecular forces on the boiling point and solubility trends of alkanes, alcohols and carboxylic acids

prompts.question: Compare the intermolecular forces in butane, butan-1-ol and butanoic acid, and relate these forces to their boiling points.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares three compounds with four carbon atoms each in a practical report on the boiling points of organic compounds.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Compares the intermolecular forces in all three compounds, explaining that hydrogen bonding in the alcohol and the paired hydrogen bonding in the acid raise their boiling points above that of the alkane, and ranks the three by boiling point
3 marks: Compares the intermolecular forces in all three compounds and relates them to boiling point, without the detail of paired hydrogen bonding in the acid
2 marks: Identifies the forces in at least two of the compounds, with some link to boiling point
1 mark: Identifies that alcohols and acids can hydrogen bond
markerNotes: Compare all three compounds, not two, and rank them by the strength of their forces before linking them to boiling points.
Name the forces: London dispersion forces in the alkane, hydrogen bonding in the alcohol, and paired hydrogen bonding in the acid, which gives the strongest effect.
commonStudentErrors: Says butane has hydrogen bonding because it has carbon-hydrogen bonds.
Says the acid boils higher only because it is larger, ignoring its hydrogen bonding.
Says covalent bonds are broken when the compounds boil.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butane is an alkane, and its molecules are held together only by London dispersion forces, which are weak because the molecules are small and non-polar. Butan-1-ol is an alcohol with an -OH group, so its molecules form hydrogen bonding with each other, a much stronger intermolecular force than London dispersion forces alone. Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid whose molecules form hydrogen-bonded pairs, which are stronger still. Because these intermolecular forces increase from butane to butan-1-ol to butanoic acid, the boiling point rises in the same order: butane boils far below the alcohol, and the carboxylic acid boils highest of the three.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by comparing the forces in all three compounds, noting the paired hydrogen bonding in the acid and ranking the boiling points.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butane has only London dispersion forces, and butan-1-ol has hydrogen bonding, so butan-1-ol has a higher boiling point.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the forces in two compounds with a link to boiling point. The acid is not compared.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butan-1-ol can hydrogen bond.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying hydrogen bonding in an alcohol. No comparison is made.

prompts.question: Analyse the solubility in water of pentane, pentan-1-ol and pentanoic acid, referring to the intermolecular forces of each compound.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student finds that pentane does not dissolve in water, while pentan-1-ol and pentanoic acid dissolve only slightly, and writes a report on the cause.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the solubility of all three compounds, explaining that pentane has only London dispersion forces that cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, while the polar -OH and -COOH groups hydrogen bond with water but are outweighed by the five carbon hydrocarbon chain
5 marks: Analyses the solubility of all three compounds with reference to hydrogen bonding with water and the effect of the hydrocarbon chain
4 marks: Explains the difference between pentane and the two polar compounds, with reference to intermolecular forces
3 marks: Describes the solubility of at least two compounds, with a limited reason
2 marks: Identifies that pentane is insoluble while the others dissolve slightly
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about solubility
markerNotes: Solubility depends on the balance between the polar group, which can hydrogen bond with water, and the non-polar hydrocarbon chain, which cannot.
Pentane cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, so it does not mix; the alcohol and acid can, but their chains limit how far they dissolve.
commonStudentErrors: Says pentane is insoluble because it is a gas.
Says pentanoic acid is insoluble because it has a higher boiling point than pentane.
Says the hydroxyl group makes pentan-1-ol non-polar, which reverses its polarity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The solubility in water of pentane is essentially nil. Pentane is a non-polar alkane, and its intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces only, which cannot form hydrogen bonding with water. Pentan-1-ol is an alcohol whose -OH group can hydrogen bond with water, so it dissolves to a limited extent. Pentanoic acid is a carboxylic acid whose carboxyl group can also hydrogen bond with water, so it dissolves slightly. In both cases the five carbon hydrocarbon chain is non-polar and limits how much of the molecule can interact with water, so the solubility is low. The analysis shows that solubility depends on the balance between the polar group and the hydrocarbon chain, not on the presence of a polar group alone, and that the longer chain of pentanoic acid is not offset by its carboxyl group.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by explaining each compound's solubility through its intermolecular forces with water and its hydrocarbon chain.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pentane has only London dispersion forces, so it does not mix with water. Pentan-1-ol and pentanoic acid can form hydrogen bonds with water, so they dissolve slightly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining the difference between pentane and the two polar compounds in terms of intermolecular forces.

sampleAnswers.answer: Pentane is insoluble, but the alcohol and acid dissolve a little.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying that pentane is insoluble while the others dissolve slightly.

prompts.question: With reference to hydrogen bonding and dispersion forces, explain the trends in the boiling point data of these compounds, within each series and between the series.
markerNotes: The top band explains both trends: boiling points rise within each series as dispersion forces increase with carbon number, and alcohols are higher than the corresponding amines because O–H hydrogen bonding is stronger than N–H.

commonStudentErrors: Says amines have stronger hydrogen bonding than alcohols because nitrogen has a lone pair.

prompts.markingCriteria:

sampleAnswers.answer: For both the alcohols and the amines, dispersion forces will increase with increasing carbon number, due to increased number of electrons present, leading to increased boiling points. However, for any given carbon number, the alcohol has stronger hydrogen bonding than the corresponding amine, as oxygen has a higher electronegativity than nitrogen, so the alcohols all have higher boiling points than the corresponding amines.

prompts.question: Demonstrate that ethyl ethanoate and methyl propanoate are isomers by writing the molecular formula and the condensed structural formula of each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is checking two esters on a worksheet to decide whether they are the same compound or isomers of each other.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates that both esters have the molecular formula C4H8O2, writes correct condensed structural formulas for both, and explains that the atoms are arranged differently, so they are isomers
2 marks: Writes correct molecular and condensed structural formulas for both esters, without explaining the isomer relationship
1 mark: Identifies that both esters have the same molecular formula
markerNotes: Isomers have the same molecular formula with different structures, so the explanation must refer to the arrangement of atoms.
Strong answers show the -COO- linkage in each ester, which is what makes each compound an ester rather than an acid.
commonStudentErrors: Writes the molecular formula of methyl propanoate as C4H10O2, which has the wrong number of hydrogen atoms.
Says the two esters are the same compound because they have the same formula, ignoring the different structures.
Draws the ester linkage as a single C-O bond only, leaving out the C=O.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethyl ethanoate has the molecular formula C4H8O2 and the condensed structural formula CH3COOCH2CH3. Its expanded structural formula shows the ester linkage, with the C=O carbon bonded to a methyl group and to an oxygen that links to an ethyl group. Methyl propanoate has the same molecular formula, C4H8O2, with the condensed structural formula CH3CH2COOCH3. Its skeletal structure has the same atoms joined in a different order, so the two esters are isomers of each other.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by showing the shared molecular formula, both condensed formulas and the different arrangement of atoms.

prompts.question: Construct the condensed structural formula and the expanded structural formula of methyl butanoate, describe its skeletal structure, and identify the ester linkage.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student is preparing a model answer on the representation of esters for a class handout, using methyl butanoate as the example.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs the molecular formula C5H10O2 and the correct condensed structural formula of methyl butanoate, describes the expanded structure with every bond shown, and describes the skeletal structure with the ester linkage identified
5 marks: Constructs the correct molecular and condensed structural formulas, with an expanded structure described and the ester linkage identified
4 marks: Constructs the correct condensed structural formula and describes the expanded structure, with the ester linkage not identified
3 marks: Constructs the correct condensed structural formula for methyl butanoate, without describing the expanded or skeletal structure
2 marks: Identifies the ester functional group in the compound, without formulas
1 mark: Identifies that the compound contains an oxygen-containing functional group
markerNotes: Methyl butanoate combines the butanoyl part from butanoic acid with the methyl part from methanol, so the molecular formula is C5H10O2.
In the condensed formula, the -COO- group must sit between the butanoyl chain and the methyl group.
commonStudentErrors: Writes the formula as CH3CH2CH2COOH, which is butanoic acid rather than the ester.
Swaps the alkyl groups around the ester linkage, giving propyl ethanoate instead.
Writes the molecular formula as C5H12O2, which has two more hydrogen atoms than correct.

sampleAnswers.answer: The molecular formula of methyl butanoate is C5H10O2. Its condensed structural formula is CH3CH2CH2COOCH3, in which the -COO- group joins the butanoyl chain to the methyl group. The expanded structural formula shows every bond: a chain of four carbon atoms, the last of which is double bonded to one oxygen and single bonded to a second oxygen that is bonded to a methyl carbon. In the skeletal structure, the chain is a zigzag of lines with a C=O at one end and an O linking to a single line that ends on the methyl group, so the ester linkage sits at the centre of the skeleton. The ester linkage is the -COO- group, which distinguishes an ester from the carboxylic acid butanoic acid and from an alcohol. Methyl butanoate is therefore an ester, consistent with its butanoyl part coming from butanoic acid and its methyl part from methanol.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by giving the molecular and condensed formulas, describing the expanded and skeletal structures and identifying the ester linkage.

prompts.question: Describe the alcohol and the carboxylic acid that react to form ethyl ethanoate, and name each one using IUPAC nomenclature.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is writing a naming key for esters for a Year 12 class and must explain how each part of the ester name is found.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes ethanol and ethanoic acid as the reactants, and explains that the alkyl part of the name comes from the alcohol and the -oate ending from the acid, using IUPAC nomenclature
2 marks: Identifies the alcohol and the carboxylic acid, without explaining how the name is built
1 mark: Identifies that an ester is formed from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid
markerNotes: The alcohol gives the alkyl name, ethyl, written first, and the acid gives the -oate ending, so ethanoic acid becomes ethanoate.
The acid part is never written first, so the name does not begin with ethanoate.
commonStudentErrors: Names the ester ethyl ethanoic acid, which keeps the acid ending.

sampleAnswers.answer: Ethyl ethanoate is formed from ethanol, the alcohol, and ethanoic acid, the carboxylic acid. Using IUPAC nomenclature, the alkyl part of the name, ethyl, comes from the alcohol and is written first. The -oate ending comes from the acid, changing ethanoic acid into ethanoate, so the ester is named ethyl ethanoate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying both reactants and explaining how the alkyl part and the -oate ending are taken from them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The alcohol is ethanol and the acid is ethanoic acid, so the ester is ethyl ethanoate.

sampleAnswers.answer: An ester forms from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the general reaction only. No reactants are named.

prompts.question: Construct the condensed structural formula and IUPAC name of the ester formed from butan-1-ol and ethanoic acid, and of the ester formed from propan-2-ol and butanoic acid.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class is building a table of esters from named alcohols and acids for a revision quiz.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs both condensed structural formulas correctly and names both esters using IUPAC nomenclature, with the alkyl part taken from the alcohol and the -oate ending from the acid, including the position number in propan-2-yl butanoate
5 marks: Constructs both formulas and names both esters correctly, with the position number in propan-2-yl butanoate missing or wrong
4 marks: Constructs both formulas correctly, with one name correct
3 marks: Constructs one formula and name correctly for an ester
2 marks: Identifies butyl ethanoate or propan-2-yl butanoate as the ester formed from the named reactants
1 mark: Identifies that an ester contains the -COO- group
markerNotes: Name the alkyl group from the alcohol, then the acid's -oate ending: butyl ethanoate, not ethyl butanoate.
For propan-2-yl butanoate, the number shows which carbon of the propane chain bonds to the ester oxygen, so it must be included.
commonStudentErrors: Names butyl ethanoate as ethyl butanoate, swapping the alcohol and acid parts.
Writes propan-2-yl butanoate as propyl butanoate, which loses the position of attachment.
Writes the formula with an -OH group still present, which is an acid or alcohol rather than an ester.

sampleAnswers.answer: Using IUPAC nomenclature, the first ester is made from butan-1-ol, a primary alcohol, and ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid. The alkyl part of the name, butyl, comes from the alcohol and the ethanoate ending comes from the acid, so the ester is butyl ethanoate, with the condensed structural formula CH3COOCH2CH2CH2CH3. The second ester is made from propan-2-ol and butanoic acid. Its alkyl group is attached to the oxygen through the middle carbon of propane, so the alkyl part is named propan-2-yl and the acid part gives butanoate. The ester is propan-2-yl butanoate, with the condensed structural formula CH3CH2CH2COOCH(CH3)2. In both names, the alcohol gives the first word and the acid gives the ending -oate, and the position of attachment is written with a number. The naming pattern is the same for both esters, so the same steps can be used to name any ester from its alcohol and acid.

prompts.question: Define functional group isomers, and give one pair of a carboxylic acid and an ester with the same molecular formula.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has written that two compounds are isomers because they look similar on a worksheet, and must correct the definition and give a valid example.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Defines functional group isomers as compounds with the same molecular formula but different functional groups, and gives a correct pair of a carboxylic acid and an ester with their formulas
2 marks: Defines functional group isomers correctly, without giving a valid example
1 mark: Identifies that the compounds share a molecular formula
markerNotes: A functional group isomer must differ in functional group, not only in the arrangement of the same group, so a carboxylic acid and an ester form a valid pair.
State the shared molecular formula in the example, since it is the link between the two compounds.
commonStudentErrors: Says functional group isomers have different molecular formulas.
Gives two alkanes as functional group isomers, which are not carboxylic acids or esters.
Gives butanoic acid and butan-1-ol as the example, which have different molecular formulas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Functional group isomers are compounds that have the same molecular formula but different functional groups. For example, butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2COOH, and ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH2CH3, both have the molecular formula C4H8O2. Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid whose carboxyl group contains an -OH, while ethyl ethanoate is an ester with no -OH group, so they are functional group isomers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by defining functional group isomers and giving a valid acid and ester pair with their formulas.

sampleAnswers.answer: Functional group isomers have the same molecular formula but different functional groups.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by defining the isomers correctly. No valid example is given.

sampleAnswers.answer: They have the same molecular formula.

prompts.question: Construct the condensed structural formula of every carboxylic acid and ester with molecular formula C4H8O2, and name each one using IUPAC nomenclature.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class is building a complete list of the functional group isomers with molecular formula C4H8O2 for a practice exam.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs all six condensed structural formulas for carboxylic acids and esters with molecular formula C4H8O2, names each correctly using IUPAC nomenclature, and identifies the acids and esters as functional group isomers
5 marks: Constructs and names five of the six isomers correctly, with the functional group isomer relationship stated
4 marks: Constructs and names four of the six isomers correctly
3 marks: Constructs and names three of the six isomers correctly
2 marks: Constructs two correct isomers, one acid and one ester
1 mark: Identifies a carboxylic acid with the molecular formula C4H8O2
markerNotes: List the acids first, then the esters grouped by their alkyl and acyl parts, so that no isomer is missed.
Methanoate esters are the easiest to miss, because they have a hydrogen directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon.
commonStudentErrors: Misses one or more esters, typically the methanoate esters.
Gives propyl ethanoate as a C4H8O2 isomer, which has the wrong number of atoms.
Names methyl propanoate as propyl methanoate, swapping the two parts.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Using IUPAC nomenclature, the six functional group isomers with molecular formula C4H8O2 are:
CH3CH2CH2COOH, butanoic acid, a carboxylic acid.
(CH3)2CHCOOH, 2-methylpropanoic acid, a carboxylic acid.
CH3CH2COOCH3, methyl propanoate, an ester.
CH3COOCH2CH3, ethyl ethanoate, an ester.
HCOOCH2CH2CH3, propyl methanoate, an ester.
HCOOCH(CH3)2, propan-2-yl methanoate, an ester.
Each of these has the molecular formula C4H8O2, so the two acids and the four esters are functional group isomers of one another. Each carboxylic acid carries the -COOH group at the end of its chain, while each ester has a -COO- linkage with no -OH group. The condensed structural formulas shown cover the full set of acids and esters, and 2-methylpropanoic acid is the only branched acid in the list, because the other acid has an unbranched chain. Naming each ester from its alcohol and acid parts, and checking that every structure has the molecular formula C4H8O2, confirms that the list is complete.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by constructing all six isomers, naming each with IUPAC nomenclature and identifying the functional group isomer relationship.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2COOH, and 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH3)2CHCOOH, are the carboxylic acids. Methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3, and ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH2CH3, are the esters.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by constructing and naming four of the six isomers.

sampleAnswers.answer: Butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2COOH, and methyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH3, are isomers.
