dotPoints.description: Compare atomic emission spectroscopy (AES) to flame tests for elemental analysis

prompts.question: Compare atomic emission spectroscopy with a flame test as methods for identifying the elements in a sample.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is asked to decide whether a flame test or atomic emission spectroscopy is the better method for identifying metal ions in a sample, for a written report on elemental analysis.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Compares atomic emission spectroscopy and flame tests, showing that both use emitted light but atomic emission spectroscopy measures specific wavelengths more precisely than the colour seen in a flame test
2 marks: Describes both methods as using emitted light from excited atoms, with limited comparison
1 mark: Identifies that a flame test shows the colour of an element
markerNotes: Compare the two methods on the same criteria, such as how the result is read and how precise it is.
State that both methods rely on light emitted by excited atoms, since that is the common basis of the comparison.
commonStudentErrors: Says a flame test measures the concentration of each element in the sample.
Says atomic emission spectroscopy only works for elements that are not metals.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both atomic emission spectroscopy and a flame test identify elements from the light emitted when excited atoms return to lower energy levels, so both are useful for elemental analysis. A flame test is qualitative, relying on the colour seen by eye, which can be ambiguous when two elements emit similar colours. Atomic emission spectroscopy records the emission at specific wavelengths, giving a more precise and reliable identification.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by comparing both methods, showing the common emission basis and that atomic emission spectroscopy is more precise.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both methods use light emitted by excited atoms to identify an element.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the shared emission basis. The difference in precision is not compared.

sampleAnswers.answer: A flame test shows the colour of an element.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the colour of a flame test. No comparison is made.

prompts.question: Analyse the advantages and limitations of atomic emission spectroscopy compared with a flame test for identifying the elements in a mixed sample.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A school technician has a mixed sample containing two metal salts, and must decide between a flame test and atomic emission spectroscopy to identify the metals.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the advantages and limitations of atomic emission spectroscopy and a flame test for the mixed sample, with a justified choice of method
4 marks: Analyses one advantage and one limitation of each method, with a sound link to the mixed sample
3 marks: Describes the methods and one advantage of atomic emission spectroscopy, with limited analysis
2 marks: Identifies that the flame test gives a colour and atomic emission spectroscopy gives wavelengths, with little analysis
1 mark: Identifies that atomic emission spectroscopy measures emitted light
markerNotes: Apply each method to the mixed sample, not to a single element, since the question asks about the mixture.
Name one limitation for each method, such as the masking of one colour by another for the flame test and the cost of the instrument for atomic emission spectroscopy.
commonStudentErrors: Says a flame test can identify every element in a mixed sample, because it shows a colour.
Says atomic emission spectroscopy cannot be used on a mixed sample because the lines overlap.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atomic emission spectroscopy has the advantage over a flame test for a mixed sample, because each element emits light at characteristic wavelengths that appear as separate emission lines, so several elements can be identified in one measurement. A flame test gives a single colour that is the combined visible emission of the elements present, which can mask one element, such as the strong yellow of sodium hiding a weaker lilac from potassium. Atomic emission spectroscopy also gives a more objective identification, since the wavelengths are measured by an instrument rather than judged by eye. Its limitations include the cost and complexity of the instrument, and the need to calibrate it with standards before results are quantitative. The flame test is simple, cheap and quick, but it is only reliable for a single element. For this mixed sample, atomic emission spectroscopy is the better method for elemental analysis.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the advantages and limitations of both methods for the mixed sample and justifying the choice of atomic emission spectroscopy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atomic emission spectroscopy records separate wavelengths, so it can identify more than one element in the mixed sample. A flame test gives only a single combined colour.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the methods and one advantage of atomic emission spectroscopy. The limitations are not analysed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atomic emission spectroscopy measures emitted light from atoms.

dotPoints.description: Relate atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) and AES to electron configuration

prompts.question: Explain how the emission of light in atomic emission spectroscopy relates to the electron configuration of an element.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 student is writing a short explanation of why each element gives a characteristic set of emission lines.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that electron transitions between energy levels release photons of specific energy, and links the pattern of lines to the electron configuration of the element
2 marks: Describes that excited electrons emit light at specific wavelengths, with limited link to electron configuration
1 mark: Identifies that atoms emit light when their electrons change energy level
markerNotes: Link each emission line to a drop between two energy levels, since the mark depends on the transition.
Connect the pattern of lines to the electron configuration, not just to the element.
commonStudentErrors: Says atomic emission spectroscopy works because the nucleus of each atom emits the light.
Says emission lines form because electrons move to a higher energy level and stay there.

sampleAnswers.answer: In atomic emission spectroscopy, electrons in excited atoms drop from higher energy levels back to lower energy levels, and each drop releases a photon with a specific energy. The energy levels available depend on the electron configuration of each element, so each element emits light at characteristic wavelengths. The pattern of emission lines therefore reflects the electron configuration of the element.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that transitions release photons of specific energy and linking the pattern of lines to electron configuration.

sampleAnswers.answer: Excited electrons emit light at specific wavelengths, which are different for each element.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the emitted light. The link to electron configuration is not explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atoms emit light when their electrons change energy level.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the energy change. The emission lines and element are not linked.

prompts.question: Apply the electron configuration of sodium to explain why atomic absorption spectroscopy and atomic emission spectroscopy use the same characteristic wavelengths for this element.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares the two spectroscopic methods for sodium, and notes that the absorption and emission measurements are made at the same characteristic wavelength.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies electron configuration and energy levels to explain that absorption and emission use the same wavelength, and distinguishes how each method excites the atoms
4 marks: Applies energy levels to explain the matching wavelengths, with a sound statement of how the atoms are excited
3 marks: Describes electron transitions in atomic absorption or atomic emission spectroscopy, with limited link to the matching wavelengths
2 marks: Identifies that electrons move between energy levels in both methods, with little application
1 mark: Identifies that atoms absorb or emit light at characteristic wavelengths
markerNotes: Apply the electron configuration to the energy gap, then use the same gap for both absorption and emission.
State how each method excites the atoms, since the question asks for the difference as well as the similarity.
commonStudentErrors: Says absorption and emission occur at different wavelengths because the atoms are in different states.
Says sodium has two electrons in its outer shell, so it has two energy gaps to absorb light.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sodium has one electron in its outer 3s subshell in the ground state, and the electron configuration determines the energy gap between this level and the next available excited level. A photon whose energy matches this gap can be absorbed to promote the electron from the ground state to the excited state, which is the basis of atomic absorption spectroscopy. The same gap defines the light emitted in atomic emission spectroscopy, since the electron drops back from the excited state to the ground state and releases a photon of exactly that energy. Because both processes involve the same pair of energy levels, the characteristic wavelengths are the same, one as absorption and one as emission. The methods differ in how the atoms are excited, since atomic emission spectroscopy relies on heating the sample to populate the excited state, whereas atomic absorption spectroscopy measures how much of a beam of light is absorbed by ground-state atoms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by applying the electron configuration and energy gap to explain the matching wavelengths, and distinguishing how each method excites the atoms.

sampleAnswers.answer: In atomic absorption spectroscopy, a photon is absorbed when an electron moves to an excited state, and in atomic emission spectroscopy the electron drops back and emits light, so both involve the same energy levels.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the electron transitions in both methods. The electron configuration is not applied to sodium.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atoms absorb or emit light at characteristic wavelengths.

dotPoints.description: Discuss the process of AAS as a quantitative method used for elemental analysis

2 marks: Describes that the sample is atomised and light is absorbed, with limited reference to calibration

sampleAnswers.answer: In atomic absorption spectroscopy, the sample is atomised in a flame or graphite furnace, so that the element is present as ground-state atoms. A hollow cathode lamp made of that element emits light at its characteristic wavelength, which passes through the atomised sample, and the absorbance is measured. Comparing the absorbance with a calibration curve made from standard solutions gives the concentration, which makes the method quantitative.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atomic absorption spectroscopy measures light absorbed by atoms.

prompts.question: Discuss atomic absorption spectroscopy as a quantitative method for elemental analysis, including the role of standards and the possible sources of error.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is asked to discuss how a school laboratory could use atomic absorption spectroscopy to measure the copper content of a water sample, and why the results can be trusted.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses the process of atomic absorption spectroscopy as a quantitative method, explaining the calibration with standards and how errors are controlled, and reaches a supported judgement on reliability
4 marks: Discusses the process and the calibration with standards, with some discussion of sources of error
3 marks: Describes the steps of atomic absorption spectroscopy and the use of standards, with limited discussion of quantitative reliability
2 marks: Identifies that atomic absorption spectroscopy measures absorbance, with little discussion of quantitative use
1 mark: Identifies that atomic absorption spectroscopy is used for elemental analysis
markerNotes: Explain the calibration curve and where the unknown sample's reading falls on it, since that is the quantitative step.
Name at least one source of error with a control for it, such as chemical interference or matching the standards to the sample.
commonStudentErrors: Says the calibration curve is unnecessary because absorbance is directly proportional to mass.
Says atomic absorption spectroscopy identifies the element only, so it cannot give a quantity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atomic absorption spectroscopy is quantitative because the amount of light absorbed by ground-state atoms is proportional to their concentration, within a working range. The sample is atomised, and light from a hollow cathode lamp of the element, here copper, passes through the atomised sample, so the absorbance can be measured. To convert absorbance into concentration, the student prepares standard solutions of known concentration and plots a calibration curve of absorbance against concentration. The unknown sample's absorbance is then read from this curve, which makes the method a reliable tool for elemental analysis. Possible sources of error include chemical interference, where other ions in the sample reduce atomisation, and a sample whose absorbance lies outside the linear range of the curve. The student can reduce these errors by matching the standards to the sample matrix and by checking the result against a blank.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by explaining the calibration with standards, identifying sources of error, and controlling them to support reliability.

sampleAnswers.answer: The sample is atomised, and the absorbance is compared with standards of known concentration to find the amount of copper. Errors can affect the reading, but these are only briefly mentioned.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the steps and the use of standards. Sources of error are only briefly mentioned, so the reliability is not discussed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Atomic absorption spectroscopy is used for elemental analysis.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the use of the method. No steps or standards are discussed.

prompts.question: Explain why atomic absorption spectroscopy can be used to determine the concentrations of Cu²⁺ and Pb²⁺ ions in a solution containing both species.
markerNotes: The top response explains that each metal absorbs light at a characteristic wavelength, so absorbance at each wavelength gives that metal’s concentration separately.
Naming the characteristic wavelength as the reason there is no interference is what separates the 2-mark answer.
commonStudentErrors: Says AAS measures the mass of each metal, rather than the light it absorbs.
Says the metals are measured together as one signal, which would not allow each concentration to be found.
Says AAS works for any ion because all metals absorb at the same wavelength.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Provides a valid explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer: AAS determines the concentration of metal ions by measuring the absorbance of light at different characteristic wavelengths for each metal. This allows the determination of the concentration of one metal without interference from the other metal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2 row: explains that each metal has its own characteristic wavelength, so the two concentrations can be found without interference.

sampleAnswers.answer: AAS measures how much light is absorbed by the sample, and the two metals absorb light at different wavelengths. This means their concentrations can be found separately.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1 row: relevant, but does not state that each metal has a characteristic wavelength that avoids interference. Naming the characteristic wavelength for each metal would lift it to the 2 row.

sampleAnswers.answer: AAS can only measure one metal at a time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Earns no marks: wrong, and does not explain why AAS works for both ions.

dotPoints.description: Describe redox reactions using the terms oxidant and reductant

prompts.question: Describe a redox reaction in terms of the transfer of electrons, identifying the oxidant and the reductant.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student adds a strip of zinc to a copper(II) sulfate solution, and sees the blue colour fade and a copper deposit form on the zinc.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes a redox reaction as electron transfer, identifying the reductant as the electron donor and the oxidant as the electron acceptor, with an example
2 marks: Describes electron transfer in a redox reaction, with one of the oxidant or reductant identified
1 mark: Identifies that a redox reaction involves oxidation and reduction
markerNotes: Name the species that loses electrons as the reductant and the species that gains them as the oxidant, not the reverse.
Use the zinc and copper example to show the electron transfer, since the scenario gives the evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Says the oxidant is the species that loses electrons, so zinc is the oxidant.
Says a redox reaction involves only the transfer of oxygen atoms.

sampleAnswers.answer: A redox reaction is one in which electrons are transferred: the reductant loses electrons and is oxidised, while the oxidant gains electrons and is reduced. In the reaction of zinc with copper(II) ions, zinc atoms lose electrons, so zinc is the reductant. Copper(II) ions gain electrons to form copper metal, so copper(II) ions are the oxidant.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the redox reaction as electron transfer, identifying the reductant and oxidant, and giving the zinc and copper example.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this redox reaction, zinc loses electrons, so zinc is the reductant.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing electron transfer and identifying one species. The oxidant is not named.

sampleAnswers.answer: A redox reaction involves oxidation and reduction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying oxidation and reduction. No species or electron transfer is identified.

prompts.question: Apply the terms oxidant and reductant to the reaction between magnesium metal and dilute hydrochloric acid, identifying the species that is oxidised and the species that is reduced.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid, and bubbles of hydrogen gas form as the magnesium dissolves. The student must identify the redox reaction and its oxidant and reductant.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies the oxidant and reductant terms to identify both species and the electron transfer in the reaction, with the evidence from the observations
4 marks: Applies the terms to identify the oxidised and reduced species, with a sound explanation of the electron transfer
3 marks: Identifies the oxidised and reduced species, with limited explanation of the electron transfer
2 marks: Identifies that magnesium is oxidised or that hydrogen is produced, with little application of the terms
1 mark: Identifies that the reaction is a redox reaction
markerNotes: Apply the terms to each species in turn, magnesium and hydrogen ions, rather than to the reaction as a whole.
Link the bubbles of hydrogen gas to the reduction, so the observation is used as evidence.
commonStudentErrors: Says magnesium is reduced because it forms a positive ion.
Says the chloride ions are the oxidant because they are in the acid.

sampleAnswers.answer: This is a redox reaction. Magnesium atoms lose two electrons each to form magnesium ions, so magnesium is oxidised and is the reductant. The hydrogen ions from the hydrochloric acid gain those electrons and form hydrogen gas, so hydrogen ions are reduced. The hydrogen ions are therefore the oxidant, because they accept electrons from magnesium. The overall ionic equation is Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂, and the electron transfer balances, since the two electrons lost by each magnesium atom are gained by the two hydrogen ions. The chloride ions are spectator ions that do not change oxidation state. The bubbles of hydrogen gas are the evidence of the reduction, and the dissolving magnesium is the evidence of the oxidation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by applying the oxidant and reductant terms to both species, explaining the electron transfer and using the observations as evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Magnesium is oxidised, because it loses electrons, and hydrogen ions are reduced, because they gain electrons to form hydrogen gas.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying the oxidised and reduced species. The oxidant and reductant are not named and the electron transfer is not explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: The reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid is a redox reaction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the reaction type. No species are identified.

dotPoints.description: Construct half-equations and balanced overall equations to represent redox reactions in galvanic cells

prompts.question: Describe the reactions at the anode and cathode of a zinc-copper galvanic cell, using half-equations.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student builds a galvanic cell with a zinc electrode in zinc sulfate solution and a copper electrode in copper(II) sulfate solution, joined by a salt bridge and an external wire.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes both half-equations at the anode and cathode, with oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode, and states that electrons flow through the external circuit
2 marks: Writes one correct half-equation, with the oxidation or reduction identified
1 mark: Identifies that zinc is oxidised in the galvanic cell
markerNotes: Write each half-equation with its electrons, then say whether it is oxidation or reduction.
State that electrons flow from the anode through the external circuit to the cathode.
commonStudentErrors: Writes the copper half-equation as Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, which reverses the reduction.
Says zinc is reduced at the anode because it loses mass.

sampleAnswers.answer: At the anode, zinc is oxidised: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Electrons flow through the external wire to the copper cathode. At the cathode, copper(II) ions are reduced: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. The two half-equations show that the electrons released at the anode are used at the cathode, so the overall reaction is a redox reaction in the galvanic cell.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by writing both half-equations, identifying oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode, and stating the electron flow.

sampleAnswers.answer: At the anode, zinc is oxidised, forming zinc ions and releasing electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying oxidation at the anode. The cathode half-equation is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Zinc is oxidised in the galvanic cell.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying oxidation of zinc. No half-equations are written.

prompts.question: Construct the half-equations and the balanced overall equation for a galvanic cell made from magnesium and silver ions, and explain why the magnesium electrode is the anode and the negative terminal.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student sets up a galvanic cell with a magnesium electrode in magnesium nitrate solution and a silver electrode in silver nitrate solution, joined by a salt bridge and a voltmeter.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Constructs both half-equations and the balanced overall equation with correct electron numbers, and explains the anode and negative terminal from the oxidation
4 marks: Constructs the half-equations and a balanced overall equation, with a sound link to the anode
3 marks: Constructs one or two half-equations, with limited balancing or explanation of the electrodes
2 marks: Identifies the magnesium electrode as the site of oxidation, with little construction
1 mark: Identifies that the cell involves a transfer of electrons
markerNotes: Balance the electrons between the two half-equations before adding them, since the overall equation depends on it.
Link the oxidation at the anode to the negative terminal, because electrons leave the anode.
commonStudentErrors: Adds the two half-equations without balancing the electrons, giving an overall equation that is not balanced.
Says the magnesium electrode is the positive terminal because magnesium is the more reactive metal.

sampleAnswers.answer: The half-equations are: at the anode, Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); at the cathode, Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (reduction), with each silver ion gaining one electron. To balance the electrons, the cathode equation is multiplied by two, giving 2Ag⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Ag. The balanced overall equation is therefore Mg + 2Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2Ag, in which the two electrons released by each magnesium atom are used by two silver ions. Magnesium is the anode because it is oxidised, releasing electrons into the external circuit, and the electrons flow from the magnesium electrode through the voltmeter to the silver electrode. Electrons leave the anode, so the magnesium electrode is the negative terminal of the galvanic cell. The salt bridge completes the circuit by allowing ions to move between the two solutions and keep each solution neutral.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by constructing both half-equations and the balanced overall equation, and explaining the anode and negative terminal from the oxidation.

sampleAnswers.answer: At the anode, Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻. At the cathode, Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. The magnesium electrode is the anode because it is oxidised.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by writing the two half-equations and identifying the anode. The electrons are not balanced and the overall equation is missing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons move from the magnesium electrode to the silver electrode.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying electron transfer. No half-equations are constructed.

Conduct a practical investigation to construct and compare the potential of different galvanic cells

prompts.question: Describe how a student could construct two galvanic cells and compare their potentials using a voltmeter.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A Year 12 class is given zinc, copper and magnesium electrodes with their salt solutions, a salt bridge and a voltmeter for a practical investigation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes constructing each galvanic cell with its two electrodes, salt bridge and voltmeter, and states that conditions are controlled so the potentials can be compared
2 marks: Describes constructing a galvanic cell and reading its potential, with limited detail of the comparison
1 mark: Identifies that a voltmeter measures the potential of a galvanic cell
markerNotes: Describe the set-up of each cell and the reading taken, then say which conditions are kept the same.
Name the variables kept constant, such as concentration and temperature, since that makes the comparison valid.
commonStudentErrors: Says the voltmeter must be connected in series with the salt bridge.
Says the potential depends on the size of the electrodes, so each cell must have the same electrode size.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student sets up each galvanic cell by placing two different metal electrodes, each in a solution of its own ions, and connects the two solutions with a salt bridge. The electrodes are joined to a voltmeter, and the reading gives the cell potential. Repeating this with each pair of electrodes allows the student to compare the potential of each galvanic cell, keeping the concentrations and temperature the same.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the set-up of each cell and the voltmeter reading, with the conditions kept constant for comparison.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student builds a galvanic cell from two metals and reads its potential with a voltmeter.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing building a cell and reading its potential. The comparison and controlled conditions are not described.

sampleAnswers.answer: A voltmeter measures the potential of a galvanic cell.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the measurement. No investigation is described.

prompts.question: Discuss the potentials you would expect when galvanic cells are made from different pairs of electrodes, and the sources of error that could make the comparison unreliable.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares galvanic cells made from zinc with copper, magnesium with copper, and zinc with magnesium electrodes, each in solutions of their own ions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses the expected potentials from the reactivity series, and the sources of error that affect the comparison, with a supported conclusion on which pairs give the largest potential
4 marks: Discusses the expected potentials and some sources of error in a sound way
3 marks: Describes the cells and the expected trend in potential, with limited discussion of error
2 marks: Identifies that the potential depends on the metals used, with little discussion
1 mark: Identifies that a voltmeter reads the potential of a galvanic cell
markerNotes: Use the reactivity series to predict the trend, then give the errors that would break that trend in practice.
Conclude which pairing gives the largest potential and why, rather than listing the pairs.
commonStudentErrors: Says the cell with the least reactive pair of metals will give the largest potential.
Says the potential is unaffected by concentration, so no control of concentration is needed.

sampleAnswers.answer: The potential of a galvanic cell depends on the difference in the tendency of the two electrodes to be oxidised, so cells made from metals further apart in the reactivity series should give a larger voltmeter reading. A magnesium with copper cell would therefore be expected to show a larger potential than a zinc with copper cell, because magnesium is more readily oxidised. The zinc with magnesium cell would show a smaller potential than magnesium with copper, since the two metals are closer together. However, the comparison is unreliable if the solutions have different concentrations, if the temperature changes, or if the salt bridge is poorly set up, because these change the potential. Other errors include oxidation of the electrode surface, poor electrical contact, and a meter of low resistance that draws current from the cell. The student should keep each variable constant and repeat the readings to make the comparison reliable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by predicting the trend from the reactivity series, identifying sources of error, and concluding which pairing gives the largest potential.

sampleAnswers.answer: A magnesium with copper cell should give a larger potential than a zinc with copper cell, because magnesium is more reactive. Changes in concentration could affect the result.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the expected trend and one source of error. The discussion of reliability is limited.

sampleAnswers.answer: A voltmeter reads the potential of a galvanic cell.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the voltmeter reading. No expected potentials or errors are discussed.

Conduct a secondary-source investigation to analyse how understanding of redox reactions has impacted battery technology

prompts.question: Describe how redox reactions at the electrodes of a lead-acid battery convert chemical energy into electrical energy.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is writing a report on how a car's lead-acid battery produces electrical energy, using a secondary source that describes its electrodes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the redox reactions at the negative and positive electrodes of the lead-acid battery, with the electron flow converting chemical energy into electrical energy
2 marks: Describes one electrode reaction in a lead-acid battery, with limited link to electrical energy
1 mark: Identifies that a battery uses redox reactions
markerNotes: Describe the reaction at each electrode, the negative one and the positive one, not just the battery as a whole.
Link the electron flow through the external circuit to the electrical energy the battery supplies.
commonStudentErrors: Says the lead-acid battery produces electricity by storing electrons in the acid.
Says the positive electrode is oxidised, because it is the electrode that releases electrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Redox reactions at the electrodes convert chemical energy into electrical energy, and the lead-acid battery is an example of this battery technology. At the negative electrode, lead is oxidised to lead(II) sulfate, releasing electrons into the external circuit. At the positive electrode, lead(IV) oxide is reduced as it gains those electrons, forming lead(II) sulfate and water, so the electrons flow through the circuit to do work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the redox reactions at both electrodes and linking the electron flow to electrical energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: At the negative electrode, lead is oxidised and releases electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing one electrode reaction. The positive electrode and the link to electrical energy are not described.

sampleAnswers.answer: A lead-acid battery uses redox reactions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying redox reactions. No electrode reactions are described.

prompts.question: Examine how an understanding of redox reactions has shaped battery technology, including rechargeable batteries such as the lithium-ion battery, and the limitations that have been identified.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A secondary-source article describes how knowledge of electrode reactions allowed engineers to design batteries that can be recharged, and how those designs are limited by materials and safety.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Examines how redox understanding shaped electrode design and rechargeable battery technology, and evaluates the limitations identified, with examples
4 marks: Examines the link between redox reactions and battery design, with one example and one limitation
3 marks: Describes how redox reactions operate in batteries, with limited link to design or limitations
2 marks: Identifies that batteries use redox reactions, with little link to technology development
1 mark: Identifies that rechargeable batteries use redox reactions
markerNotes: Give one example of a rechargeable battery and one limitation, since the question asks for both the shaping and the limitations.
Link each design change to the redox understanding that made it possible.
commonStudentErrors: Says rechargeable batteries do not use redox reactions because they store charge rather than react.
Says lithium-ion batteries are limited only by their cost, with no chemical limitations.

sampleAnswers.answer: Understanding redox reactions showed that a battery works by oxidation at one electrode and reduction at the other, with electrons passing through the external circuit and ions moving through the electrolyte. This knowledge shaped battery technology, allowing engineers to choose electrode materials with a large difference in their tendency to be oxidised and reduced, which gives a higher cell potential and more energy. The lead-acid battery is an early rechargeable battery, because its redox reactions can be reversed by applying an external current. In the lithium-ion battery, lithium is oxidised at one electrode and reduced at the other as ions move between electrodes, allowing a high energy density in a light and rechargeable battery. The same understanding also identified limitations, such as the gradual loss of capacity when the electrode reactions are not fully reversible, and the risk of overheating when electrode materials react with the electrolyte.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by examining how redox understanding shaped electrode design and rechargeable batteries, and evaluating the limitations with examples.

sampleAnswers.answer: Batteries use redox reactions, with oxidation at one electrode and reduction at the other. Rechargeable batteries can be recharged because their reactions can be reversed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing how redox reactions operate in rechargeable batteries. The link to design and the limitations are not examined.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rechargeable batteries use redox reactions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying redox reactions in rechargeable batteries. No examples or limitations are given.
